# BOOTSTRAP-607
## Native Application Scheduling, Threading, Async Runtime, Executors & Work-Stealing Runtime 5.0

**Status:** Architecture Specification  
**Phase:** Native Runtime / Execution Model  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600 → 606

---

# 607.0 — Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-607 defines the Axiom execution and scheduling runtime.

Its responsibility is to transform executable work into actual CPU/GPU execution while respecting:

- resource limits from BOOTSTRAP-606;
- security boundaries from BOOTSTRAP-603;
- service lifecycle from BOOTSTRAP-605;
- IPC from BOOTSTRAP-604;
- configuration from BOOTSTRAP-601;
- diagnostics from BOOTSTRAP-602;
- application state/recovery from BOOTSTRAP-600.

The central separation is:

```text
BOOTSTRAP-606
Resource Governance
        │
        │ "How much?"
        ▼
BOOTSTRAP-607
Scheduling / Execution
        │
        │ "When / where / how?"
        ▼
CPU / OS / GPU
```

---

# 607.1 — Design Goals

Axiom scheduling shall provide:

1. very low scheduling overhead;
2. native OS thread execution;
3. lightweight Axiom tasks;
4. async I/O;
5. work stealing;
6. structured concurrency;
7. cancellation;
8. deadlines;
9. CPU affinity;
10. priority;
11. bounded queues;
12. backpressure;
13. blocking-operation isolation;
14. deterministic shutdown;
15. resource-governor integration;
16. optional real-time scheduling;
17. NUMA awareness;
18. GPU work submission;
19. minimal runtime overhead;
20. no mandatory garbage collector.

---

# 607.2 — Execution Hierarchy

Axiom shall distinguish four levels:

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Executor
    │
    ▼
Task
    │
    ▼
Execution Context
    │
    ▼
OS Thread
```

GPU introduces another execution domain:

```text
Task
  │
  ├── CPU Executor → CPU Thread
  │
  └── GPU Executor → GPU Queue
```

---

# 607.3 — OS Thread

An OS thread is a platform execution resource.

It has:

```text
ThreadId
Generation
Stack
CPU affinity
Scheduling priority
Resource scope
Execution context
```

Axiom shall not expose platform-specific thread internals in ordinary code.

---

# 607.4 — Axiom Task

A task is the primary unit of logical work.

A task is substantially cheaper than an OS thread.

Conceptually:

```text
Task {
    id
    generation
    state
    priority
    executor
    parent
    resource_scope
    cancellation
    deadline
}
```

---

# 607.5 — Task States

Canonical states:

```text
Created
Queued
Running
Waiting
Sleeping
Blocked
Completed
Failed
Cancelled
```

Transitions:

```text
Created
   ↓
Queued
   ↓
Running
   ├──→ Completed
   ├──→ Failed
   ├──→ Cancelled
   ├──→ Waiting
   ├──→ Sleeping
   └──→ Blocked
```

---

# 607.6 — Task Identity

Task identity:

```text
(TaskId, Generation)
```

Generation prevents stale task handles from referencing a newly reused task slot.

---

# 607.7 — Task Handle

Public task references shall be opaque.

```text
TaskHandle<T>
```

A handle contains no exposed pointer.

Invalid handles produce:

```text
InvalidTaskHandle
```

---

# 607.8 — Executor

An executor owns execution capacity.

```text
Executor {
    id
    policy
    workers
    queues
    resource_scope
}
```

Executors may be:

```text
CpuExecutor
IoExecutor
BlockingExecutor
GpuExecutor
RealtimeExecutor
```

---

# 607.9 — Executor Responsibilities

An executor manages:

- runnable tasks;
- worker threads;
- task queues;
- stealing;
- wakeups;
- task admission;
- shutdown;
- scheduling policy.

The executor does **not** own application business logic.

---

# 607.10 — Default CPU Executor

Every native Axiom application may have a default CPU executor.

Default worker count:

```text
available_cpu_capacity
```

as reported by BOOTSTRAP-606 and the platform.

It shall not blindly create one worker per logical CPU if resource policy prohibits that.

---

# 607.11 — Worker

A worker is an execution loop associated with an executor.

Conceptually:

```text
worker_loop():
    while executor.running:
        task = acquire_local()
        if none:
            task = steal()
        if none:
            wait_for_work()

        execute(task)
```

---

# 607.12 — Local Worker Queue

Each worker should have a local deque.

Typical behavior:

```text
owner:
    push/pop bottom

thieves:
    steal top
```

This minimizes contention.

---

# 607.13 — Work Stealing

When a worker becomes idle:

```text
Worker A
    queue empty
       ↓
Worker B
    queue has work
       ↓
A steals work from B
```

Work stealing shall be bounded and resource-aware.

---

# 607.14 — Why Work Stealing

Work stealing is preferred for general parallel workloads because:

- local scheduling is cheap;
- independent tasks naturally distribute;
- contention is reduced;
- load imbalance can be corrected dynamically.

The implementation shall remain replaceable.

---

# 607.15 — Global Injection Queue

External producers need a safe way to submit tasks.

Axiom shall provide an injection queue:

```text
external producer
       ↓
global injection queue
       ↓
worker
       ↓
local queue
```

The queue must be bounded or governed by BOOTSTRAP-606.

---

# 607.16 — Queue Capacity

Every executor queue shall have a resource limit.

Example:

```text
tasks.max = 100000
queue_bytes.max = 64 MiB
```

An unbounded task queue is forbidden in the core runtime.

---

# 607.17 — Queue Overflow

Possible policies:

```text
Reject
Block
Await
ExecuteInline
Drop
Escalate
```

For normal application tasks:

```text
Reject / Await
```

should be preferred over silent dropping.

---

# 607.18 — Inline Execution

For latency-sensitive or already-saturated executors:

```text
submit()
```

may execute the task inline when explicitly permitted.

This avoids:

```text
enqueue
→ wake worker
→ context switch
→ execute
```

for tiny operations.

---

# 607.19 — Inline Execution Guard

Inline execution must not cause uncontrolled recursion.

The executor shall track:

```text
inline_depth
```

and fall back to queueing beyond a bounded depth.

---

# 607.20 — Task Cost Hint

Tasks may optionally declare:

```text
Tiny
Small
Normal
Large
Blocking
```

This is a scheduling hint.

The scheduler must not depend on the hint for correctness.

---

# 607.21 — Task Priority

Canonical priority levels:

```text
Critical
High
Normal
Low
Background
```

Priority affects scheduling order.

Priority does not grant:

- security capabilities;
- additional resource quota;
- unrestricted CPU;
- memory beyond policy.

---

# 607.22 — Priority and Resource Governor

The scheduler asks:

```text
Can this task run?
```

The governor answers:

```text
Is its resource usage permitted?
```

Therefore:

```text
Priority ≠ Resource Permission
```

---

# 607.23 — Fair Scheduling

Within the same priority class, scheduling should provide fairness.

The scheduler may use:

```text
FIFO
round-robin
weighted fair scheduling
aging
work stealing
```

depending on executor policy.

---

# 607.24 — Priority Aging

Low-priority tasks may gradually gain scheduling eligibility after waiting for a bounded period.

This reduces starvation.

Aging shall not exceed the priority policy's defined maximum.

---

# 607.25 — CPU Affinity

Executors may specify:

```text
allowed_cpus
preferred_cpus
```

Workers shall respect:

```text
security policy
resource policy
executor policy
platform topology
```

---

# 607.26 — Affinity Hierarchy

Effective affinity:

```text
platform
    ∩ deployment
    ∩ resource group
    ∩ executor
    ∩ task
```

An empty intersection is a configuration error.

---

# 607.27 — NUMA Awareness

On NUMA systems, executors may have locality domains:

```text
NumaDomain
```

Tasks may prefer:

```text
memory locality
CPU locality
GPU locality
```

The scheduler should avoid unnecessary migration across NUMA nodes.

---

# 607.28 — NUMA Policy

Possible policies:

```text
Local
Preferred
Interleave
Any
```

The default for latency-sensitive workloads should favor locality.

---

# 607.29 — CPU Cache Locality

The scheduler should prefer keeping a recently runnable task on its previous worker when practical.

This improves:

- cache locality;
- branch predictor locality;
- thread-local state locality.

Correctness must never depend on this behavior.

---

# 607.30 — Task Migration

Tasks may migrate between workers.

Migration should occur when:

```text
worker overloaded
worker idle
affinity changes
NUMA balancing required
executor policy changes
```

---

# 607.31 — Thread Pinning

A task may explicitly request:

```text
pinned_worker
```

but pinning is a scarce resource.

It must consume a resource reservation where appropriate.

---

# 607.32 — OS Thread Pool

Axiom shall not create unnecessary OS threads.

Default model:

```text
many Tasks
        ↓
small number of Workers
        ↓
OS Threads
```

---

# 607.33 — Thread Count Control

Thread creation must go through BOOTSTRAP-606.

Therefore:

```text
spawn worker
     ↓
ResourceGovernor.acquire(Thread)
```

If denied:

```text
executor remains at current capacity
```

rather than bypassing the quota.

---

# 607.34 — Dynamic Worker Scaling

Executors may dynamically scale worker count.

Signals:

```text
queue depth
CPU utilization
task wait time
resource pressure
I/O blocking
```

Scaling must respect:

```text
minimum_workers
maximum_workers
resource quota
```

---

# 607.35 — Worker Idle Timeout

Workers may terminate after being idle for:

```text
idle_timeout
```

except reserved workers.

---

# 607.36 — Reserved Workers

An executor may maintain a minimum worker reserve for latency-sensitive tasks.

Example:

```text
workers:
    minimum = 2
    maximum = 8
    reserved = 1
```

---

# 607.37 — Blocking Operations

Axiom must explicitly distinguish:

```text
nonblocking task
blocking task
```

Blocking code must not silently consume the entire normal executor.

---

# 607.38 — Blocking Executor

A dedicated blocking executor shall exist:

```text
BlockingExecutor
```

Example:

```text
await blocking {
    legacy_file_operation()
}
```

The blocking executor has its own:

```text
thread quota
resource scope
queue quota
priority
```

---

# 607.39 — Blocking Detection

Debug builds may detect a task that blocks inside a normal CPU executor.

Possible diagnostic:

```text
BlockingOperationOnCpuExecutor
```

Production behavior may be configurable.

---

# 607.40 — Async I/O

Axiom shall provide asynchronous I/O abstractions:

```text
AsyncRead
AsyncWrite
AsyncConnect
AsyncAccept
AsyncFile
AsyncSocket
```

Platform adapters translate these into native completion mechanisms.

---

# 607.41 — I/O Completion

Preferred platform-native models include:

```text
Windows → IOCP
Linux → io_uring / epoll / native mechanisms
macOS → kqueue / native mechanisms
Android → platform facilities
iOS → platform facilities
WASM → host callbacks
```

The API must not expose these directly.

---

# 607.42 — Completion Queue

I/O completion events enter the executor through a bounded completion mechanism.

```text
OS completion
      ↓
Axiom I/O backend
      ↓
completion queue
      ↓
task wakeup
```

---

# 607.43 — Async Task

An async function represents resumable work.

Conceptually:

```text
async fn fetch_data(...) -> Result<Data>
```

does not require one OS thread per invocation.

---

# 607.44 — Future

The result of asynchronous execution is represented by:

```text
Future<T>
```

A future is a state machine.

It contains:

```text
state
result
waker
cancellation
deadline
resource_scope
```

---

# 607.45 — No Hidden Heap Requirement

The compiler should lower async functions into explicit state machines.

Where lifetime analysis permits, the state machine may live:

```text
stack
caller-provided storage
inline task storage
```

rather than requiring a heap allocation.

---

# 607.46 — Async State Machine

Conceptually:

```text
Created
 ↓
Poll
 ↓
Pending
 ↓
Wake
 ↓
Poll
 ↓
Ready
```

The executor drives the state machine.

---

# 607.47 — Poll Contract

Conceptually:

```text
Poll<T> {
    Ready(T)
    Pending(Waker)
}
```

A task returning `Pending` must register a valid wakeup source.

---

# 607.48 — Waker

A `Waker` schedules the associated task.

```text
Waker {
    task_id
    generation
    executor_id
}
```

A stale waker shall be rejected.

---

# 607.49 — Wake Coalescing

Multiple wakeups may be collapsed:

```text
wake
wake
wake
wake
```

into:

```text
one runnable event
```

if the task is already queued.

This prevents wake storms.

---

# 607.50 — Wake Storm Protection

The executor shall track:

```text
queued
running
waiting
```

so a task cannot accidentally be queued thousands of times simultaneously.

---

# 607.51 — Async Cancellation

Cancellation shall be explicit.

```text
CancellationToken
```

Cancellation states:

```text
Active
Requested
Cancelled
Completed
```

---

# 607.52 — Cooperative Cancellation

A cancellation request does not forcibly terminate arbitrary CPU code.

Instead:

```text
cancel request
     ↓
task observes
     ↓
cleanup
     ↓
Cancelled
```

This preserves memory/resource safety.

---

# 607.53 — Cancellation Propagation

Structured concurrency shall propagate cancellation:

```text
Parent
  ├── Child A
  ├── Child B
  └── Child C
```

If the parent scope is cancelled:

```text
A → cancel
B → cancel
C → cancel
```

unless explicitly detached.

---

# 607.54 — Detached Tasks

Detached tasks may exist but must explicitly declare lifetime ownership.

Example:

```text
spawn_detached(...)
```

A detached task belongs to an executor/application scope rather than the lexical parent.

Detached work must not silently survive application shutdown.

---

# 607.55 — Structured Concurrency

Default concurrency should be structured.

Conceptual:

```text
scope {
    a = spawn(...)
    b = spawn(...)
    c = spawn(...)

    await a
    await b
    await c
}
```

Leaving the scope requires child tasks to:

```text
complete
cancel
or explicitly detach
```

---

# 607.56 — Child Failure

If one child fails, the structured scope may use policies:

```text
CancelSiblings
Continue
CollectErrors
FailFast
```

The default should be explicitly defined by the language/runtime rather than left ambiguous.

---

# 607.57 — Error Aggregation

Multiple child failures may be collected:

```text
TaskGroupError {
    primary
    secondary[]
}
```

No error should be silently discarded.

---

# 607.58 — Async Exception Boundary

A failed task stores its failure in its future/result.

It must not crash the entire process merely because the task failed.

Process-level termination remains an explicit supervisor/runtime policy.

---

# 607.59 — Deadline

Tasks may specify:

```text
deadline: Time
```

Deadline is absolute monotonic time.

Example:

```text
deadline = now + 500.ms
```

---

# 607.60 — Timeout

Timeout is syntactic sugar over a deadline.

```text
with_timeout(500.ms, operation)
```

shall internally use the same deadline model.

---

# 607.61 — Deadline Propagation

A child task inherits the parent's deadline unless explicitly shortened.

A child may not extend the parent's deadline automatically.

---

# 607.62 — Timer Integration

BOOTSTRAP-606 governs timer resources.

BOOTSTRAP-607 uses timers to wake tasks.

Therefore:

```text
timer request
→ ResourceGovernor admission
→ Timer backend
→ task wakeup
```

---

# 607.63 — Timer Wheel

The runtime may use:

```text
hierarchical timer wheel
```

for large numbers of timers.

Alternative structures may be used if benchmarked superior.

The API remains independent.

---

# 607.64 — Sleeping Tasks

Sleeping shall not occupy an OS thread.

```text
sleep(1.s)
```

should become:

```text
task → Waiting
timer → registered
thread → available
```

---

# 607.65 — Event Waiting

Tasks may wait for:

```text
IPC
I/O
timer
channel
mutex
condition
process
GPU completion
```

without consuming an OS worker thread where the backend supports asynchronous waiting.

---

# 607.66 — Async Mutex

Axiom shall provide async-compatible synchronization:

```text
AsyncMutex
AsyncRwLock
AsyncSemaphore
AsyncEvent
```

Waiting must yield the task instead of blocking the worker thread.

---

# 607.67 — Synchronous Mutex

Synchronous primitives remain available:

```text
Mutex
RwLock
Semaphore
Event
```

They are appropriate for short critical sections.

---

# 607.68 — Blocking Mutex Detection

Debug diagnostics may detect prolonged lock ownership or blocking.

Example:

```text
LongCriticalSection
PotentialPriorityInversion
BlockingInsideAsyncTask
```

---

# 607.69 — Priority Inversion

The scheduler/runtime shall cooperate with platform synchronization mechanisms where possible.

For Axiom primitives:

```text
priority inheritance
```

may be enabled.

---

# 607.70 — Deadlock Prevention

Axiom shall not attempt to make arbitrary user locking mathematically deadlock-free.

Instead, runtime facilities provide:

- lock ordering metadata;
- timeout;
- cancellation;
- diagnostics;
- deadlock detection in diagnostic builds.

---

# 607.71 — Executor Isolation

Separate workloads may use separate executors:

```text
InteractiveExecutor
BackgroundExecutor
IoExecutor
BlockingExecutor
GpuExecutor
```

This prevents one workload class from monopolizing another.

---

# 607.72 — Executor Resource Groups

Each executor belongs to a BOOTSTRAP-606 resource scope.

Example:

```text
Application
 ├── InteractiveExecutor
 │     └── CPU budget 50%
 │
 └── BackgroundExecutor
       └── CPU budget 20%
```

---

# 607.73 — Executor Backpressure

When an executor reaches its resource limit:

```text
submit
 ↓
admission
 ↓
accepted
```

or:

```text
submit
 ↓
quota exceeded
 ↓
await / reject
```

Tasks must not silently accumulate forever.

---

# 607.74 — Work-Stealing and Resource Groups

Workers may steal tasks only when permitted by resource policy.

A task belonging to a restricted resource group must not be executed by a worker in a way that bypasses its group's CPU/accounting policy.

---

# 607.75 — Cross-Executor Stealing

Default:

```text
same executor → allowed
different executor → forbidden
```

unless explicitly configured.

This keeps workload isolation predictable.

---

# 607.76 — Executor Affinity

An executor can define:

```text
cpu_set
numa_nodes
priority
resource_scope
```

Tasks submitted to that executor inherit these constraints unless explicitly narrowed.

---

# 607.77 — Task Migration Between Executors

A task may migrate if:

```text
executor policy permits
resource scopes compatible
security policy permits
task not pinned
```

Migration must preserve:

```text
cancellation
deadline
resource ownership
priority
```

---

# 607.78 — Thread-Local Storage

Axiom may provide:

```text
ThreadLocal<T>
```

but task migration means thread-local state must not be treated as task-local state.

For async workflows:

```text
TaskLocal<T>
```

should be available.

---

# 607.79 — Task Local Context

Task-local state may contain:

```text
correlation_id
locale
diagnostic_context
cancellation
deadline
resource_scope
```

This integrates with BOOTSTRAP-602.

---

# 607.80 — Context Propagation

When spawning a child:

```text
parent context
      ↓
child context
```

selected context fields propagate.

Sensitive capabilities must not automatically propagate unless explicitly delegated according to BOOTSTRAP-603.

---

# 607.81 — Security Context

The scheduler shall not use ordinary task-local context as a security authority.

Security capabilities remain opaque and explicit.

---

# 607.82 — CPU Yield

A task may voluntarily yield:

```text
yield()
```

The scheduler places it back into an appropriate runnable queue.

---

# 607.83 — Cooperative Long Tasks

Long CPU tasks should periodically provide scheduling points when practical.

Example:

```text
for item in data {
    process(item)

    if scheduler.should_yield():
        yield()
}
```

---

# 607.84 — Preemption

OS threads remain preemptively scheduled by the OS.

Axiom tasks are primarily cooperatively suspended at:

- await;
- yield;
- blocking boundary;
- synchronization wait;
- explicit scheduler point.

The runtime must not claim that every arbitrary task is safely preemptible at instruction granularity.

---

# 607.85 — CPU-Bound Task Isolation

A long-running CPU task may be marked:

```text
cpu_bound
```

The executor can dedicate workers or scheduling policy accordingly.

---

# 607.86 — Real-Time Executor

Axiom may expose an optional:

```text
RealtimeExecutor
```

for supported platforms.

Features:

```text
deadline
priority
CPU affinity
bounded allocations
preallocated queues
```

Real-time guarantees shall only be claimed when the underlying platform can provide them.

---

# 607.87 — Real-Time Restrictions

Inside a strict real-time scope, the runtime may forbid:

```text
unbounded allocation
blocking I/O
dynamic resource discovery
unbounded locks
unbounded queue growth
```

---

# 607.88 — Real-Time Resource Reservation

Realtime execution shall require BOOTSTRAP-606 reservations.

Example:

```text
cpu reservation = 1 core
thread reservation = 2
memory reservation = 64 MiB
```

---

# 607.89 — Energy-Aware Scheduling

On mobile/embedded platforms, scheduler decisions may incorporate:

```text
thermal pressure
battery state
energy class
```

from BOOTSTRAP-606.

---

# 607.90 — GPU Executor

GPU work shall use an executor abstraction.

```text
GpuExecutor {
    device
    queues
    resource_scope
}
```

---

# 607.91 — GPU Task

A GPU task may contain:

```text
kernel
buffers
dependencies
stream
```

# 607.213 — Scheduler Recursion Protection

# 607.214 — Tail Scheduling

# 607.216 — False Sharing Avoidance

# 607.219 — Global Scheduler Lock

# 607.220 — Worker Locality

# 607.221 — Cross-Worker Coordination

# 607.222 — Scheduler Correctness

Mandatory invariants:

1. a task is never simultaneously owned by two executors;
2. a task cannot run after completion;
3. a cancelled task cannot resume after cancellation completion;
4. stale wakeups cannot access a reused task;
5. worker count never exceeds resource policy;
6. executor queues remain bounded;
7. task resource ownership remains stable during migration;
8. task deadlines never move later implicitly;
9. child tasks cannot outlive structured scopes;
10. shutdown eventually terminates owned workers.

---

# 607.223 — Async Correctness

Mandatory invariants:

1. a future completes at most once;
2. a waker cannot resurrect a completed task;
3. a cancellation request is idempotent;
4. a late I/O completion cannot mutate freed task state;
5. async frames are released exactly once;
6. every `Pending` operation has a valid wakeup path;
7. task state is valid across every suspension point.

---

# 607.227 — Deterministic Virtual Time

Tests shall support:

```text
clock.advance(100.ms)
```

without sleeping the host.

Timers and deadlines then advance deterministically.

# 607.228 — Deterministic Executor

Example:

```text
executor = DeterministicExecutor(
    workers = 4
)
```

The test may explicitly choose which worker/task executes next.

# 607.229 — Model Checking

Small scheduler state machines should be suitable for exhaustive exploration of:

```text
wake
cancel
complete
migrate
shutdown
```

interleavings.

# 607.230 — Fuzzing

Fuzz:

```text
task submission
task cancellation
wake ordering
I/O completions
timer events
executor shutdown
resource quota changes
```

# 607.231 — Race Detector Integration

Debug builds should optionally integrate with:

```text
Axiom synchronization metadata
```

to detect races involving Axiom-managed synchronization.

The core runtime must not require a third-party race detector.

# 607.232 — Failure Injection

Inject:

```text
thread creation failure
I/O registration failure
I/O completion delay
queue allocation failure
timer registration failure
GPU submission failure
executor crash
resource quota exhaustion
```

# 607.233 — Executor Crash Recovery

If an executor fails internally:

```text
detect
→ stop admission
→ recover runnable tasks
→ release workers
→ rebuild executor
→ requeue recoverable tasks
```

Only tasks whose state is provably recoverable may be requeued.

---

# 607.234 — Task Recovery

Tasks shall declare:

```text
Recoverable
NonRecoverable
```

A non-recoverable task must fail rather than execute twice.

---

# 607.235 — Exactly-Once Execution

The scheduler shall not claim exactly-once execution across crashes.

Within one healthy runtime, however:

```text
task execution state
```

must prevent accidental duplicate execution.

---

# 607.236 — Idempotency

Higher-level application operations requiring retry safety should use explicit idempotency mechanisms.

The scheduler itself does not invent business-level idempotency.

---

# 607.237 — Scheduler State Checkpoint

```text
executor configuration
persistent task metadata
```

but ordinary in-memory task execution stacks are not assumed checkpointable.

---

# 607.238 — Restart Semantics

After application restart:

```text
old transient tasks
→ lost
```

---

# 607.239 — Durable Jobs

A higher-level runtime may build:

```text

```

on top of:

```text
BOOTSTRAP-600 state
+
607 executor
```

---

# 607.240 — Scheduler and Persistence

Persistence must never silently turn every task into a durable task.

Durability is opt-in.

---

# 607.241 — Scheduler and IPC

```text
IPC message
 ↓
decode
 ↓
spawn/queue task
 ↓
execute

response
```

---

# 607.242 — IPC Handler Isolation

A service may specify:

```text
handler_executor
```

so expensive IPC handlers cannot monopolize unrelated application tasks.

---

# 607.243 — IPC Handler Backpressure

If the handler executor is saturated:

```text

→ backpressure
```

rather than unlimited task creation.

---

# 607.244 — Network Server Model

A native Axiom server should support:

```text

→ async task
→ bounded worker pool
```

rather than:

```text
one thread per connection
```

as the default.

---

# 607.245 — High-Performance Server Path

The optimized path:

```text
socket event
 ↓
parse
 ↓
small task
 ↓
worker local queue
 ↓
response
```

should avoid unnecessary heap allocation and context switching.

---

# 607.246 — Scheduler and Memory

Task frames, queues, synchronization objects and worker metadata are charged to BOOTSTRAP-606.

The scheduler cannot allocate outside its declared memory budget.

---

# 607.247 — Scheduler and GPU

GPU queues and task frames are governed separately.

CPU workers waiting for GPU completion should yield.

---

# 607.248 — Scheduler and Diagnostics

Diagnostics must preserve:

```text
task_id
generation
executor
worker
resource_scope
```

# 607.249 — Scheduler and Configuration

```text

queue_limits

affinity

blocking_executor
```

# 607.250 — Scheduler and Security

# 607.251 — Scheduler and Supervisor

Supervisor owns lifecycle.

Executor owns execution.

```text

Executor:
```

is emitted.

# BOOTSTRAP-607 — Native Application Scheduling, Threading, Async Runtime & Executor 5.0

**Status:** ARCHITECTURE SPECIFICATION  
**Layer:** Native Runtime / Execution  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600, 601, 602, 603, 604, 605, 606  
**Primary concern:** CPU execution, OS threads, tasks, async/await, executors, scheduling, I/O waiting and cancellation.

---

## 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-607 defines the Axiom execution engine responsible for deciding:

- which work executes;
- on which worker;
- on which OS thread;
- when work runs;
- when work suspends;
- when work resumes;
- how blocking operations are isolated;
- how asynchronous I/O is integrated;
- how cancellation and deadlines propagate;
- how CPU and resource budgets from BOOTSTRAP-606 are enforced.

The runtime must support both:

```text
Traditional native threading
```

and:

```text
Lightweight Axiom tasks + async/await
```

without forcing applications to use either model exclusively.

The architecture must permit:

```text
Application
 ├── ordinary synchronous function
 ├── OS thread
 ├── lightweight task
 ├── async task
 ├── blocking worker
 ├── I/O operation
 └── GPU operation
```

to coexist.

---

# 2. Design Goals

### G1 — Native performance

Thread execution must map directly to native OS primitives.

### G2 — Cheap tasks

An Axiom task should be substantially cheaper than creating an OS thread.

### G3 — No mandatory GC

The scheduler must not depend on garbage collection.

### G4 — No mandatory borrow checker

Concurrency safety must primarily come from:

- ownership/lifetime rules already defined by Axiom;
- explicit synchronization;
- structured concurrency;
- capability/resource boundaries.

### G5 — Async without callback hell

The language should expose:

```axiom
async function load() -> Data
```

rather than requiring manual callback state machines.

### G6 — Compiler-generated state machines

`async/await` should normally compile into explicit state-machine IR.

The runtime should execute the generated machine rather than implement a heavyweight coroutine object model.

### G7 — Blocking isolation

A blocking syscall must never silently consume an async executor worker indefinitely.

### G8 — Cancellation

Cancellation must be explicit, composable and cooperative.

### G9 — Fairness

A task must not be able to monopolize an executor indefinitely.

### G10 — Resource-aware scheduling

The scheduler must cooperate with BOOTSTRAP-606 rather than bypassing resource limits.

---

# 3. Non-Goals

BOOTSTRAP-607 does not define:

- distributed scheduling;
- cluster scheduling;
- operating-system process orchestration;
- GPU kernel programming language;
- network protocol semantics;
- application-level actor frameworks.

Those belong to higher layers.

---

# 4. Execution Hierarchy

Axiom defines four execution levels.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Executor
    │
    ├── Worker
    │      │
    │      └── OS Thread
    │
    └── Task
           │
           ├── synchronous execution
           └── async state machine
```

Conceptually:

```text
OS Thread
   ↓
Worker
   ↓
Executor
   ↓
Task
   ↓
Function / Async State Machine
```

---

# 5. Execution Entities

## 5.1 Thread

A `Thread` represents an OS execution thread.

Properties:

```text
ThreadId
Generation
Name
Priority
Affinity
Stack
ResourceGroup
State
```

Identity:

```text
ThreadKey {
    id: ThreadId
    generation: u32
}
```

Generation prevents stale handles from referring to a recycled OS thread identity.

---

# 6. Thread States

```text
Created
Starting
Running
Parked
Stopping
Stopped
Failed
```

Transitions:

```text
Created → Starting → Running
Running → Parked
Parked → Running
Running → Stopping
Stopping → Stopped
Running → Failed
```

A stopped thread can never become running again.

A new OS thread receives a new generation.

---

# 7. Thread Stack

Each native thread has an explicitly allocated native stack.

Configuration:

```axiom
ThreadOptions {
    stack_size: Bytes
    guard_pages: u32
}
```

Default stack size is platform-specific.

The runtime must not require segmented stacks.

For async tasks, suspension does **not** preserve the native thread stack.

Instead:

```text
async task
    ↓
compiler-generated state machine
    ↓
heap/arena/task-frame storage
```

---

# 8. Task

A `Task` represents schedulable logical work.

A task is not necessarily an OS thread.

A typical executor may contain:

```text
8 OS threads
100,000 tasks
```

provided resource limits permit it.

Task identity:

```text
TaskKey {
    id: TaskId
    generation: u32
}
```

---

# 9. Task States

```text
Created
Queued
Running
Waiting
Sleeping
Completed
Cancelled
Failed
Detached
```

State machine:

```text
Created
   ↓
Queued
   ↓
Running
 ┌─┴─────────────┐
 ▼               ▼
Waiting         Completed
 │
 ▼
Queued

Running → Sleeping → Queued

Running → Failed
Running → Cancelled
```

---

# 10. Task Ownership

Tasks should normally have an owning parent task or executor scope.

Example:

```axiom
async function main() {
    let a = spawn work_a()
    let b = spawn work_b()

    await a
    await b
}
```

The parent owns the lifetime of `a` and `b`.

This produces structured concurrency.

---

# 11. Structured Concurrency

Default rule:

> A child task must not outlive its structured parent scope unless explicitly detached.

Example:

```axiom
async function process() {
    let task = spawn worker()
    await task
}
```

The scope cannot finish while `task` remains active.

---

# 12. Detached Tasks

Detached execution is explicit:

```axiom
detach spawn background_cleanup()
```

A detached task becomes owned by an executor/application scope.

Detached tasks must not silently inherit arbitrary stack-local resources.

Therefore:

```text
stack-local value
       X
       │
       └── cannot outlive parent scope
```

The compiler must reject unsafe lifetime escapes according to the Axiom lifetime/value model.

---

# 13. Task Failure

An uncaught task failure becomes:

```text
TaskFailure {
    task_id
    parent_task_id
    service_id
    process_id
    error
    stack_trace
}
```

For structured children:

```text
child failure
    ↓
parent task cancellation
    ↓
sibling cancellation
    ↓
parent receives failure
```

This is the default failure-propagation policy.

---

# 14. Executor

An `Executor` owns schedulable tasks and workers.

Core structure:

```axiom
struct Executor {
    id: ExecutorId
    workers: WorkerSet
    scheduler: Scheduler
    timers: TimerService
    reactor: IoReactor
    resource_group: ResourceGroup
}
```

Struct-only methods:

```axiom
function Executor.spawn(self: Executor, task: TaskFn) -> JoinHandle
function Executor.shutdown(self: Executor) -> Result
function Executor.stats(self: Executor) -> ExecutorStats
```

---

# 15. Executor Types

Axiom defines four standard executor modes.

### 15.1 CPU executor

Optimized for CPU-bound work.

### 15.2 Async executor

Optimized for large numbers of suspended I/O tasks.

### 15.3 Blocking executor

Dedicated to blocking operations.

### 15.4 Deterministic executor

Used for testing and reproducibility.

Applications may create custom executors.

---

# 16. Worker

A worker is a scheduler entity normally backed by one OS thread.

```axiom
struct Worker {
    id: WorkerId
    thread: ThreadKey
    queue: TaskQueue
    state: WorkerState
}
```

Worker states:

```text
Starting
Running
Parking
Parked
Stopping
Stopped
```

---

# 17. Scheduler Architecture

Default scheduler:

```text
                    Global Queue
                        │
          ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
          ▼             ▼             ▼
       Worker 0      Worker 1      Worker 2
       Local Q       Local Q       Local Q
          ↕             ↕             ↕
       stealing      stealing      stealing
```

Each worker owns a local deque.

Benefits:

- reduced contention;
- cache locality;
- scalable task submission;
- efficient child-task execution.

---

# 18. Local Queue

Default policy:

```text
owner:
    LIFO

thief:
    FIFO
```

The worker executes recently-created tasks first.

Other workers steal older tasks.

This generally improves locality while preventing abandoned old work.

---

# 19. Global Queue

The global queue handles:

- external submissions;
- cross-executor submissions;
- overflow;
- tasks with explicit global scheduling requirements.

The global queue must be bounded or governed by BOOTSTRAP-606.

---

# 20. Work Stealing

If a worker has no local task:

```text
1. check local queue
2. check global queue
3. inspect I/O completions
4. inspect timers
5. steal from another worker
6. park
```

Victim selection should avoid deterministic hot spots.

Possible implementation:

```text
pseudo-random victim
+
topology-aware preference
```

Deterministic mode replaces randomness with a deterministic sequence.

---

# 21. CPU Topology

The scheduler may detect:

```text
CPU package
NUMA node
physical core
logical CPU
performance class
```

The information becomes:

```axiom
CpuTopology
```

The scheduler may use topology to improve locality.

Correctness must never depend on topology information.

---

# 22. NUMA

NUMA-aware scheduling is optional.

Default behavior:

```text
task → worker local node
```

Memory placement may remain controlled by the memory/resource subsystem.

Axiom must not require NUMA APIs.

---

# 23. Worker Parking

When no work exists:

```text
worker
  ↓
short spin
  ↓
yield
  ↓
park
```

The spin duration should be adaptive.

Parking must use native OS primitives rather than busy-waiting indefinitely.

---

# 24. Worker Wakeup

Submitting work to a parked executor:

```text
enqueue task
      ↓
wake one worker
```

If work exceeds available workers:

```text
wake additional workers
```

Wakeups must be coalesced to avoid thundering-herd behavior.

---

# 25. Fairness

A task cannot indefinitely monopolize a worker.

For CPU tasks, the runtime tracks:

```text
execution time
queue wait time
preemption/yield count
```

A task exceeding its scheduling quantum should:

```text
yield
```

or, for compiler-generated safe points:

```text
scheduler checkpoint
```

The scheduler must not asynchronously terminate arbitrary native code.

---

# 26. Cooperative CPU Yield

Axiom provides:

```axiom
yield()
```

and:

```axiom
await yield()
```

depending on execution context.

The compiler may insert safe scheduler checkpoints into:

- async state machines;
- generated loops when enabled;
- runtime-managed execution regions.

It must not silently insert expensive checks into every instruction.

---

# 27. Priority

Task priority:

```text
Critical
High
Normal
Low
Background
```

Priority is a scheduling hint, not a security authority.

A task cannot use:

```axiom
priority = Critical
```

to bypass resource limits.

---

# 28. Priority Inversion

Synchronization primitives must support priority inheritance or priority-aware mitigation where the platform provides it.

At minimum:

```text
high-priority waiter
        ↓
low-priority lock owner
        ↓
temporary priority boost
```

The exact mechanism is platform-specific.

---

# 29. Resource Governor Integration

Every executor and worker belongs to a BOOTSTRAP-606 resource group.

```text
Application
   │
ResourceGroup
   │
Executor
   │
Worker
   │
Task
```

CPU consumption is charged to the logical owner.

---

# 30. Task Resource Attribution

For:

```text
Task A
 └── CPU
```

CPU accounting charges Task A's resource group.

For a task performing IPC:

```text
Task A
 └── IPC
      └── ResourceGroup A
```

Shared resources use defined attribution rules rather than double-counting.

---

# 31. CPU Budget

BOOTSTRAP-606 may specify:

```axiom
CpuBudget {
    period: Duration
    quota: CpuTime
}
```

When exhausted:

```text
task remains logically runnable
        ↓
scheduler throttles execution
        ↓
budget replenishes
```

The runtime must not busy-spin waiting for budget replenishment.

---

# 32. Thread Quota

Executor creation is rejected when:

```text
current_threads + requested_threads > hard_limit
```

Soft limits produce diagnostics or admission pressure.

---

# 33. Task Quota

Tasks are counted separately from threads.

Example:

```text
max_tasks = 100_000
```

This protects the process from accidental task explosions.

---

# 34. Task Frame

An async function is lowered into a state machine.

Example conceptual transformation:

```axiom
async function fetch() -> Data
```

becomes approximately:

```text
FetchState {
    state
    local_1
    local_2
    pending_operation
}
```

with:

```text
poll(FetchState)
```

The exact ABI is compiler-defined.

---

# 35. Async State Machine ABI

Every generated async state machine provides:

```text
poll()
drop()
cancel()
```

Conceptually:

```text
PollResult =
    Pending
    Ready(Value)
    Failed(Error)
```

No general-purpose coroutine runtime is required.

---

# 36. Suspension

At:

```axiom
let x = await io_operation()
```

the compiler generates:

```text
save live locals
save state number
register continuation
return Pending
```

When the operation completes:

```text
resume state machine
```

---

# 37. No Native Stack Preservation

The default async runtime does not save the entire native stack.

Therefore:

```text
async task
```

can support very large numbers of suspended tasks without allocating one native stack per task.

---

# 38. Async Allocation Policy

A simple async function should avoid unnecessary heap allocation.

Possible implementation:

```text
caller-owned frame
```

for directly awaited operations.

A detached task may require:

```text
executor-owned task frame
```

The compiler chooses the smallest valid representation.

---

# 39. JoinHandle

```axiom
struct JoinHandle<T> {
    task: TaskKey
}
```

Operations:

```axiom
function JoinHandle.await(self) -> Result<T>
function JoinHandle.cancel(self)
function JoinHandle.is_done(self) -> bool
```

A join handle does not itself own an OS thread.

---

# 40. Cancellation

Axiom defines:

```axiom
struct CancelToken {
    source: CancelSource
}
```

Cancellation is cooperative.

Propagation:

```text
parent cancelled
      ↓
child token cancelled
      ↓
awaiting operation notified
      ↓
task resumes
      ↓
task returns Cancelled
```

---

# 41. Cancellation Safety

Cancellation must occur at defined cancellation points.

Typical cancellation points:

- `await`;
- channel wait;
- timer wait;
- I/O wait;
- semaphore wait;
- explicit `check_cancel()`;
- executor yield.

The runtime must not arbitrarily interrupt native instructions.

---

# 42. Non-Cancellable Region

Some operations require atomic completion.

Axiom provides:

```axiom noncancelable {
    commit_transaction()
}
```

The region should be short.

The cancellation request remains pending and becomes observable after the region.

---

# 43. Deadlines

Cancellation and timeout are separate concepts.

```axiom
await operation()
    with deadline = now() + 5s
```

The runtime represents:

```text
Deadline
```

rather than creating one OS timer per operation where unnecessary.

---

# 44. Timer Service

Timers use a centralized timer subsystem.

Possible implementation:

```text
timer wheel
```

for large numbers of timers, with a heap or hierarchical wheel depending on workload.

Required properties:

- monotonic clock;
- bounded overhead;
- cancellation;
- deadline ordering;
- efficient bulk timers.

---

# 45. Timer Integration

```text
Task
 ↓
TimerService
 ↓
timer expires
 ↓
enqueue task
 ↓
Executor
```

Timer expiration never executes arbitrary user code directly from the timer interrupt context.

---

# 46. I/O Reactor

Axiom defines:

```axiom trait IoReactor {
    function submit(...)
    function cancel(...)
    function poll(...)
}
```

Platform backends include:

### Windows

IOCP.

### Linux

epoll and optionally io_uring.

### macOS

kqueue.

### Android

native platform facilities plus supported Linux mechanisms.

### iOS

native asynchronous APIs mapped through the platform adapter.

### WASM

host-provided asynchronous callbacks/promises.

### Embedded

host/platform-defined event source.

---

# 47. Reactor vs Proactor

The abstraction must support both:

```text
Reactor:
    readiness notification
```

and:

```text
Proactor:
    completion notification
```

Therefore the common abstraction is:

```text
AsyncOperation
```

rather than exposing epoll/io_uring/IOCP semantics directly to application code.

---

# 48. I/O Completion

Conceptual flow:

```text
Task
 ↓
submit I/O
 ↓
Pending
 ↓
OS
 ↓
completion
 ↓
IoReactor
 ↓
enqueue continuation
 ↓
Worker
 ↓
Task resumes
```

---

# 49. Blocking Operations

Axiom distinguishes:

```text
async operation
```

from:

```text
blocking operation
```

Blocking operations must be submitted to a blocking executor.

Example:

```axiom
await blocking {
    legacy_library_call()
}
```

---

# 50. Blocking Executor

The blocking executor has its own:

- worker pool;
- thread quota;
- CPU budget;
- queue;
- admission control.

It must not silently consume all async workers.

---

# 51. Blocking Pool Growth

Default:

```text
minimum workers
maximum workers
idle timeout
```

Growth occurs only when:

```text
queued blocking work > available blocking workers
```

and BOOTSTRAP-606 permits additional threads.

---

# 52. Blocking Pool Protection

If maximum blocking workers are exhausted:

```text
new blocking task → queued
```

rather than:

```text
create unlimited threads
```

This prevents thread explosions.

---

# 53. Synchronization

BOOTSTRAP-607 consumes synchronization primitives from the concurrency subsystem.

Required primitives include:

```text
Mutex
RwLock
Semaphore
Event
Condition
Barrier
Latch
Atomic
Channel
```

The detailed primitive ABI may be split into a subsequent specification.

---

# 54. Atomic Operations

Axiom supports:

```text
load
store
exchange
compare_exchange
fetch_add
fetch_sub
fetch_and
fetch_or
fetch_xor
```

Memory order:

```text
Relaxed
Acquire
Release
AcqRel
SeqCst
```

The compiler maps these to the target ISA.

---

# 55. Lock-Free Scheduler Structures

The scheduler should use:

- atomic indices;
- per-worker deques;
- low-contention wakeup state;
- bounded queues where possible.

A global mutex must not guard every task submission or execution.

---

# 56. Channels

Channels provide message-oriented synchronization.

Core forms:

```text
Unbounded
Bounded
SingleProducer
MultiProducer
SingleConsumer
MultiConsumer
```

However, "unbounded" is still subject to BOOTSTRAP-606 resource limits.

---

# 57. Backpressure

A bounded channel:

```axiom
channel<T>(capacity: 1024)
```

must provide:

```text
send()
try_send()
receive()
try_receive()
```

and async forms:

```text
send_async()
receive_async()
```

When full:

```text
sender waits
```

rather than allocating unlimited memory.

---

# 58. Async Channel Wakeups

Channel operations integrate with task scheduling.

```text
send
 ↓
enqueue receiver continuation
 ↓
worker executes receiver
```

No polling loop should be required.

---

# 59. Thread-Local Storage

Axiom provides:

```axiom thread_local<T>
```

for data tied to an OS thread.

Thread-local state must not be confused with task-local state.

---

# 60. Task-Local Context

Async execution also requires task-local state:

```text
TaskLocal<T>
```

Examples:

- correlation ID;
- trace context;
- locale;
- request metadata;
- cancellation token.

When a task migrates between workers:

```text
worker-local state ≠ task-local state
```

Task-local context follows the task.

---

# 61. Diagnostics Integration

Every task may carry:

```text
TaskId
ParentTaskId
ExecutorId
WorkerId
TraceId
SpanId
ServiceId
ResourceGroupId
```

BOOTSTRAP-602 can therefore report:

```text
task queue latency
task execution time
await latency
I/O latency
worker utilization
blocked-worker count
task cancellation
executor saturation
```

---

# 62. Deadlock Diagnostics

Debug/diagnostic builds may construct a wait graph:

```text
Task A → Mutex X
Task B → Mutex Y
Task C → Task A
```

Potential cycles are reported.

The runtime must not add expensive graph tracking to production unless explicitly enabled.

---

# 63. Starvation Detection

Diagnostics can detect:

```text
task waiting unusually long
```

based on configurable thresholds.

Report:

```text
queue age
priority
resource throttling
lock wait
I/O wait
worker availability
```

The system should identify possible causes rather than claiming that a particular cause is always responsible.

---

# 64. Configuration

BOOTSTRAP-601 supplies:

```text
executor.worker_count
executor.max_tasks
executor.queue_capacity
executor.policy
executor.spin_duration
blocking.min_workers
blocking.max_workers
blocking.idle_timeout
timer.granularity
scheduler.priority_enabled
```

Configuration is loaded once into an immutable runtime snapshot.

---

# 65. Dynamic Configuration

Changes that cannot safely occur live are deferred until executor recreation.

Examples:

```text
worker stack size
```

Changes that can safely occur live:

```text
queue limit
diagnostic sampling
priority policy
```

must use atomic configuration snapshots.

---

# 66. Service Lifecycle Integration

BOOTSTRAP-605 controls:

```text
start
ready
stop
restart
```

BOOTSTRAP-607 controls the execution infrastructure used by the service.

Startup:

```text
Supervisor
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Executor
 ↓
Workers
 ↓
Service initialization task
 ↓
Ready
```

---

# 67. Shutdown

Shutdown sequence:

```text
Supervisor requests drain
        ↓
stop accepting new tasks
        ↓
cancel structured children
        ↓
finish allowed work
        ↓
cancel remaining waits
        ↓
stop I/O
        ↓
stop workers
        ↓
Executor stopped
```

---

# 68. Drain Mode

Executor states:

```text
Running
Draining
Stopped
```

During draining:

```text
new application tasks → rejected
existing tasks → allowed to finish according to policy
```

---

# 69. Shutdown Deadline

The supervisor supplies:

```text
shutdown deadline
```

When deadline expires:

```text
cooperative cancellation
        ↓
forced executor termination
```

Native thread termination must be avoided where possible because arbitrary thread termination can leave locks/resources inconsistent.

---

# 70. Crash Handling

If a worker encounters an unrecoverable process fault:

```text
BOOTSTRAP-602 crash handler
        ↓
process diagnostics
        ↓
BOOTSTRAP-605 supervisor
        ↓
service recovery
```

The executor itself must not attempt to continue from arbitrary memory corruption.

---

# 71. IPC Integration

BOOTSTRAP-604 operations can return asynchronous handles.

Example:

```axiom
let message = await channel.receive()
```

Flow:

```text
IPC
 ↓
OS event
 ↓
IoReactor
 ↓
Task continuation
```

Backpressure is enforced by BOOTSTRAP-604 + BOOTSTRAP-606.

---

# 72. Zero-Copy Integration

When IPC supplies a shared buffer:

```text
SharedBuffer
 ↓
Task
```

the task receives a resource handle rather than copying payload bytes.

Lifetime remains governed by the buffer ownership rules.

---

# 73. State/Checkpoint Integration

BOOTSTRAP-600 cannot snapshot arbitrary running task stacks.

Therefore checkpointing occurs at safe quiescence points.

A service may request:

```text
executor.quiesce()
```

The executor:

```text
stop new work
 ↓
wait for tasks to reach safe points
 ↓
flush I/O state
 ↓
checkpoint application state
```

Tasks that cannot reach a safe point are reported.

---

# 74. GPU Execution

CPU and GPU execution are separate scheduling domains.

```text
CPU Executor
     │
     └── GPU submission
             ↓
        GPU Executor
             ↓
        GPU Stream
```

A CPU worker must not remain blocked waiting for a GPU operation when asynchronous completion is possible.

---

# 75. GPU Task

Conceptual API:

```axiom
let result = await gpu.submit(kernel)
```

GPU resources are charged to BOOTSTRAP-606.

Required accounting:

```text
VRAM
GPU context
stream
command queue
kernel time where measurable
```

---

# 76. CPU/GPU Synchronization

Preferred:

```text
GPU event
 ↓
completion callback/event
 ↓
resume task
```

rather than:

```text
CPU busy wait
```

---

# 77. Security Integration

Thread creation, affinity and priority changes are capability-controlled where required by BOOTSTRAP-603.

Example:

```text
ThreadCapability
CpuAffinityCapability
SchedulingPriorityCapability
```

Untrusted code cannot self-grant elevated scheduling authority.

---

# 78. Resource Capability Checks

Before:

```text
create worker
```

the executor checks:

```text
Thread capability
ResourceGroup quota
```

Before:

```text
GPU submission
```

it checks:

```text
GPU capability
GPU budget
```

Before:

```text
I/O operation
```

it checks:

```text
I/O capability
resource budget
```

---

# 79. Platform Mapping — Windows

Primary mechanisms:

```text
CreateThread
Threadpool APIs where appropriate
Waitable objects
IOCP
native synchronization
thread affinity APIs
priority APIs
```

Axiom should prefer native facilities where they provide better integration.

---

# 80. Platform Mapping — Linux

Possible mechanisms:

```text
pthread
futex
epoll
io_uring
eventfd
timerfd
sched APIs
CPU affinity
cgroup integration
```

The runtime must gracefully fall back when optional kernel facilities are unavailable.

---

# 81. Platform Mapping — macOS

Use:

```text
pthread
Grand Central Dispatch integration where useful
kqueue
mach/native synchronization where required
native QoS
```

The abstraction must remain Axiom-owned.

---

# 82. Android

Android imposes application lifecycle and background-execution restrictions.

Axiom therefore maps:

```text
Executor
Worker
Task
```

onto Android-supported execution facilities.

The runtime must not assume unrestricted background threads.

---

# 83. iOS

The runtime must respect:

- application lifecycle;
- background execution restrictions;
- system scheduling;
- energy constraints.

The Axiom scheduler may reduce or suspend execution according to platform lifecycle signals.

---

# 84. WASM

WASM execution depends on host capabilities.

Possible model:

```text
Axiom Task
 ↓
WASM state machine
 ↓
host async event
 ↓
resume
```

If threads are unavailable:

```text
single-thread executor
```

remains valid.

---

# 85. Embedded

Axiom supports a reduced execution profile:

```text
single worker
static task storage
static queues
no dynamic thread creation
```

This permits the same execution model on constrained systems.

---

# 86. Single-Thread Executor

A single-thread executor is a first-class configuration.

```text
Executor
 └── Worker 0
```

This is useful for:

- embedded;
- WASM;
- deterministic tests;
- GUI event loops.

Async still works because tasks can suspend/resume cooperatively.

---

# 87. GUI Integration

GUI applications may use:

```text
GuiExecutor
```

with:

```text
UI thread
```

as a special executor.

Background tasks can submit:

```axiom
ui.post(...)
```

No background worker may directly manipulate UI state unless the platform explicitly permits it.

---

# 88. External Event Loops

Axiom allows integration with external event loops through:

```axiom trait EventSource {
    function poll(...)
    function wake(...)
}
```

Examples:

```text
GUI loop
embedded loop
host application loop
foreign runtime loop
```

---

# 89. FFI Threads

Foreign code may create threads outside the Axiom runtime.

Such threads must attach explicitly:

```axiom
Thread.attach_external()
```

Attachment establishes:

- diagnostics context;
- resource accounting where possible;
- TLS;
- capability context;
- runtime registration.

---

# 90. Foreign Async Runtime

Axiom does not assume that a foreign async runtime can directly resume Axiom state machines.

Adapters must explicitly bridge:

```text
ForeignFuture
 ↕
AxiomFuture
```

---

# 91. ABI

The stable native ABI for async boundaries must not expose implementation-specific scheduler structures.

FFI should use:

```text
opaque handles
callbacks
explicit completion objects
```

rather than requiring foreign code to understand Axiom task frames.

---

# 92. Compiler IR

The compiler introduces execution-related IR operations:

```text
task.spawn
task.await
task.cancel
task.detach
task.yield

executor.submit
executor.shutdown

io.submit
io.await

timer.await
sync.wait
sync.signal
```

---

# 93. Async Lowering

Input:

```axiom
async function foo() {
    let a = await read()
    return transform(a)
}
```

Compiler pipeline:

```text
AST
 ↓
Semantic async analysis
 ↓
Coroutine/state-machine transformation
 ↓
Axiom IR
 ↓
native lowering
```

The state machine contains only variables live across suspension points.

---

# 94. Frame Optimization

The compiler should:

- eliminate dead locals;
- split state frames;
- avoid storing values that do not cross suspension;
- use stack storage when provably safe;
- inline trivial futures;
- eliminate unnecessary task allocation.

---

# 95. Async Fusion

When:

```axiom
await foo()
```

is immediately awaited by the caller, the compiler may fuse state machines.

Goal:

```text
fewer allocations
fewer scheduler transitions
fewer continuation objects
```

This is an optimization, not a semantic requirement.

---

# 96. Synchronous Fast Path

If an async operation completes immediately:

```text
submit
 ↓
Ready
```

the runtime should continue synchronously without:

```text
queue
→ worker
→ dequeue
```

unless scheduling semantics require a yield.

This is critical for low-latency async code.

---

# 97. Task Allocation Fast Path

Task frames should preferably come from:

```text
worker-local allocator
```

or:

```text
executor arena
```

where lifetime permits.

Cross-thread freeing must remain safe.

---

# 98. No Hidden GC Requirement

Task-frame lifetime is governed by:

```text
ownership
join handle
parent scope
executor ownership
reference counts only where explicitly required
```

No tracing garbage collector is required.

---

# 99. Task Handle Safety

Handles use:

```text
index + generation
```

rather than raw pointers exposed to application code.

Stale handles produce:

```text
InvalidHandle
```

rather than undefined access.

---

# 100. Memory Visibility

Scheduler queues, task states and synchronization primitives must establish the required memory-ordering semantics.

For example:

```text
producer writes task data
Release
    ↓
queue publication
    ↓
Acquire
    ↓
consumer reads task data
```

The compiler must not reorder operations across defined synchronization boundaries.

---

# 101. Deterministic Executor

Testing requires:

```axiom DeterministicExecutor
```

Features:

- single logical scheduler;
- deterministic task IDs;
- deterministic queue order;
- deterministic timer clock;
- controlled task interleaving;
- explicit scheduling points.

This allows reproducible concurrency tests.

---

# 102. Virtual Clock

The deterministic executor provides:

```axiom clock.advance(10ms)
```

Timers should fire without waiting for real time.

This eliminates slow timing-based tests.

---

# 103. Fault Injection

The scheduler must support controlled faults:

```text
worker creation failure
queue full
thread quota exceeded
CPU budget exhausted
I/O completion failure
timer failure
task cancellation
worker crash
executor shutdown
```

---

# 104. Testing Model

Required test classes:

### Unit tests

Each scheduler component independently.

### Stress tests

Millions of task submissions.

### Race tests

Concurrent submission/stealing/cancellation.

### Fuzz tests

Random task state transitions.

### Model tests

Small deterministic scheduling state spaces.

### Performance tests

Task creation, await, wakeup, queue operations.

---

# 105. Required Stress Scenarios

At minimum:

```text
1M task submissions
100K suspended tasks
mass cancellation
worker churn
executor restart
queue saturation
blocking-pool saturation
timer storm

nested task trees
deep structured concurrency
```

# 106. Cancellation Race Tests

Test:

```text

cancel during queueing
cancel while running
cancel during await
cancel simultaneously with completion
cancel after completion
parent cancellation during child creation
```

# 107. Completion Race

If:

```text
I/O completion
```

and:

```text
cancellation
```

occur simultaneously, exactly one terminal state wins.

The losing event becomes an ignored/stale event.

No double-resume is permitted.

---

# 108. Double Resume Prevention

Every async frame has an execution-state guard.

Invariant:

```text
one continuation
→ at most one active execution
```

Concurrent completion notifications must be coalesced or rejected.

---

# 109. Executor Shutdown Race

Test:

```text
spawn
cancel
shutdown
completion
```

in every meaningful ordering.

No task may:

```text
resume after executor destruction
```

---

# 110. Queue Capacity

Every queue has explicit capacity semantics.

A queue cannot silently grow without BOOTSTRAP-606 accounting.

When capacity is reached:

```text
reject
wait
spill to governed storage
```

according to queue policy.

# 111. Admission Control

Before accepting work:

```text

 ↓
ResourceGovernor
 ↓

 ↓
```

# 147. Runtime Invariants

### INV-1

No task executes concurrently on two workers unless explicitly designed as parallel work.

### INV-2

A completed task cannot resume.

### INV-3

A cancelled task cannot resume after terminal cancellation.

### INV-4

An executor cannot accept work after entering stopped state.

### INV-5

No worker exceeds its resource-group thread limit.

### INV-6

No queue bypasses resource accounting.

### INV-7

A detached task has explicit ownership.

### INV-8

No arbitrary thread is asynchronously killed.

### INV-9

Every task completion is observed at most once.

### INV-10

A stale task handle cannot access a recycled task.

### INV-11

I/O completion cannot double-resume a task.

### INV-12

Shutdown eventually reaches a terminal state unless the OS itself prevents progress.

# 148. Performance Targets

The implementation should target:

```text

local task submission:

work stealing:
    O(1) amortized

timer insertion:
    O(1) amortized for wheel implementation

task wakeup:
    O(1) amortized

scheduler contention:
    independent of total task count in the common local-queue case
```

Exact numerical benchmarks are platform-specific and belong to implementation validation.

# 149. Hot-Path Rules

The scheduler hot path must avoid:

```text
global mutex
system call per task
heap allocation per await
logging per task
capability lookup through complex maps
```

unless explicitly required.

# 150. Cache Locality

Prefer:

```text
worker-local queue
worker-local allocator
worker-local scheduler state
```

before shared global structures.

# 151. False Sharing

Scheduler structures must use cache-line-aware layout where beneficial.

Frequently modified worker state should not unnecessarily share cache lines.

---

# 152. Memory Reclamation

Scheduler nodes use:

```text
ownership
generation handles
epoch/hazard mechanisms
or deferred worker-local reclamation
```

as appropriate.

No tracing GC is required.

---

# 153. Async Frame Reclamation

A frame is destroyed only after:

```text
task terminal state
+
no outstanding join/operation ownership
```

Foreign I/O completions must hold explicit references to the frame/resource state they may resume.

# 154. Stale Completion Protection

Each asynchronous operation receives:

```text
OperationId
Generation
```

A completion for an obsolete operation is ignored.

This prevents:

```text

reuse memory
old completion
→ resume new task
```

If the OS supports cancellation:


If not:


```text

 ↓
release task frame
 ↓
release task handle state
 ↓

```

Foreign operations must not retain destroyed state.

```text
timer subsystem

```

```text
 ↓
```

# 186. Resource Pressure

When BOOTSTRAP-606 reports:

```text
Normal
Warning
High
Critical
Emergency
```

the scheduler can progressively:

```text
reduce worker creation
reject detached tasks
delay background tasks
throttle CPU work
cancel optional work
```

# 187. Background Priority

Background tasks are suitable for:

```text
prefetch
analytics
maintenance
```

# 188. Admission Under Pressure

The scheduler may reject:

```text

```

while continuing already accepted critical tasks.

# 200. Architectural Conclusion

BOOTSTRAP-607 establishes the execution foundation of Axiom without forcing a single concurrency style.

The intended model is:

```text
OS Thread
    = expensive, explicit native execution resource

Task
    = cheap logical unit of execution

async/await
    = compiler-generated state machine

Executor
    = scheduler + workers

I/O
    = event/completion-driven

Blocking
    = isolated execution domain

Cancellation
    = explicit + cooperative

Resource control
    = BOOTSTRAP-606

Security
    = BOOTSTRAP-603

Lifecycle
    = BOOTSTRAP-605
```

The critical architectural decision is that **Axiom does not make threads and async competing language models**.

Instead:

```text
Thread
  ↓
Worker
  ↓
Executor
  ↓
Task
  ↓
async state machine
```

forms one unified execution hierarchy.

This preserves the ability to write low-level native threaded code while making high-concurrency applications possible without one OS thread per operation.
