:::writing{variant="document" id="58327" title="BOOTSTRAP-614 — Native Device, Hardware, Peripheral, Sensor, GPU/Accelerator & OS Resource I/O Runtime 5.0"}

# BOOTSTRAP-614 — Native Device, Hardware, Peripheral, Sensor, GPU/Accelerator & OS Resource I/O Runtime 5.0

**Status:** Architecture Specification — Completed  
**Layer:** Native Hardware / Device / OS Integration  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600..613  
**Primary dependencies:** 603 Security, 606 Resource Governor, 607 Scheduler, 608 Synchronization, 609 Networking, 610 Cryptography, 611 Storage, 613 Packaging

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-614 defines Axiom's unified native abstraction for interacting with:

- CPUs;
- memory and NUMA topology;
- GPUs;
- NPUs;
- AI accelerators;
- displays;
- keyboards;
- mice;
- touch devices;
- cameras;
- microphones;
- speakers;
- audio devices;
- serial ports;
- USB devices;
- Bluetooth devices;
- HID devices;
- game controllers;
- sensors;
- timers/clocks;
- storage devices;
- network interfaces;
- PCI/PCIe devices;
- platform-specific hardware;
- embedded peripherals;
- OS device resources.

The design must expose hardware without turning the language runtime into an enormous platform-specific framework.

The central abstraction is:

```text
Axiom Application
       ↓
Device / Hardware API
       ↓
Capability
       ↓
Resource Governor
       ↓
Device Backend
       ↓
Operating System
       ↓
Hardware
```

---

# 2. Design Goals

614 must provide:

1. native performance;
2. predictable overhead;
3. capability-controlled access;
4. asynchronous operation;
5. zero-copy where possible;
6. explicit resource ownership;
7. deterministic device lifetime;
8. cross-platform abstractions;
9. platform-specific escape hatches;
10. GPU/accelerator support;
11. CPU topology discovery;
12. device enumeration;
13. hot-plug handling;
14. event-driven I/O;
15. bounded resource consumption;
16. safe device handles;
17. no mandatory garbage collector;
18. no mandatory third-party runtime;
19. struct-only APIs;
20. compiler-visible hardware metadata.

---

# 3. Non-Goals

614 does not attempt to become:

- a complete graphics engine;
- a complete audio engine;
- a complete ML framework;
- a complete OS kernel API;
- a universal device-driver framework;
- a hardware abstraction that hides every platform difference;
- a mandatory GUI toolkit.

Those may be built above 614.

---

# 4. Fundamental Principle

Axiom exposes a **common semantic layer**, not a lowest-common-denominator API.

Therefore:

```text
common capability
+
common lifetime model
+
common synchronization
+
common scheduling
+
common resource accounting
+
platform-specific extension
```

is preferred over forcing every platform into identical semantics.

---

# 5. Device Model

Every device is represented logically as:

```text
Device {
    id
    class
    generation
    state
    capabilities
    properties
}
```

Identity:

```text
DeviceId = {
    provider
    physical_id
    generation
}
```

Generation prevents stale handles from accidentally referencing a newly attached device.

---

# 6. Device Classes

Base classes:

```text
CPU
Memory
GPU
NPU
Accelerator
Display
Camera
Microphone
Speaker
AudioInput
AudioOutput
HID
Keyboard
Mouse
Touch
Gamepad
Sensor
USB
Bluetooth
Serial
Network
Storage
PCI
Virtual
Other
```

New classes can be added without changing the core handle model.

---

# 7. Device State

Common states:

```text
Discovered
Available
Opening
Open
Suspended
Reconnecting
Unavailable
Removed
Faulted
Closed
```

State transitions are explicit.

---

# 8. Device Discovery

API:

```text
DeviceManager.enumerate()
DeviceManager.find()
DeviceManager.watch()
```

Enumeration returns metadata without necessarily opening the device.

This is important for security and performance.

---

# 9. Device Metadata

Metadata may include:

```text
vendor
model
serial
bus
driver
firmware
architecture
features
memory
power_state
location
permissions
```

Sensitive identifiers are policy-controlled.

---

# 10. Device Provider

Platform backend:

```text
trait DeviceProvider {
    fn enumerate(...)
    fn open(...)
    fn close(...)
    fn watch(...)
}
```

Implementations:

```text
WindowsDeviceProvider
LinuxDeviceProvider
MacOSDeviceProvider
AndroidDeviceProvider
IOSDeviceProvider
WasmDeviceProvider
EmbeddedDeviceProvider
```

---

# 11. Device Capabilities

A device exposes capabilities:

```text
DeviceCapability {
    read
    write
    stream
    configure
    control
    map_memory
    execute
    reset
}
```

Possessing a `DeviceHandle` does not automatically imply every operation.

---

# 12. Capability Integration

Opening a device requires BOOTSTRAP-603 authority.

Examples:

```text
camera.open()
```

requires:

```text
camera.read
```

GPU compute requires:

```text
gpu.compute
```

Microphone input:

```text
microphone.capture
```

USB raw access:

```text
device.usb.raw
```

---

# 13. Capability Attenuation

A device handle can be restricted:

```text
read_only = device.attenuate(Read)
```

A child component must never receive more authority than its parent.

---

# 14. Device Handle

Device handles are opaque:

```text
DeviceHandle<T>
```

Internally:

```text
slot
generation
rights
provider
```

Stale generation detection prevents use-after-remove.

---

# 15. Device Lifetime

Default:

```text
open
→ use
→ close
```

No implicit finalizer is required.

Resource lifetime is deterministic.

---

# 16. Device Removal

If hardware disappears:

```text
Open
 ↓
Removed
```

existing operations return:

```text
DeviceRemoved
```

The handle becomes invalid for new operations.

---

# 17. Hot Plug

Device watchers emit:

```text
DeviceAdded
DeviceRemoved
DeviceChanged
DeviceSuspended
DeviceResumed
DeviceFaulted
```

Events are delivered asynchronously through BOOTSTRAP-607.

---

# 18. Device Event Ordering

Events from one physical device are ordered.

Across unrelated devices no global ordering is guaranteed.

This avoids a global synchronization bottleneck.

---

# 19. Device I/O Model

All I/O should support:

```text
synchronous
asynchronous
streaming
buffered
zero-copy
```

where supported by the underlying device.

---

# 20. Common I/O Interface

```text
trait DeviceIo {
    fn read(...)
    fn write(...)
    fn submit(...)
    fn cancel(...)
    fn flush(...)
}
```

Device-specific operations remain separate.

---

# 21. Async Device Operations

Every async operation returns a scheduler-compatible handle:

```text
IoOperation<T>
```

It integrates with:

```text
await
CancelToken
Deadline
Executor
```

from BOOTSTRAP-607.

---

# 22. DMA Model

Devices may transfer data using DMA.

Axiom abstracts:

```text
DmaBuffer
DmaRegion
DmaMapping
```

The application does not manipulate physical addresses directly.

---

# 23. DMA Security

DMA mappings require explicit capability.

The runtime must prevent arbitrary device DMA from accessing unrelated application memory.

---

# 24. DMA Ownership

A DMA buffer has:

```text
owner
device
direction
size
state
mapping
```

Directions:

```text
HostToDevice
DeviceToHost
Bidirectional
```

---

# 25. DMA Synchronization

On platforms requiring cache maintenance:

```text
flush_for_device()
invalidate_from_device()
```

are explicit backend operations.

Architectures with coherent DMA may implement them as no-ops.

---

# 26. Shared Buffers

A buffer can be shared between:

```text
CPU
GPU
NPU
camera
audio
network
storage
```

when the platform supports it.

The runtime tracks ownership and synchronization.

---

# 27. Buffer State

```text
CPUOwned
DeviceOwned
Shared
Pending
Mapped
Unmapped
Invalid
```

Invalid transitions are rejected.

---

# 28. Zero-Copy

Zero-copy is preferred when:

```text
same physical storage
compatible device mapping
compatible lifetime
correct synchronization
```

can be guaranteed.

Otherwise a copy is explicit or internally performed.

---

# 29. Copy Semantics

Axiom must not falsely promise zero-copy.

APIs may expose:

```text
copy_required()
```

or capability metadata.

---

# 30. Memory Integration

Device memory is integrated with BOOTSTRAP's memory model as a distinct memory domain:

```text
HostMemory
DeviceMemory
UnifiedMemory
MappedMemory
PinnedHostMemory
SharedMemory
```

---

# 31. Device Memory

GPU/NPU memory:

```text
DeviceAllocation<T>
```

is not an ordinary CPU pointer.

CPU access requires an explicit mapping or unified-memory capability.

---

# 32. Address Model

Axiom must not expose arbitrary physical addresses as ordinary application values.

Physical addresses belong to privileged driver/kernel boundaries.

This preserves safety and portability.

---

# 33. CPU Topology

614 exposes:

```text
CpuTopology {
    logical_cpus
    physical_cores
    packages
    numa_nodes
    cache_levels
    feature_sets
}
```

---

# 34. CPU Features

Feature discovery:

```text
SSE
SSE2
AVX
AVX2
AVX512
NEON
SVE
SVE2
AES
SHA
FMA
```

and future features.

Compiler can specialize code based on these capabilities.

---

# 35. CPU Dispatch

Axiom supports:

```text
if cpu.has(AVX2)
    fast_path()
else
    fallback()
```

The compiler may generate multi-versioned functions:

```text
generic
SSE
AVX2
AVX512
NEON
SVE
```

---

# 36. Compile-Time CPU Features

Compiler target metadata:

```text
@target(cpu = "x86-64-v3")
```

or:

```text
@requires_cpu("avx2")
```

The compiler must reject unsupported deployment targets when the requirement is mandatory.

---

# 37. Runtime CPU Dispatch

For portable binaries:

```text
dispatch(feature_set)
```

selects the best supported implementation.

The dispatch result may be cached.

---

# 38. NUMA

If supported:

```text
NumaTopology
NumaNode
```

provide:

```text
memory_size
cpu_set
distance
```

Scheduler and allocator can use this information.

---

# 39. NUMA Allocation

Optional:

```text
allocate_on(node)
allocate_local_to(cpu)
interleave(nodes)
```

These are performance hints unless policy makes them strict.

---

# 40. Cache Topology

Expose:

```text
L1
L2
L3
```

sizes and sharing relationships.

Applications can use this for high-performance algorithms without depending on hard-coded CPU assumptions.

---

# 41. Power and Thermal Information

Where available:

```text
PowerState
Temperature
ThermalState
BatteryState
```

are read-only device/system metrics.

They are advisory unless explicitly documented by the platform.

---

# 42. GPU Architecture

GPU is represented as:

```text
GpuDevice
GpuContext
GpuQueue
GpuBuffer
GpuTexture
GpuPipeline
GpuFence
GpuEvent
```

---

# 43. GPU Backend Boundary

Supported conceptual backends:

```text
Direct3D
Vulkan
Metal
OpenGL
OpenCL
CUDA
HIP
WebGPU
Platform-specific
```

No single API is mandatory.

---

# 44. GPU Runtime Principle

Axiom's core runtime defines:

```text
resource lifetime
memory model
command submission
synchronization
capabilities
```

while backend modules implement actual API translation.

---

# 45. GPU Adapter Discovery

```text
GpuManager.enumerate()
```

returns:

```text
vendor
model
driver
VRAM
shared_memory
compute_units
features
queues
formats
limits
```

---

# 46. GPU Context

A GPU context owns:

```text
queues
allocators
pipelines
descriptor state
device synchronization
```

Context lifetime is explicit.

---

# 47. GPU Queue

Queue types:

```text
Graphics
Compute
Transfer
Copy
VideoDecode
VideoEncode
```

Actual availability is device-dependent.

---

# 48. GPU Command Buffer

Commands are recorded:

```text
CommandBuffer.begin()
...
CommandBuffer.end()
queue.submit(command_buffer)
```

Command buffers are reusable only when the backend guarantees it.

---

# 49. GPU Synchronization

GPU synchronization uses:

```text
Fence
Semaphore
Event
Barrier
TimelineValue
```

where supported.

These integrate with BOOTSTRAP-608.

---

# 50. GPU/CPU Synchronization

Example:

```text
CPU writes buffer
→ memory barrier
→ GPU reads
→ GPU fence
→ CPU reads
```

The runtime must make ownership transitions explicit.

---

# 51. GPU Memory Allocation

Allocation classes:

```text
DeviceLocal
HostVisible
HostCoherent
HostCached
Unified
Transient
```

Backend reports actual properties.

---

# 52. GPU Memory Pools

The runtime may use:

```text
PageAllocator
SlabAllocator
BuddyAllocator
Suballocator
```

internally.

Applications see logical allocations.

---

# 53. GPU Memory Budget

GPU allocations count against BOOTSTRAP-606.

Metrics:

```text
allocated
resident
committed
mapped
evicted
```

where supported.

---

# 54. GPU Out-of-Memory

Failure:

```text
GpuOutOfMemory
```

must not silently fall back to arbitrary host allocation.

Fallback requires explicit application policy.

---

# 55. GPU Pipeline

Pipeline objects represent compiled device programs:

```text
ComputePipeline
GraphicsPipeline
RayTracingPipeline
```

where supported.

---

# 56. Shader Model

614 only defines loading and execution boundaries.

A future graphics/shader subsystem defines:

```text
shader language
reflection
pipeline layout
material system
render graph
```

---

# 57. GPU Program Security

GPU executable code requires:

```text
gpu.execute
```

and may require package trust.

Unsigned/untrusted shader packages can be blocked by deployment policy.

---

# 58. GPU Binary Cache

Compiled GPU pipelines can use BOOTSTRAP-613 content-addressed cache.

Cache key includes:

```text
shader hash
driver version
GPU identity
pipeline configuration
compiler version
```

---

# 59. GPU Cache Invalidity

Driver updates may invalidate GPU binary caches.

The cache must therefore be disposable.

---

# 60. NPU / AI Accelerator

Generic abstraction:

```text
AcceleratorDevice
AcceleratorContext
AcceleratorBuffer
AcceleratorGraph
AcceleratorCommand
```

---

# 61. Accelerator Backends

Examples:

```text
DirectML
Core ML
NNAPI
TensorRT
CUDA
ROCm
Metal
Vulkan Compute
WebGPU
vendor-specific NPU
```

These are optional providers.

---

# 62. Accelerator Model

The core API should support:

```text
tensor
buffer
graph
operator
compiled graph
queue
event
```

without forcing one tensor framework into the language core.

---

# 63. Accelerator Memory

AI workloads commonly use:

```text
Host → Device
Device → Device
Device → Host
```

and should reuse 614's shared-buffer and DMA model.

---

# 64. Accelerator Graph

A graph:

```text
input
 ↓
operator
 ↓
operator
 ↓
output
```

can be compiled into backend-specific executable state.

---

# 65. Accelerator Compilation

Compiled graphs may be cached through BOOTSTRAP-613.

Cache key:

```text
graph fingerprint
device fingerprint
backend version
compiler options
```

---

# 66. Accelerator Synchronization

Accelerator completion integrates with:

```text
Future
Fence
Event
Task
```

so CPU threads do not need busy waiting.

---

# 67. Display Devices

Generic:

```text
DisplayDevice
DisplayMode
DisplaySurface
DisplayFrame
```

Metadata:

```text
resolution
refresh_rate
pixel_format
HDR
color_space
orientation
```

---

# 68. Display Enumeration

Applications can enumerate:

```text
primary display
secondary display
virtual display
headless target
```

without assuming a GUI exists.

---

# 69. Presentation

Display subsystem exposes:

```text
acquire_frame()
present(frame)
```

Synchronization may use:

```text
vsync
fence
present_event
```

---

# 70. Windowing Boundary

Window creation belongs above the low-level display API.

614 provides the display/device primitives needed by a future GUI/windowing subsystem.

---

# 71. Camera Model

```text
CameraDevice
CameraFormat
CameraStream
CameraFrame
```

Metadata:

```text
resolution
pixel_format
fps
exposure
gain
focus
orientation
```

---

# 72. Camera Capture

Pipeline:

```text
Camera
 ↓
DMA buffer
 ↓
Frame
 ↓
Application / GPU / Encoder
```

Zero-copy paths should be preferred where supported.

---

# 73. Camera Permissions

Opening camera requires:

```text
camera.capture
```

and OS-level user permission where applicable.

Axiom capability does not bypass OS consent.

---

# 74. Camera Hot Plug

USB cameras may appear/disappear.

The stream must emit:

```text
CameraDisconnected
```

rather than blocking indefinitely.

---

# 75. Microphone

```text
AudioInputDevice
AudioFormat
AudioStream
AudioBuffer
```

supports:

```text
sample_rate
channels
sample_format
buffer_size
```

---

# 76. Speaker

```text
AudioOutputDevice
```

supports:

```text
play
pause
flush
drain
```

with explicit buffering semantics.

---

# 77. Audio Clock

Audio devices may have independent clocks.

The runtime must expose:

```text
AudioClock
```

for synchronization with:

```text
system clock
video clock
network clock
```

---

# 78. Audio Latency

Applications can request:

```text
low_latency
balanced
power_efficient
```

The backend reports actual achievable latency.

---

# 79. Audio Real-Time Safety

Real-time audio callbacks must avoid:

- blocking locks;
- arbitrary allocation;
- filesystem access;
- network access;
- unbounded operations.

The compiler/runtime should provide annotations to detect violations where possible.

---

# 80. HID Devices

Generic HID:

```text
HidDevice
HidReport
HidDescriptor
```

supports:

```text
input
output
feature
```

---

# 81. Keyboard

Keyboard events:

```text
KeyDown
KeyUp
TextInput
ModifierChanged
```

Physical key identity and logical text input must remain distinct.

---

# 82. Mouse

Events:

```text
Move
ButtonDown
ButtonUp
Wheel
DeviceAdded
DeviceRemoved
```

Raw mouse input may be exposed under a separate capability.

---

# 83. Touch

Touch point:

```text
TouchId
position
pressure
contact_size
phase
timestamp
```

Phases:

```text
Down
Move
Up
Cancel
```

---

# 84. Game Controller

Generic controller:

```text
button
axis
trigger
hat
rumble
```

Rumble/output requires explicit device write capability.

---

# 85. Sensor Model

Generic:

```text
SensorDevice
SensorSample
SensorStream
```

Examples:

```text
accelerometer
gyroscope
magnetometer
barometer
proximity
light
temperature
GPS/GNSS
```

---

# 86. Sensor Timestamping

Every sample should contain:

```text
device_timestamp
host_timestamp?
sequence
```

Device time and host time must not be conflated.

---

# 87. Sensor Sampling

Applications can request:

```text
frequency
batch_size
latency
accuracy
power_mode
```

Actual values are reported by the backend.

---

# 88. Sensor Privacy

Location, microphone, camera and biometric-related sensors require explicit capabilities and platform permission.

---

# 89. Serial Devices

```text
SerialDevice
SerialConfig
```

supports:

```text
baud_rate
data_bits
stop_bits
parity
flow_control
```

---

# 90. USB

USB abstraction:

```text
UsbDevice
UsbInterface
UsbEndpoint
UsbTransfer
```

Raw USB access is privileged.

---

# 91. USB Transfer Types

```text
Control
Bulk
Interrupt
Isochronous
```

where supported.

---

# 92. USB Hot Plug

USB watcher:

```text
UsbAdded
UsbRemoved
UsbReset
UsbPermissionChanged
```

---

# 93. Bluetooth

Generic:

```text
BluetoothAdapter
BluetoothDevice
BluetoothService
BluetoothConnection
```

Higher-level profiles can be separate modules.

---

# 94. Bluetooth Security

Pairing/authentication is delegated to the OS/provider.

Raw key handling belongs to BOOTSTRAP-610 where cryptographic material is exposed.

---

# 95. Network Interface Devices

614 exposes hardware/network interface metadata:

```text
NetworkInterface
InterfaceAddress
LinkState
LinkSpeed
HardwareAddress
```

Actual socket networking remains BOOTSTRAP-609.

---

# 96. Storage Devices

614 exposes device-level information:

```text
StorageDevice
Volume
BlockDevice
```

while filesystem operations remain BOOTSTRAP-611.

---

# 97. Block Device Boundary

Privileged environments may expose:

```text
read_blocks
write_blocks
flush
discard
```

Raw block access requires elevated capability.

---

# 98. PCI/PCIe

Privileged/device-driver environments may enumerate:

```text
PciDevice {
    vendor_id
    device_id
    class
    bus
    slot
    function
}
```

---

# 99. PCI Memory Mapping

BAR regions are not exposed as ordinary pointers.

A privileged backend may provide:

```text
MappedDeviceRegion
```

with explicit bounds and access rights.

---

# 100. Interrupts

Hardware interrupt handling is a driver/kernel responsibility.

User-space applications receive:

```text
event
completion
notification
```

rather than arbitrary interrupt vectors.

---

# 101. Driver Boundary

614 does not require Axiom applications to implement kernel-mode drivers.

Driver development can use a separate privileged Axiom profile in future work.

---

# 102. Driver ABI

Future driver ABI should use:

```text
fixed-width ABI types
opaque handles
versioned interfaces
capabilities
explicit ownership
```

rather than compiler-private layouts.

---

# 103. Platform Device Backends

### Windows

Potential sources:

```text
SetupAPI
CM APIs
WMI where appropriate
DirectX
WASAPI
Media Foundation
WinUSB
HID
IOCP
```

### Linux

Potential sources:

```text
sysfs
udev
evdev
ALSA
V4L2
DRM
Vulkan
CUDA/ROCm
io_uring
```

### macOS

Potential sources:

```text
IOKit
CoreAudio
AVFoundation
Metal
CoreBluetooth
```

### Android

Potential sources:

```text
Camera2
AAudio
AudioTrack
USB Host
Bluetooth
Sensor APIs
Vulkan
NNAPI
```

### iOS

Potential sources:

```text
AVFoundation
CoreAudio
Metal
CoreMotion
CoreML
ExternalAccessory where permitted
```

### WASM

Host APIs provide device access.

### Embedded

Board-specific providers implement the same semantic interfaces.

---

# 104. Platform Extensions

Applications can explicitly request backend-specific functionality:

```text
device.native<Windows>()
device.native<Linux>()
device.native<Metal>()
```

Such code is clearly marked platform-dependent.

---

# 105. Native Handle Wrapping

Platform handles remain opaque:

```text
NativeHandle<T>
```

Examples:

```text
HANDLE
file descriptor
Mach port
CoreFoundation object
JNI reference
WASM host handle
```

---

# 106. Native Handle Ownership

Every wrapped handle declares:

```text
Owned
Borrowed
Shared
Transferred
```

The wrapper must not accidentally double-close a borrowed handle.

---

# 107. FFI Handle Transfer

Handle transfer through FFI must specify:

```text
ownership
close responsibility
thread affinity
validity lifetime
```

---

# 108. Device Thread Affinity

Some platform devices are thread-affine.

A device can declare:

```text
ThreadAffine
TaskAffine
AnyThread
```

Scheduler integration enforces the declared constraint.

---

# 109. Device Task Affinity

For devices that require a particular event loop:

```text
DeviceTaskAffinity
```

binds operations to the appropriate executor.

---

# 110. Blocking Device APIs

If an OS API blocks:

```text
blocking_pool
```

from BOOTSTRAP-607 must be used.

Blocking device calls must never silently occupy async workers.

---

# 111. Device Timeouts

Every potentially blocking operation supports:

```text
Deadline
Timeout
CancelToken
```

where the hardware/backend permits cancellation.

---

# 112. Device Reset

Reset capability:

```text
device.reset()
```

must require explicit privilege.

It may invalidate:

```text
buffers
contexts
streams
handles
```

and therefore emits a generation change.

---

# 113. Device Fault Recovery

Possible recovery:

```text
retry
reconnect
reset
reinitialize
disable
```

Recovery policy integrates with BOOTSTRAP-605.

# 120. Resource Reservation

through BOOTSTRAP-606.

# 156. Device Context Cache

Disposable cache:

# 159. Unified Memory

If platform supports unified memory:

may avoid explicit transfer.

can execute copies asynchronously.

# 163. Peer Transfer Fallback

If direct transfer is unavailable:

```text
device A
→ host staging
→ device B
```

may be used.

# 164. Staging Buffers

# 166. Pool Lifetime

```text
application
```

# 167. No Hidden Infinite Pool

All pools have:

```text
maximum capacity
current usage
```

# 168. Memory Fragmentation

```text
pooling
```

# 169. CPU Memory for DMA

# 170. Pinned Memory API

```text
PinnedBuffer<T>
```

requires explicit allocation.

# 171. Device Mapping

Mapping a device buffer into CPU space:

```text
map()
```

returns a scoped mapping.

---

# 172. Mapping Rules

A buffer may not be simultaneously:

```text
CPU mutable
+
GPU exclusive write
```

unless synchronization semantics explicitly permit concurrent access.

---

# 173. Data Race Model

Device/CPU concurrent access is considered a data race unless synchronization establishes ordering.

This extends BOOTSTRAP-608's memory model to device memory.

---

# 174. Device Memory Ordering

Device APIs define:

```text
HostWrite
DeviceRead
DeviceWrite
HostRead
```

transitions.

Conceptually:

# 176. Accelerator Barrier

semantics.

---

# 177. Device Event Loop

Device backends can integrate:

```text
IOCP
epoll
kqueue
dispatch
Android Looper
iOS run loop
WASM callbacks
```

with BOOTSTRAP-607.

# 178. Event Loop Ownership

An event loop may be:

```text
ApplicationOwned
RuntimeOwned
PlatformOwned
```

# 179. Callback Safety

Documentation identifies:

```text
executor
thread
task
```

context.

# 180. Callback to Async Conversion

```text

→ promise completion
```

is the preferred application-facing model.

```text
→ backoff
```

under low activity.

```text
priority
```

# 183. Interrupt Coalescing

Where supported, applications may request latency/throughput tradeoffs.

# 184. Device Batching

Batch APIs reduce overhead:

```text
submit_many()
read_many()
write_many()
```

Useful for:

- sensor samples;
- network packets;
- GPU commands;
- accelerator jobs.

# 185. Vectorized Device Access

The compiler can optimize batches without changing semantic ordering.

---

# 186. Device Queue Depth

Every asynchronous device queue has a bounded or policy-controlled depth.

Overflow returns:

```text
QueueFull
```

rather than unlimited allocation.

---

# 187. Device Backpressure

Backpressure integrates with channels from 608.

A producer can await capacity:


# 188. Device Cancellation

Cancellation of hardware operations is backend-dependent.

# 189. Completion Semantics

An operation has exactly one terminal state:

```text
Success
Failed
Cancelled
TimedOut
DeviceLost
```

# 190. Duplicate Completion

Backend events must not complete the same operation twice.

Generation-safe operation IDs are used.

# 191. Operation Identity

```text
IoOperationId {
    device_generation

}
```

prevents stale completion events.

---

# 192. Device Restart

After device restart:

```text
old generation
→ invalid
new generation
→ new handles
```

---

# 193. Supervisor Integration

A service can declare:

```text

requires device gpu
```

---

# 194. Device Dependency

Service dependency states may include:

```text

DeviceReady

```

---

# 195. Device Recovery

Example:

```text

→ service degraded
→ reinitialize GPU
→ recreate resources
→ service ready
```

---

# 196. Checkpoint Boundary

Hardware contexts generally cannot be checkpointed.

Checkpoint stores:

```text
configuration
resource descriptors
logical state
```

not:

```text

DMA transaction state
device register state
```

# 197. Recovery Reconstruction

```text
→ recreate device resources
→ replay initialization
```

# 198. Device State Serialization

Serializable descriptors use BOOTSTRAP-612.

Opaque native handles are never serialized as persistent application state.

---

# 199. Security Boundary for Native APIs

Raw native access requires:

```text
unsafe
+
capability
+
platform permission
```

where appropriate.

`unsafe` alone does not grant authority.

---

# 200. Unsafe Device Operations

Examples:

```text

DMA configuration
firmware flashing
device reset
MMIO mapping
```

# 201. No Ambient Hardware Authority

```text
microphone
GPU

serial
```

# 204. Mobile Security


# BOOTSTRAP-614 — Native Device, Hardware, Peripheral, Sensor, GPU/Accelerator & OS Resource I/O Runtime 5.0

**Status:** Architecture Specification — Completed  
**Layer:** Native Hardware / Device / OS Integration  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600..613  
**Primary dependencies:** 603 Security, 606 Resource Governor, 607 Scheduler, 608 Synchronization, 609 Networking, 610 Cryptography, 611 Storage, 613 Packaging

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-614 defines Axiom's unified native abstraction for interacting with:

- CPUs;
- memory and NUMA topology;
- GPUs;
- NPUs;
- AI accelerators;
- displays;
- keyboards;
- mice;
- touch devices;
- cameras;
- microphones;
- speakers;
- audio devices;
- serial ports;
- USB devices;
- Bluetooth devices;
- HID devices;
- game controllers;
- sensors;
- timers/clocks;
- storage devices;
- network interfaces;
- PCI/PCIe devices;
- platform-specific hardware;
- embedded peripherals;
- OS device resources.

The design must expose hardware without turning the language runtime into an enormous platform-specific framework.

The central abstraction is:

```text
Axiom Application
       ↓
Device / Hardware API
       ↓
Capability
       ↓
Resource Governor
       ↓
Device Backend
       ↓
Operating System
       ↓
Hardware
```

---

# 2. Design Goals

614 must provide:

1. native performance;
2. predictable overhead;
3. capability-controlled access;
4. asynchronous operation;
5. zero-copy where possible;
6. explicit resource ownership;
7. deterministic device lifetime;
8. cross-platform abstractions;
9. platform-specific escape hatches;
10. GPU/accelerator support;
11. CPU topology discovery;
12. device enumeration;
13. hot-plug handling;
14. event-driven I/O;
15. bounded resource consumption;
16. safe device handles;
17. no mandatory garbage collector;
18. no mandatory third-party runtime;
19. struct-only APIs;
20. compiler-visible hardware metadata.

---

# 3. Non-Goals

614 does not attempt to become:

- a complete graphics engine;
- a complete audio engine;
- a complete ML framework;
- a complete OS kernel API;
- a universal device-driver framework;
- a hardware abstraction that hides every platform difference;
- a mandatory GUI toolkit.

Those may be built above 614.

---

# 4. Fundamental Principle

Axiom exposes a **common semantic layer**, not a lowest-common-denominator API.

Therefore:

```text
common capability
+
common lifetime model
+
common synchronization
+
common scheduling
+
common resource accounting
+
platform-specific extension
```

is preferred over forcing every platform into identical semantics.

---

# 5. Device Model

Every device is represented logically as:

```text
Device {
    id
    class
    generation
    state
    capabilities
    properties
}
```

Identity:

```text
DeviceId = {
    provider
    physical_id
    generation
}
```

Generation prevents stale handles from accidentally referencing a newly attached device.

---

# 6. Device Classes

Base classes:

```text
CPU
Memory
GPU
NPU
Accelerator
Display
Camera
Microphone
Speaker
AudioInput
AudioOutput
HID
Keyboard
Mouse
Touch
Gamepad
Sensor
USB
Bluetooth
Serial
Network
Storage
PCI
Virtual
Other
```

New classes can be added without changing the core handle model.

---

# 7. Device State

Common states:

```text
Discovered
Available
Opening
Open
Suspended
Reconnecting
Unavailable
Removed
Faulted
Closed
```

State transitions are explicit.

---

# 8. Device Discovery

API:

```text
DeviceManager.enumerate()
DeviceManager.find()
DeviceManager.watch()
```

Enumeration returns metadata without necessarily opening the device.

This is important for security and performance.

---

# 9. Device Metadata

Metadata may include:

```text
vendor
model
serial
bus
driver
firmware
architecture
features
memory
power_state
location
permissions
```

Sensitive identifiers are policy-controlled.

---

# 10. Device Provider

Platform backend:

```text
trait DeviceProvider {
    fn enumerate(...)
    fn open(...)
    fn close(...)
    fn watch(...)
}
```

Implementations:

```text
WindowsDeviceProvider
LinuxDeviceProvider
MacOSDeviceProvider
AndroidDeviceProvider
IOSDeviceProvider
WasmDeviceProvider
EmbeddedDeviceProvider
```

---

# 11. Device Capabilities

A device exposes capabilities:

```text
DeviceCapability {
    read
    write
    stream
    configure
    control
    map_memory
    execute
    reset
}
```

Possessing a `DeviceHandle` does not automatically imply every operation.

---

# 12. Capability Integration

Opening a device requires BOOTSTRAP-603 authority.

Examples:

```text
camera.open()
```

requires:

```text
camera.read
```

GPU compute requires:

```text
gpu.compute
```

Microphone input:

```text
microphone.capture
```

USB raw access:

```text
device.usb.raw
```

---

# 13. Capability Attenuation

A device handle can be restricted:

```text
read_only = device.attenuate(Read)
```

A child component must never receive more authority than its parent.

---

# 14. Device Handle

Device handles are opaque:

```text
DeviceHandle<T>
```

Internally:

```text
slot
generation
rights
provider
```

Stale generation detection prevents use-after-remove.

---

# 15. Device Lifetime

Default:

```text
open
→ use
→ close
```

No implicit finalizer is required.

Resource lifetime is deterministic.

---

# 16. Device Removal

If hardware disappears:

```text
Open
 ↓
Removed
```

existing operations return:

```text
DeviceRemoved
```

The handle becomes invalid for new operations.

---

# 17. Hot Plug

Device watchers emit:

```text
DeviceAdded
DeviceRemoved
DeviceChanged
DeviceSuspended
DeviceResumed
DeviceFaulted
```

Events are delivered asynchronously through BOOTSTRAP-607.

---

# 18. Device Event Ordering

Events from one physical device are ordered.

Across unrelated devices no global ordering is guaranteed.

This avoids a global synchronization bottleneck.

---

# 19. Device I/O Model

All I/O should support:

```text
synchronous
asynchronous
streaming
buffered
zero-copy
```

where supported by the underlying device.

---

# 20. Common I/O Interface

```text
trait DeviceIo {
    fn read(...)
    fn write(...)
    fn submit(...)
    fn cancel(...)
    fn flush(...)
}
```

Device-specific operations remain separate.

---

# 21. Async Device Operations

Every async operation returns a scheduler-compatible handle:

```text
IoOperation<T>
```

It integrates with:

```text
await
CancelToken
Deadline
Executor
```

from BOOTSTRAP-607.

---

# 22. DMA Model

Devices may transfer data using DMA.

Axiom abstracts:

```text
DmaBuffer
DmaRegion
DmaMapping
```

The application does not manipulate physical addresses directly.

---

# 23. DMA Security

DMA mappings require explicit capability.

The runtime must prevent arbitrary device DMA from accessing unrelated application memory.

---

# 24. DMA Ownership

A DMA buffer has:

```text
owner
device
direction
size
state
mapping
```

Directions:

```text
HostToDevice
DeviceToHost
Bidirectional
```

---

# 25. DMA Synchronization

On platforms requiring cache maintenance:

```text
flush_for_device()
invalidate_from_device()
```

are explicit backend operations.

Architectures with coherent DMA may implement them as no-ops.

---

# 26. Shared Buffers

A buffer can be shared between:

```text
CPU
GPU
NPU
camera
audio
network
storage
```

when the platform supports it.

The runtime tracks ownership and synchronization.

---

# 27. Buffer State

```text
CPUOwned
DeviceOwned
Shared
Pending
Mapped
Unmapped
Invalid
```

Invalid transitions are rejected.

---

# 28. Zero-Copy

Zero-copy is preferred when:

```text
same physical storage
compatible device mapping
compatible lifetime
correct synchronization
```

can be guaranteed.

Otherwise a copy is explicit or internally performed.

---

# 29. Copy Semantics

Axiom must not falsely promise zero-copy.

APIs may expose:

```text
copy_required()
```

or capability metadata.

---

# 30. Memory Integration

Device memory is integrated with BOOTSTRAP's memory model as a distinct memory domain:

```text
HostMemory
DeviceMemory
UnifiedMemory
MappedMemory
PinnedHostMemory
SharedMemory
```

---

# 31. Device Memory

GPU/NPU memory:

```text
DeviceAllocation<T>
```

is not an ordinary CPU pointer.

CPU access requires an explicit mapping or unified-memory capability.

---

# 32. Address Model

Axiom must not expose arbitrary physical addresses as ordinary application values.

Physical addresses belong to privileged driver/kernel boundaries.

This preserves safety and portability.

---

# 33. CPU Topology

614 exposes:

```text

    logical_cpus
    physical_cores
    packages
    numa_nodes
    cache_levels
    feature_sets
}
```

```text
SVE

AES
```

and future features.

# 35. CPU Dispatch

Axiom supports:

```text

    fast_path()
else
```

```text
generic
SSE
AVX2
AVX512
```

The compiler must reject unsupported deployment targets when the requirement is mandatory.

# 38. NUMA

---

# 40. Cache Topology

Expose:


# 41. Power and Thermal Information

# 42. GPU Architecture

GPU is represented as:

```text

GpuContext
GpuQueue

GpuTexture
GpuPipeline
```

```text
Platform-specific
```

No single API is mandatory.

# 44. GPU Runtime Principle

Axiom's core runtime defines:

```text
command submission
synchronization
capabilities
```

while backend modules implement actual API translation.

# 45. GPU Adapter Discovery

```text
GpuManager.enumerate()
```

returns:

```text
vendor

VRAM
shared_memory

features
queues
formats
limits
```

# 46. GPU Context

A GPU context owns:


# 47. GPU Queue

Queue types:

# 48. GPU Command Buffer

Commands are recorded:

GPU synchronization uses:

where supported.

# 50. GPU/CPU Synchronization

Example:

```text
→ memory barrier

→ GPU fence
→ CPU reads
```

# 51. GPU Memory Allocation

Allocation classes:

```text

HostCoherent
HostCached
Unified
Transient
```

Backend reports actual properties.

# 52. GPU Memory Pools

The runtime may use:

```text
+
```

# 295. Architectural Invariants

The 614 subsystem is valid only if these invariants hold:

```text
Device handle != physical address

Device identity != permission

Capability != device availability

Package presence != hardware authority

GPU memory != ordinary CPU memory

Device generation != process generation

Device failure != automatic application failure

Native handle != persistent application state

DMA mapping != unrestricted memory access

Unsafe != privileged

Async operation != dedicated thread

Device event != arbitrary callback execution

Hardware reset != handle resurrection
```

The central security/resource chain is:

```text
OS / Hardware
      ↓
Platform Driver
      ↓
Axiom Device Backend
      ↓
Capability 603
      ↓
Resource Admission 606
      ↓
Device Handle
      ↓
Scheduler 607
      ↓
Synchronization 608
      ↓
Application
```

The central data path is:

```text
Device
   ↓
DMA / Shared Buffer
   ↓
Axiom Buffer
   ↓
GPU / NPU / CPU
   ↓
Synchronization
   ↓
Application / Storage / Network
```

Axiom now has a native hardware boundary covering:

```text
CPU
NUMA
memory topology
GPU
NPU
AI accelerators
display
camera
microphone
audio
HID
keyboard
mouse
touch
gamepad
sensors
USB
Bluetooth
serial
network interfaces
storage devices
PCI/PCIe
embedded buses
GPIO
I2C
SPI
UART
CAN
PWM
ADC/DAC
timers
```

while maintaining:

```text
capability security
resource quotas
async scheduling
device synchronization
zero-copy buffers
DMA isolation
device generations
hot-plug
device recovery
package integration
GPU/accelerator caching
cross-process device sharing
mobile/WASM/embedded portability
```

The architecture deliberately leaves **device drivers, graphics engines, GUI frameworks, media frameworks and ML frameworks above the low-level 614 boundary**, preventing the Axiom core runtime from becoming unnecessarily large.

**Target:** Windows / Linux / macOS / Android / iOS / WASM / Embedded

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-613 defines Axiom's native infrastructure for:

- compression;
- decompression;
- archive handling;
- native Axiom packages;
- executable/resource bundles;
- immutable resource objects;
- content-addressed storage;
- chunking and deduplication;
- Merkle trees;
- package manifests;
- package verification;
- package signing;
- optional package encryption;
- package mounting through VFS;
- deterministic package generation;
- reproducible package identity;
- offline deployment;
- package caching;
- resource indexing;
- lazy resource loading;
- large-file/model/asset packaging;
- atomic package installation and activation;
- package generations and rollback;
- package patch/delta infrastructure.

The subsystem must remain independent from any particular package manager.

---

# 2. Core Design Principle

Axiom separates four concepts:

```text
Compression
    ↓
Archive
    ↓
Package
    ↓
Content-Addressed Object Store
```

They are related but must not be conflated.

A compressed byte stream is not an archive.

An archive is not necessarily a package.

A package is not necessarily an object store.

An object store is not a package manager.

---

# 3. Non-Goals

BOOTSTRAP-613 does not define:

- public package registries;
- package marketplace;
- dependency marketplace;
- centralized repository infrastructure;
- source-code dependency resolution;
- build-system semantics;
- language-level module semantics;
- arbitrary package-install scripts;
- automatic execution of package contents;
- automatic code execution during package inspection;
- a mandatory third-party compression library;
- a mandatory third-party package manager;
- garbage collection of language memory.

Storage-object reclamation is distinct from language memory management.

---

```text
│ Application / Compiler / Linker             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤

├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤

├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Archive Layer                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Compression Layer                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Content-Addressed Object Store               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤

├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤

└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

# 5. Terminology

## 5.1 Blob

An immutable byte sequence.

## 5.2 Chunk

A bounded portion of a blob.

## 5.3 Object

A content-addressed immutable storage unit.

## 5.4 Entry

A named item inside an archive or package.

## 5.5 Package

A versioned, structured, verifiable collection of entries.

## 5.6 Resource

A package entry exposed to an application.

## 5.7 Manifest

Machine-readable package metadata.

## 5.8 Package generation

One immutable installed version of a package.

## 5.9 Activation

The atomic operation that makes one package generation current.

---

# 6. Fundamental Invariants

1. Package paths are normalized.
2. Package paths cannot escape the package root.
3. Package opening never executes package code.
4. Package inspection never requires executing package contents.
5. Package contents are immutable after finalization.
6. Package identity is deterministic.
7. Package signatures cover canonical package identity.
8. Content-addressed objects are immutable.
9. Object IDs derive from cryptographic content identity.
10. Corrupted objects are detected before use.
11. Installation is atomic.
12. Activation is atomic.
13. Failed installation cannot partially activate a package.
14. Untrusted packages cannot acquire capabilities automatically.
15. Package metadata cannot silently grant OS privileges.
16. Compression cannot bypass security validation.
17. Decompression is resource-bounded.
18. Archive extraction is sandboxed.
19. No mandatory garbage collector exists.
20. No mandatory package registry exists.

---

# 7. Compression Abstraction

The compiler/runtime exposes:

```text
CompressionCodec
CompressionEncoder
CompressionDecoder
CompressionOptions
CompressionStats
```

Example:

```text
codec = CompressionCodec.zstd
encoder = codec.encoder(options)
encoder.write(data)
encoder.finish()
```

Decoding:

```text
decoder = codec.decoder(options)

while decoder.has_data():
    data = decoder.read()
```

---

# 8. Codec Model

The logical codec identifiers are:

```text
store
deflate
zstd
lz4
brotli
axiom-native
```

`store` means no compression.

Axiom must not make all codecs mandatory.

The minimal runtime profile may contain only:

```text
store
axiom-native
```

Platform/full profiles may add others.

---

# 9. Native Compression Codec

Axiom may define an internally implemented codec optimized for:

- package resources;
- deterministic output;
- streaming;
- low memory;
- fast decompression;
- random-access chunks.

The codec must have:

```text
encode()
decode()
stream_encode()
stream_decode()
```

and an explicit format version.

---

# 10. Third-Party Codec Boundary

External codecs may be provided through:

```text
CompressionProvider
```

but:

```text
Axiom core != third-party codec dependency
```

An external provider must not become a mandatory dependency of the compiler or minimal runtime.

---

# 11. Compression Levels

Logical levels:

```text
Fastest
Fast
Balanced
Dense
Maximum
```

A codec maps these to implementation-specific parameters.

The package metadata stores the actual codec and format version, not merely the logical level.

---

# 12. Deterministic Compression

Deterministic mode must guarantee identical output when:

- input is identical;
- codec version is identical;
- options are identical;
- architecture-independent mode is selected.

Non-deterministic metadata such as:

- timestamps;
- process IDs;
- random seeds;
- host paths

must not affect deterministic package output.

---

# 13. Streaming Compression

The encoder operates incrementally:

```text
Input → Encoder → Output
```

without requiring the entire input in memory.

Requirements:

- bounded buffers;
- backpressure;
- cancellation;
- async support;
- partial write handling;
- error propagation.

---

# 14. Streaming Decompression

Decoder requirements:

- bounded output;
- maximum expansion ratio;
- maximum output size;
- cancellation;
- truncated-input detection;
- checksum validation.

A decompressor must reject malicious expansion exceeding configured limits.

---

# 15. Compression Statistics

Optional statistics:

```text
input_bytes
output_bytes
compression_ratio
codec
level
elapsed_time
```

Statistics are diagnostic only and must not alter package identity.

---

# 16. Checksums

Package components may contain:

```text
CRC32C
SHA-256
SHA-512
BLAKE3
```

depending on profile.

Cryptographic package identity should use the algorithm selected by the package format.

The hash abstraction is supplied by BOOTSTRAP-610.

---

# 17. Archive Abstraction

Axiom defines:

```text
ArchiveReader
ArchiveWriter
ArchiveEntry
ArchiveEntryMetadata
```

Reader:

```text
open()
entry_count()
find(path)
read(entry)
stream(entry)
```

Writer:

```text
create()
add()
add_stream()
finish()
```

---

# 18. Archive Entry

Each entry contains:

```text
path
type
size
stored_size
compression
checksum
offset
flags
attributes
```

Optional:

```text
content_type
language
variant
target
permissions
```

---

# 19. Archive Types

Logical archive types:

```text
AXPK
ZIP
TAR
```

ZIP and TAR are compatibility formats.

AXPK is the native format.

---

# 20. ZIP Compatibility

Axiom may read/write conventional ZIP where required.

Compatibility must not change the semantics of the native AXPK format.

ZIP-specific limitations must be represented explicitly.

---

# 21. TAR Compatibility

TAR support is useful for:

- Unix interoperability;
- source bundles;
- container-like distribution;
- archival exports.

TAR does not provide all AXPK security or indexing guarantees.

---

# 22. Native Package Format

The native package format is named:

```text
AXPK
```

Logical layout:

```text
┌─────────────────────┐
│ Header              │
├─────────────────────┤
│ Manifest            │
├─────────────────────┤
│ Entry Index         │
├─────────────────────┤
│ Chunk/Object Index  │
├─────────────────────┤
│ Data                │
├─────────────────────┤
│ Merkle Metadata     │
├─────────────────────┤
│ Signature Block     │
└─────────────────────┘
```

---

# 23. AXPK Header

Required fields:

```text
magic
format_version
header_size
flags
package_id
package_version
target
architecture
manifest_offset
manifest_size
index_offset
index_size
data_offset
data_size
root_hash
signature_offset
signature_size
```

---

# 24. Package Identity

A package has:

```text
PackageId
PackageVersion
PackageBuildId
PackageRootHash
```

The immutable identity is:

```text
PackageIdentity =
    Hash(canonical package content)
```

The human-readable package ID is metadata.

---

# 25. Package Version

Axiom uses explicit version components:

```text
major
minor
patch
revision
```

Additional pre-release/build metadata may exist.

Version ordering is deterministic.

---

# 26. Package Target

A package may declare:

```text
os
architecture
abi
cpu_features
gpu_features
runtime_profile
```

Examples:

```text
windows-x64
linux-x64
linux-arm64
macos-arm64
android-arm64
ios-arm64
wasm32
```

---

# 27. Manifest

The package manifest is canonical AXBIN/AXSCHEMA-compatible data.

Example:

```text
package {
    id: "com.example.app"
    version: 1.4.0

    targets {
        windows-x64
        linux-x64
    }

    resources {
        "/assets/main.bin"
        "/models/model.axmodel"
    }
}
```

The actual canonical representation must use field IDs rather than textual field order.

---

# 28. Manifest Requirements

Manifest fields include:

```text
package identity
version
build identity
targets
dependencies
resources
capabilities
signing information
compression policy
encryption policy
minimum runtime
maximum runtime
compatibility flags
```

---

# 29. Resource Entry

A resource entry contains:

```text
resource_id
logical_path
content_type
size
compressed_size
compression
hash
chunking
flags
```

---

# 30. Resource IDs

Resource IDs should be stable across package versions when the logical resource remains the same.

Example:

```text
resource_id = Hash(package_id || normalized_path)
```

Alternative explicitly assigned IDs are permitted.

---

# 31. Path Normalization

Package paths use:

```text
UTF-8
/
```

Rules:

- no drive letters;
- no absolute OS paths;
- no `..`;
- no NUL;
- no platform separator ambiguity;
- canonical Unicode normalization policy;
- reserved package metadata paths.

Example:

```text
assets/logo.png
models/text_encoder.bin
locales/vi-VN.axres
```

---

# 32. Path Traversal Prevention

The following are invalid:

```text
../file
a/../../file
C:\file
\\server\file
/absolute/file
```

Validation occurs before:

- indexing;
- extraction;
- mounting;
- installation.

---

# 33. Symlinks

Native AXPK does not require symlink entries.

If supported, symlinks must be:

- explicitly marked;
- sandboxed;
- unable to escape the package root;
- disabled by default for untrusted packages.

---

# 34. Package Permissions

A package manifest may declare required capabilities:

```text
filesystem.read
network.connect
gpu.compute
camera.read
microphone.read
```

These are requests, not grants.

Actual authority comes from BOOTSTRAP-603.

---

# 35. Capability Principle

Package installation must never imply:

```text
package capability declaration
→ OS permission
```

Instead:

```text
package requirement
→ deployment policy
→ application capability
→ runtime operation
```

---

# 36. Package Signing

AXPK supports signatures based on BOOTSTRAP-610.

Signature covers:

```text
format version
manifest
entry index
content root
package identity
```

Mutable transport metadata must not be included.

---

# 37. Publisher Identity

A signature contains:

```text
publisher_id
key_id
algorithm
signature
certificate/reference metadata
```

Private keys are never stored in the package.

---

# 38. Verification

Verification sequence:

```text
parse
 ↓
validate bounds
 ↓
validate paths
 ↓
validate manifest
 ↓
compute content root
 ↓
verify signature
 ↓
verify policy
 ↓
accept package
```

No executable package content is loaded during verification.

---

# 39. Trust Policies

Policies may include:

```text
TrustedPublisher
TrustedKey
TrustedCertificate
UnsignedAllowed
SignatureRequired
PinnedPublisher
PinnedKey
```

Policy is controlled by BOOTSTRAP-603/610.

---

# 40. Encrypted Package Contents

AXPK may encrypt:

- complete data region;
- selected resources;
- selected chunks.

Encryption must use authenticated encryption.

Example:

```text
resource ciphertext
→ AEAD
→ authentication tag
```

---

# 41. Encryption Metadata

Metadata includes:

```text
algorithm
key_id
nonce/nonce derivation identifier
key version
encrypted range
```

Secrets are never stored directly in package metadata.

---

# 42. Selective Encryption

A package can leave public resources unencrypted while encrypting:

```text
models/*
private/*
license/*
```

This enables:

- fast package inspection;
- public metadata;
- protected large assets.

---

# 43. Compression + Encryption Ordering

Correct order:

```text
plaintext
 ↓
compress
 ↓
encrypt
```

Not:

```text
plaintext
 ↓
encrypt
 ↓
compress
```

because encrypted data generally compresses poorly.

---

# 44. Chunking

Large resources may be divided into chunks.

Each chunk contains:

```text
chunk_id
logical_offset
logical_size
stored_size
compression
encryption
hash
```

---

# 45. Chunk Size

Profiles may use:

```text
64 KiB
256 KiB
1 MiB
4 MiB
8 MiB
```

Adaptive chunking is permitted.

The package manifest records the actual chunking scheme.

---

# 46. Random Access

Chunking enables:

```text
read(resource, offset, size)
```

without decompressing the entire resource.

Example:

```text
model.bin
 ├─ chunk 0
 ├─ chunk 1
 ├─ chunk 2
 └─ ...
```

Only required chunks are loaded.

---

# 47. Memory Mapping

Uncompressed, aligned resources may be memory-mapped directly.

Requirements:

- immutable mapping;
- capability authorization;
- lifetime-bound package mount;
- package generation remains active while mapping exists.

Compressed resources cannot be directly memory-mapped as their logical representation.

---

# 48. Resource Streaming

API:

```text
Resource.open_stream()
Resource.read(offset, length)
Resource.map()
Resource.load()
```

Large resources should default to streaming.

---

# 49. Lazy Loading

A resource should not be loaded merely because its package was mounted.

Loading occurs on:

```text
open()
read()
map()
load()
```

This is important for:

- models;
- textures;
- audio;
- video;
- large language-model data;
- scientific datasets.

---

# 50. Resource Cache

The runtime provides:

```text
ResourceCache
```

with:

```text
memory cache
compressed chunk cache
decoded cache
disk cache
```

Caches are optional.

---

# 51. Cache Identity

Cache keys are content-based:

```text
ObjectId
ChunkId
PackageRootHash
```

not only:

```text
filename
```

This prevents stale-resource ambiguity.

---

# 52. Content-Addressed Storage

Axiom defines:

```text
ObjectStore
ObjectId
ObjectReader
ObjectWriter
ObjectLease
```

An object is immutable.

Example:

```text
ObjectId = SHA-256(content)
```

---

# 53. Object Store Layout

Logical layout:

```text
objects/
    ab/
       cdef...
```

The physical layout is backend-dependent.

---

# 54. Object Immutability

After:

```text
put(object)
```

the object cannot be modified.

Replacing content creates another object ID.

This provides strong cache correctness.

---

# 55. Deduplication

If two resources contain identical content:

```text
resource A → object X
resource B → object X
```

Only one physical object is required.

---

# 56. Chunk-Level Deduplication

Large files can deduplicate at chunk level:

```text
file A:
A B C D

file B:
A B X D
```

Only `X` is new.

---

# 57. Merkle Tree

A package may use:

```text
leaf = Hash(chunk)
parent = Hash(left || right)
root = Hash(tree)
```

The root becomes the package content identity.

---

# 58. Merkle Proof

A resource can be verified using:

```text
chunk
sibling hashes
root hash
```

without reading the entire package.

This is useful for:

- remote downloads;
- partial synchronization;
- large model distribution;
- cache validation.

---

# 59. Object References

Package index entries may reference:

```text
ObjectId
```

instead of physical offsets.

This permits:

- deduplication;
- package reconstruction;
- local cache reuse;
- remote object retrieval.

---

# 60. Object Store Modes

```text
Embedded
Local
Shared
Remote-backed
ReadOnly
Ephemeral
```

Only local embedded storage is required by the core runtime.

---

# 61. Storage Garbage Collection

Object-store reclamation is not language garbage collection.

Logical process:

```text
roots
 ↓
reachable objects
 ↓
unreachable objects
 ↓
reclaim
```

---

# 62. Object Store Roots

Roots include:

```text
active packages
installed generations
pinned packages
explicit leases
cache pins
checkpoint references
deployment references
```

---

# 63. Leases

An object may be temporarily protected by:

```text
ObjectLease
```

A lease prevents reclamation while a consumer is using the object.

---

# 64. Pinning

Long-lived applications may pin objects:

```text
store.pin(object_id)
```

Pins must be bounded and observable.

---

# 65. Reclamation Algorithms

Allowed implementations:

```text
reference counting
mark/sweep
generation-based reclamation
lease-based reclamation
hybrid
```

The public API must not expose the implementation.

---

# 66. Package Cache

The package cache contains:

```text
package metadata
manifest
signature verification result
object references
decoded indexes
compressed chunks
```

---

# 67. Cache Namespaces

Separate namespaces:

```text
system
user
application
build
temporary
deployment
```

Security boundaries must prevent cross-application unauthorized reuse.

---

# 68. Offline Deployment

A package may be installed from:

```text
local file
USB/storage
network download
IPC transfer
embedded resource
object store
```

No network access is required during installation if all objects are local.

---

# 69. Dependency Metadata

AXPK can declare:

```text
dependency {
    id
    version_constraint
    target
    optional
    feature
}
```

BOOTSTRAP-613 does not define full dependency resolution.

---

# 70. Dependency Resolution Boundary

Resolution belongs to a higher-level package/deployment system.

The runtime only needs:

```text
resolved dependency set
```

at activation time.

---

# 71. Resource Variants

One logical resource may contain variants:

```text
texture.png
 ├─ desktop
 ├─ mobile
 ├─ retina
 └─ low-memory
```

Selection can depend on:

```text
platform
architecture
locale
screen density
GPU capabilities
feature set
```

---

# 72. Localization

Resources may declare:

```text
locale = vi-VN
locale = en-US
```

Fallback:

```text
vi-VN
→ vi
→ default
```

The exact fallback chain is explicit and deterministic.

---

# 73. Target-Specific Resources

Example:

```text
bin/windows-x64/app.exe
bin/linux-x64/app
bin/macos-arm64/app
```

Only the active target's resources need to be activated.

---

# 74. Executable Bundles

An application package may contain:

```text
application executable
dynamic libraries
configuration
resources
debug symbols
licenses
metadata
```

The package runtime itself does not automatically execute the executable.

---

# 75. Native Executable Loading Boundary

Executable loading belongs to:

```text
Process/Supervisor
OS loader
Security capability layer
```

Package runtime provides the bytes and metadata.

---

# 76. Dynamic Libraries

Libraries can be package entries:

```text
.dll
.so
.dylib
```

Loading requires explicit security policy.

A package cannot silently replace a system library.

---

# 77. Platform Bundle Mapping

## Windows

Possible deployment:

```text
app.axpkg
 → app.exe
 → *.dll
 → resources
```

## Linux

Possible:

```text
app.axpkg
 → ELF
 → .so
 → resources
```

## macOS

Possible:

```text
App.app/
    Contents/
        MacOS/
        Frameworks/
        Resources/
```

AXPK may serve as the build/deployment source.

---

# 78. iOS

AXPK is a build/deployment abstraction.

The final platform bundle must obey Apple platform signing and bundle rules.

AXPK cannot bypass platform security.

---

# 79. Android

AXPK may be used internally for:

- application resources;
- native libraries;
- asset staging.

Final packaging must obey Android platform requirements.

---

# 80. WASM

A package may expose resources through:

```text
virtual filesystem
embedded byte ranges
host-provided resources
```

No assumption of native filesystem access is permitted.

---

# 81. Embedded Systems

AXPK can be compiled into:

```text
firmware image
read-only resource image
flash partition
ROM resource table
```

A minimal profile may remove:

- package installation;
- object reclamation;
- signatures;
- encryption;
- dynamic mounting.

---

# 82. Package Mounting

A package can be mounted as a read-only VFS:

```text
mount(package, "/app")
```

Example:

```text
/app/assets/logo.png
/app/models/model.bin
```

---

# 83. Mount Security

Mounting verifies:

- package integrity;
- path validity;
- package policy;
- capability requirements;
- signature policy.

---

# 84. Read-Only Package Filesystem

AXPK mounts are immutable.

Write operations return:

```text
ReadOnlyFilesystem
```

An overlay can provide writable state.

---

# 85. Overlay Filesystem

Logical structure:

```text
Writable Overlay
       ↑
AXPK Package
       ↑
Base Package
```

Read resolution searches upper layers first.

---

# 86. Atomic Activation

Installation:

```text
download
 ↓
verify
 ↓
stage
 ↓
validate
 ↓
commit
 ↓
activate
```

The active package pointer changes atomically.

---

# 87. Package Generations

Example:

```text
generation 41
generation 42
generation 43
```

Only one generation is active for a package identity unless explicitly configured otherwise.

---

# 88. Rollback

Rollback is:

```text
activate(previous_generation)
```

not:

```text
modify(active_package)
```

Old generations remain until reclamation policy permits deletion.

---

# 89. Interrupted Installation

If installation terminates unexpectedly:

```text
staged generation != active generation
```

Therefore the active version remains unchanged.

---

# 90. Secure Temporary Installation

Temporary package files use BOOTSTRAP-611 secure temporary-file mechanisms.

Rules:

- unpredictable temporary identity;
- exclusive creation;
- restrictive permissions;
- no unsafe shared directory;
- cleanup after completion.

---

# 91. Package Uninstall

Uninstall means:

```text
remove active reference
remove package metadata
remove unused object references
```

It does not necessarily immediately delete shared content.

---

# 92. Shared Objects

If:

```text
Package A → Object X
Package B → Object X
```

uninstalling A must not delete X while B still references it.

---

# 93. Package Garbage Collection

Package reclamation must consider:

```text
active generations
dependencies
pins
leases
snapshots
object references
```

---

# 94. Delta Packages

A delta package may contain:

```text
added objects
removed references
changed manifest
new signature
```

It should avoid transmitting unchanged content.

---

# 95. Binary Delta Boundary

Binary delta algorithms are optional.

The preferred base mechanism is object/chunk reuse.

This provides a simple and robust delta model without requiring a complex binary-diff engine.

---

# 96. Delta Verification

A delta must verify:

```text
base package root
target package root
new object hashes
signature
```

before activation.

---

# 97. Reproducible Package Builds

The package builder must normalize:

- entry ordering;
- paths;
- timestamps;
- ownership;
- permissions;
- compression settings;
- manifest serialization;
- padding;
- metadata ordering.

---

# 98. Canonical Entry Ordering

Default:

```text
lexicographic UTF-8 byte order
```

using canonical normalized paths.

---

# 99. Timestamp Policy

Reproducible mode uses:

```text
timestamp = SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH
```

or:

```text
timestamp = 0
```

if no build timestamp is supplied.

---

# 100. Host Independence

The following must not affect reproducible package identity:

```text
username
hostname
absolute build path
temporary directory
OS-specific local path
process ID
build machine ID
```

---

# 101. Package Root Hash

Conceptually:

```text
PackageRootHash =
    Hash(
        canonical manifest ||
        canonical entry index ||
        Merkle root
    )
```

The exact format is versioned.

---

# 102. Package Fingerprint

Human-readable fingerprint:

```text
axpk:<algorithm>:<hex>
```

Example:

```text
axpk:sha256:...
```

---

# 103. AI-Readable Metadata

Every package should optionally contain:

```text
package.axmeta
```

containing:

```text
package ID
version
targets
resources
schemas
dependencies
capabilities
ABI
exports
entrypoints
build identity
source mapping
```

# 104. Machine-Readable Package Inspection

A resource handle keeps its package generation alive as required.

Unmounting a package with active mapped resources must either:

- reject unmount.

```text
package.install
package.activate
package.extract
```

# 142. Missing Object


```text
no visible package generation
```

```text
new generation exists
```


---

# 221. No Silent Recovery

If integrity validation fails, the runtime must not silently substitute arbitrary data.

Recovery must be explicit:

```text
alternate object source
cache repair
re-download
rollback
```

---

# 222. Package Trust Levels

Optional policy classifications:

```text
Untrusted
Verified
TrustedPublisher
SystemTrusted
EmbeddedTrusted
```

These are policy metadata, not intrinsic properties of the bytes.

---

# 223. Package Isolation

Package contents must not automatically share:

- capabilities;
- secrets;
- process authority;
- filesystem access;
- network authority.

Package code inherits authority only from its execution context.

---

# 224. Package-to-Package Isolation

Two packages may share immutable objects safely because object identity is content-based.

Mutable runtime state remains outside the package object store.

---

# 225. Package Metadata Versioning

Every schema has:

```text
schema_id
schema_version
schema_fingerprint
```

using BOOTSTRAP-612.

---

# 226. Package Metadata Evolution

New optional fields may be added.

Required fields must remain compatible according to schema rules.

Old readers must reject incompatible required semantics explicitly.

---

# 227. Package Resource ABI

Resources can expose typed schemas:

```text
Texture2D
AudioClip
Shader
Model
Font
LocalizationTable
BinaryBlob
```

These are metadata types, not necessarily language-level classes.

---

# 228. Shader Resources

GPU shader packages may contain:

```text
SPIR-V
DXIL
MSL
WGSL
```

depending on target.

Actual GPU execution belongs to a later hardware/GPU subsystem.

---

# 229. Resource Compilation Pipeline

Example:

```text
model.fbx
 ↓
asset compiler
 ↓
model.axmesh
 ↓
chunk/compress
 ↓
AXPK
```

The package layer does not need to understand every source format.

---

# 230. Package as Build Artifact

Compiler output can be:

```text
app.exe
app.axpkg
app.debug.axpkg
```

Debug symbols should be separately packaged when desired.

---

# 231. Debug Package

Debug package may contain:

```text
symbols
source maps
type metadata
resource source mappings
compiler diagnostics
```

It must not be shipped accidentally in release profiles.

---

# 232. Symbol Package Identity

Debug package can reference release binary by:

```text
BuildId
```

rather than filename alone.

---

# 233. Package Signing Profiles

Profiles:

```text
Development
Testing
Release
System
```

Each can define different signature requirements.

---

# 234. Development Mode

May permit:

```text
unsigned packages
local keys
debug metadata
```

only when explicitly enabled.

---

# 235. Release Mode

May require:

```text
signature
trusted publisher
verified dependencies
reproducible build metadata
```

---

# 236. No Install Scripts

AXPK does not support arbitrary:

```text
install.sh
postinstall.exe
package.js
```

inside the core format.

Installation is declarative.

This prevents package opening from becoming arbitrary code execution.

---

# 237. Declarative Hooks

If platform deployment requires actions, those actions are represented as typed manifest operations handled by trusted system code.

---

# 238. Package Resource Permissions

Resource declarations can specify:

```text
public
private
secret
executable
system
```

Security policy determines actual treatment.

---

# 239. Secret Resources

Secret resources must not be included as ordinary plaintext assets in release packages unless policy explicitly permits it.

Preferred mechanism:

```text
package → key reference
runtime → secure key provider
```

---

# 240. Secure Resource Deletion

Deletion of encrypted package objects follows storage guarantees from BOOTSTRAP-611.

The runtime must not falsely claim that flash/SSD data has been physically erased.

---

# 241. Package Compression Security

Compression codecs must enforce:

```text
output limit
memory limit
CPU budget
nested archive depth
```

Nested archives are not automatically recursively extracted.

---

# 242. Nested Packages

An AXPK may contain another AXPK as a resource.

It is treated as data until explicitly opened.

Opening the nested package creates a new trust boundary.

---

# 243. Package-in-Package Mount

Optional:

```text
mount(parent:/packages/a.axpkg, "/a")
```

Capability and resource limits apply independently.

---

# 244. Archive Compatibility Security

ZIP/TAR importers must normalize and validate paths before exposing entries.

Legacy archive semantics must not weaken AXPK security.

---

# 245. Package Cache Security

Cache entries are validated by content identity.

Cache poisoning cannot change content without changing its hash.

---

# 246. Publisher Cache

Signature verification results may be cached using:

```text
package_root_hash
publisher_key_id
policy_fingerprint
```

Changing policy invalidates the cached authorization result.

---

# 247. Trust Cache Invalidation

Changing:

```text
trust store
key revocation
security policy
```

must invalidate affected verification results.

---

# 248. Package Policy Fingerprint

Deployment records should include:

```text
package_policy_fingerprint
```

so that activation decisions remain auditable.

---

# 249. Object Store Compaction

If physical object storage uses packed files, compaction must:

- preserve object identity;
- use atomic replacement;
- tolerate interruption;
- preserve active objects.

---

# 250. Packed Object Store

Objects may be physically packed:

```text
pack-001
pack-002
pack-003
```

with an index:

```text
ObjectId → pack + offset + length
```

This reduces filesystem overhead.

---

# 251. Object Index

Object index can use:

```text
hash table
B-tree
sorted table
minimal perfect hash
```

depending on profile.

---

# 252. Object Store Integrity

Pack files contain:

```text
header
object records
checksum/footer
```

Corruption must be detectable.

---

# 253. Object Store Crash Recovery

A crash during pack creation must leave:

```text
old valid pack
```

or:

```text
new valid pack
```

never a silently accepted partial pack.

---

# 254. Object Store Snapshot

Snapshots may record:

```text
root set
package generations
object index version
```

and integrate with BOOTSTRAP-600.

---

# 255. Snapshot Semantics

Snapshotting the object store does not imply snapshotting arbitrary external filesystem state.

---

# 256. Resource Versioning

A resource can have:

```text
resource_id
version
content_hash
```

but content hash remains the authoritative immutable identity.

---

# 257. Package Aliases

Deployment systems may define:

```text
current
stable
testing
```

aliases.

The core package store treats aliases as mutable references to immutable generations.

---

# 258. Atomic Alias Update

Alias update must be atomic:

```text
stable → generation 42
```

No intermediate partially updated state is visible.

---

# 259. Package Channel Metadata

Channels are higher-level deployment metadata.

AXPK itself does not decide whether a package is “stable” or “beta”.

---

# 260. Remote Object Protocol Boundary

A later networking/deployment subsystem may define:

```text
GET object_id
GET package manifest
GET chunk
```

613 only defines the local object abstraction.

---

# 261. HTTP Integration

A package may be downloaded over BOOTSTRAP-609 HTTP.

Download pipeline:

```text
HTTP
 ↓
stream
 ↓
verify chunk
 ↓
store object
```

No need to hold the whole package in memory.

---

# 262. Resumable Download

Content-addressed chunks allow:

```text
download missing chunks only
```

after interruption.

---

# 263. Parallel Download

Independent chunks may be fetched concurrently.

BOOTPSTRAP-606 limits:

```text
CPU
network
memory
open connections
```

---

# 264. Package Prefetch

Deployment systems may prefetch packages without activation.

Prefetched packages remain:

```text
Committed but Inactive
```

until activation.

---

# 265. Rollback Storage Budget

The resource governor may enforce a maximum number of retained generations.

Example policy:

```text
keep_last = 3
```

The package layer only exposes the primitives.

---

# 266. Package Lifecycle

```text
Unknown
 ↓
Discovered
 ↓
Downloaded
 ↓
Verified
 ↓
Staged
 ↓
Committed
 ↓
Active
 ↓
Retired
 ↓
Reclaimable
 ↓
Reclaimed
```

---

# 267. Invariant: Immutable Content

Once:

```text
ObjectId = H(content)
```

the object represented by that ID must never change.

---

# 268. Invariant: Atomic Activation

At every observable point:

```text
active package = valid generation
```

---

# 269. Invariant: Verified Consumption

An application must never consume package content that violates configured integrity policy.

---

# 270. Invariant: Capability Separation

Package metadata can request capabilities but cannot grant them.

---

# 271. Invariant: Bounded Expansion

Decompression must respect resource limits.

---

# 272. Invariant: No Hidden Execution

Parsing, verification, extraction and mounting never execute package-provided code.

---

# 273. Invariant: Deterministic Identity

Given identical canonical inputs:

```text
package root hash
```

must be identical.

---

# 274. Invariant: Shared Content Safety

Removing one package cannot remove objects still referenced by another package.

---

# 275. Invariant: Cache Non-Authority

Deleting all caches cannot make a valid installed package invalid.

---

# 276. Invariant: Crash Safety

A process crash during install cannot expose a partial active package.

---

# 277. Invariant: Memory Bound

Package opening must not require memory proportional to total package content.

---

# 278. Invariant: Platform Independence

AXPK logical semantics must remain independent from:

```text
Windows path syntax
Linux permissions
macOS bundle structure
Android package structure
iOS bundle structure
```

# 288. Final Design Decision

BOOTSTRAP-613 establishes **AXPK + immutable content-addressed objects + chunked resources** as the native packaging foundation.

The critical separation is:

```text
AXPK
    = package/container identity

ObjectStore
    = immutable content storage

VFS
    = resource namespace

Compression
    = storage/transport optimization

Crypto
    = integrity/confidentiality/trust

Package Manager
    = higher-level dependency/deployment policy
```

This prevents the core runtime from becoming coupled to a monolithic package-manager design.

# BOOTSTRAP-614
## Native Device, Hardware, Peripheral, Sensor, GPU/Accelerator & OS Resource I/O Runtime 5.0

**Status:** Architecture Specification  
**Layer:** Native Hardware / Device Runtime  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600 → 613  
**Primary dependencies:** 603 Security, 606 Resource Governor, 607 Scheduler, 608 Synchronization, 609 Networking, 610 Cryptography, 611 Storage, 612 Serialization, 613 Packaging  
**Target:** Windows / Linux / macOS / Android / iOS / WASM / Embedded

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-614 defines Axiom's native abstraction for physical and OS-managed devices.

It covers:

- device discovery;
- device identity;
- device capabilities;
- device handles;
- device lifetime;
- hardware resources;
- peripheral access;
- buses;
- USB;
- PCI/PCIe;
- Bluetooth;
- serial devices;
- HID/input;
- display;
- audio;
- cameras;
- sensors;
- GPU;
- accelerators;
- DMA;
- device memory;
- command queues;
- synchronization;
- device events;
- hot-plug;
- power state;
- thermal state;
- device reset;
- device loss;
- embedded peripherals;
- platform-specific device backends.

The design must provide a common Axiom model without pretending that all platforms expose identical hardware capabilities.

---

# 2. Core Principle

The architecture separates:

```text
Physical Device
      ↓
OS Device Object
      ↓
Axiom Device Backend
      ↓
Typed Device Handle
      ↓
Capability
      ↓
Device API
```

Axiom never assumes that possession of a device handle automatically grants unrestricted hardware access.

---

# 3. Non-Goals

This specification does not define:

- a universal GPU shader language;
- a complete graphics API;
- a complete audio DSP framework;
- a complete camera-processing framework;
- a universal driver-development language;
- kernel implementation;
- replacement for OS device managers;
- firmware implementation;
- automatic hardware overclocking;
- unsafe raw MMIO by default.

Those can be built above this layer.

---

# 4. Fundamental Invariants

1. Every device has a stable runtime identity.
2. Device handles are generation-safe.
3. A closed/lost device cannot be used.
4. Device capabilities are explicit.
5. Device operations obey BOOTSTRAP-603.
6. Device resource consumption obeys BOOTSTRAP-606.
7. Blocking device operations do not block async executors unnecessarily.
8. Device buffers have explicit ownership/lifetime.
9. DMA mappings are explicitly represented.
10. GPU device loss is recoverable where the platform permits.
11. Hot-plug does not invalidate unrelated device handles.
12. Device removal produces deterministic events.
13. Raw physical addresses are not exposed to ordinary application code.
14. MMIO requires explicit privileged capability.
15. Driver boundaries remain platform-specific.
16. No mandatory global device lock exists.
17. Device enumeration is deterministic within a snapshot.
18. Device metadata is inspectable without opening the device.
19. Device discovery never executes device-provided code.
20. Unsupported hardware features fail explicitly.

---

# 21. Backend Architecture

```text

    ↓

    ↓

    ├── Windows
```

```text
Device
 └── Session
      ├── Queue

      ├── Mapping

```

# 225. Structured Device Ownership

Axiom can use structured lifetime:

```text

    ...
```

without requiring a garbage collector.

# 226. Device Handle RAII

Compiler-generated cleanup may release:

```text
queues
mappings
```

at deterministic scope exit.

# 227. No Hidden Finalizer

may be returned.

# 230. Device Scope

A structured scope can ensure:

```text

→ use
→ drain
→ close
```

before leaving the scope.

---

# 231. Compiler Lifetime Metadata

The compiler may track:

```text
resource owner
in-flight use
close state
```

without implementing a global borrow checker.

rather than raw pointers.
