# 139. Memory Budget

Document loading must respect 606 memory budgets.

---

# 140. Memory-Mapped Documents

611 memory mapping can be used for suitable formats.

---

# 141. Copy-On-Write

Large immutable document regions may use structural sharing.

---

# 142. Rope / Chunked Structures

Text editors can use ropes/chunked buffers to avoid O(n) insertion.

---

# 143. Binary Large Documents

Binary editors can use sparse/chunked representations.

---

# 144. Object Documents

Structured editors can use object graphs with stable IDs.

---

# 145. Stable Object Identity

```text
DocumentObjectId
```

must survive non-semantic reordering when the application requires it.

---

# 146. Structural Changes

Objects may be:

```text
Created
Deleted
Moved
Reparented
Modified
```

---

# 147. Schema Version

Structured documents include schema versions through 612.

---

# 148. Migration

Document migrations are explicit and versioned.

---

# 149. Migration Backup

Before destructive migration, a recovery snapshot may be created.

---

# 150. Migration Failure

Original content remains available.

---

# 151. Import

Import converts an external format into the document model.

---

# 152. Export

Export converts the model into an external format.

---

# 153. Lossy Export

Export may explicitly report:

```text
Lossy
UnsupportedFeature
DroppedMetadata
```

---

# 154. Export Validation

Applications can require zero loss before allowing save.

---

# 155. Document Capabilities

Formats declare:

```text
CanRead
CanWrite
CanStream
CanPatch
CanMerge
CanRecover
CanIncrementalSave
```

---

# 156. Capability Negotiation

DocumentManager selects operations based on format capabilities.

---

# 157. Save Strategy

Strategies include:

```text
FullRewrite
IncrementalPatch
AppendLog
CopyOnWrite
```

---

# 158. Transaction Journal

A document can maintain a journal of changes before snapshotting.

---

# 159. Journal

```text
DocumentJournal
```

stores:

```text
revision
operation_id
change
checksum
```

---

# 160. Journal Recovery

Valid journal entries can reconstruct state after a crash.

---

# 161. Journal Truncation

After a durable snapshot, obsolete journal entries can be compacted.

---

# 162. Journal Integrity

Each entry can contain a chained checksum/hash.

---

# 163. Corruption

Corrupt journal entries stop replay at the last valid boundary.

---

# 164. No Silent Corruption

The application receives a recovery diagnostic.

---

# 165. Checkpoint

A checkpoint represents a durable document reconstruction boundary.

---

# 166. Checkpoint Metadata

```text
checkpoint_id
revision
snapshot_hash
storage_location
```

---

# 167. Checkpoint Frequency

Controlled by resource budget and autosave policy.

---

# 168. History Compaction

Compaction:

```text
old revisions
    ↓
snapshot
    ↓
new base
```

---

# 169. History Integrity

Compaction must preserve reconstructibility of retained revisions.

---

# 170. History Garbage Collection

History storage reclamation is storage-object reclamation, not language GC.

---

# 171. CAS Integration

Old snapshots may be retained by CAS pins/leases through 613.

---

# 172. Document Export

Export can directly stream to:

```text
File
Memory
Network
IPC
```

through 611/609/604.

---

# 173. Document Import

Import can stream from those same sources.

---

# 174. Security

Opening an untrusted document must not execute document-provided code.

---

# 175. Parser Sandbox

Complex parsers may run in isolated processes through 603/604/605.

---

# 176. Resource Limits

Untrusted documents have limits for:

```text
size
depth
object count
decompression
CPU
memory
```

---

# 177. Zip/Package Bomb Protection

---

# 178. External References

A document referencing external files must use explicit capabilities.

---

# 179. Missing References

Missing resources are represented as explicit unresolved references.

---

# 180. Secret References

Sensitive resources cannot be silently embedded into exported documents.

---

# 181. Diagnostics

```text

load duration
save duration
revision
autosave
recovery
merge conflict
parse error
external modification
```

---

# 182. Performance Metrics

Applications can inspect:

```text
load throughput
save throughput
diff time
merge time
serialization time
history size
autosave latency
```

---

# 183. Trace Integration

Document operations can create tracing spans.

---

# 184. AI Metadata

621 may generate:

```text
.axdoc
.axformat
.axhistory
```

metadata.

# 185. `.axdoc`

```text
document type
schema
revision

dependencies
```

---

# 186. `.axhistory`

---

# 187. Compiler Integration

The compiler may generate document serializers, patch structures and stable IDs for typed document models.

# 192. Format Detection

# 193. Ambiguous Format

# 196. Reload

```text
   +
```

# 200. Merge UI

# 201. Conflict Resolution State

# 202. Collaboration Transport

# 203. IPC Collaboration

# 204. Authentication

# 205. Authorization

# 206. Capability Model

```text
DocumentRead
DocumentWrite
DocumentSave
DocumentExport
DocumentShare
DocumentHistory
DocumentRecover
DocumentMerge
```

---

# 207. Least Privilege

A view that only displays a document should not receive write capability.

---

# 208. Read-Only Mode

Read-only documents reject mutations at transaction start.

---

# 209. Temporary Edit

---

# 210. Draft

Draft state may be persisted separately from the canonical document.

---

# 211. Draft Identity

is separate from `DocumentId`.

---

# 212. Draft Recovery

Drafts use the recovery infrastructure.

---

# 213. Publish

An application can explicitly promote a draft into the canonical document.

---

# 214. Version Tags

Human-readable labels can reference revisions:

---

# 215. Branch

Applications may create:

for experimental editing.

# 216. Branch Merge

Branches merge through the same three-way merge engine.

# 217. No Mandatory Git Dependency

621 does not depend on Git or another VCS.

# 218. VCS Integration Boundary

# 219. Version Control Adapter

may provide:

```text
checkout
branch
diff
merge
```

# 220. Local History

Applications can implement local history without a VCS.

# 221. Autosave + History

Autosave protects current work.

# 222. Crash Recovery + Undo

# 223. Recovery Compatibility

Undo history must only be restored when its base revision matches the recovered document.

---

# 224. Recovery Mismatch

Mismatched history is discarded or exposed separately; it must not be applied blindly.

---

# 225. Workspace Recovery

600 can persist workspace state:

```text
open documents
active document
unsaved drafts
```

---

# 226. Application Restart

The application may restore its previous workspace.

---

# 227. Shutdown

On graceful shutdown:

```text

close sessions
flush history
```

according to policy.

---

# 228. Forced Shutdown

Recovery records remain available for unsaved documents.

---

# 229. Resource Governor

606 may terminate or constrain:

```text
history
autosave frequency
diff workers
merge workers
document cache
```

# 230. Scheduler

Large diff/merge/save operations should execute asynchronously.

---

# 231. UI Responsiveness

UI-affine document operations must not perform unbounded blocking I/O.

---

# 232. Background Save

# 233. Completion Safety

---

# 234. Stale Save

the completion must not mark the newer state as saved.

---

# 235. Concurrent Saves

At most one durable save pipeline per document unless the format explicitly supports concurrent versions.

---

# 236. Save Cancellation

Cancellation must preserve the existing durable document.

---

# 237. Save Temporary Files

Temporary files use secure creation through 611.

---

# 238. Atomic Replacement

Final replacement uses filesystem atomicity guarantees.

---

# 239. Durability

The implementation must not claim durable persistence until the configured durability operation succeeds.

# 240. Testing

- document lifecycle;
- transaction atomicity;
- revision tracking;
- save failure;
- save race;
- autosave;
- recovery;
- crash;
- journal replay;

- diff;

# 242. Property Tests

Properties include:

```text
apply(diff(A,B), A) == B
```

# 243. Merge Property

For non-conflicting changes:

```text
merge(base, A, B)
```

must preserve both changes.

---

# 244. Undo Property

For reversible transaction `T`:

```text
undo(T(apply(S))) == S
```

within declared semantic equivalence.

# 245. Save Property

After successful durable save:

```text
persisted_revision == saved_revision
```

---

# 246. Crash Property

# 247. Recovery Property

Recovered content must pass checksum and schema validation before becoming active.

# 248. Collaboration Property

Duplicate operation IDs must not duplicate mutations.

# 249. Security Property

Untrusted documents cannot execute arbitrary application code merely by being parsed.

# 250. Performance Property

Small document edits should not require full-document serialization unless the format requires it.

# 253. Architectural Decisions

Axiom adopts the following document architecture:

1. `DocumentId` is independent of filesystem path.
2. Document revisions are immutable.
3. Mutations occur through transactions.
4. Dirty state is revision-based.
5. Save is distinct from autosave.
6. Recovery is distinct from normal persistence.
7. Undo is distinct from recovery.
8. History is optional.
9. Diff/merge are provider-extensible.
10. Three-way merge is the canonical generic merge model.
11. Collaboration is an optional provider layer.
12. OT/CRDT are not built into the language core.
13. Document models are ordinary structs/data.
14. Views are independent from documents.
15. Multiple views can share one document.
16. External changes never silently destroy local edits.
17. Save completion is revision-aware.
18. No third-party VCS is required.
19. No mandatory GC is introduced.
20. No mandatory reflection is introduced.

Tiếp tục với **BOOTSTRAP-622** — lớp presentation/workspace phía trên Document và GUI, tập trung vào navigation, docking, multi-window và quản lý bố cục ứng dụng phức tạp.

# BOOTSTRAP-622 — Native Application Navigation, Routing, Workspace Layout, Docking, Multi-Window, MDI/SDI & Document/View Presentation Runtime 5.0

**Status:** SPECIFIED  
**Layer:** Native Application Presentation / Workspace Runtime  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600 → 621

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-622 defines the application-level presentation runtime above:

- BOOTSTRAP-619 GUI;
- BOOTSTRAP-620 State/Binding/Commands;
- BOOTSTRAP-621 Documents/History/Recovery.

It provides the infrastructure for applications containing:

- multiple windows;
- documents and document views;
- navigation;
- routes;
- tabs;
- docking panels;
- split views;
- tool windows;
- floating windows;
- MDI/SDI/hybrid presentation;
- workspaces;
- layout persistence;
- window restoration;
- presentation history;
- modal/non-modal navigation;
- deep links;
- URI-based application state.

It does **not** mandate a particular application UI architecture.

---

# 2. Design Principle

The core separation is:

```text
Document
    ≠
DocumentView
    ≠
Window
    ≠
Workspace
    ≠
NavigationEntry
```

A document may have multiple views.

A view may move between windows.

A window may belong to different workspaces over time.

Navigation state records presentation history, not ownership of domain data.

---

# 3. Layering

```text
Application
     │
     ▼
ApplicationShell
     │
 ┌───┼──────────────┐
 ▼   ▼              ▼
Router Workspace  WindowManager
 │      │              │
 ▼      ▼              ▼
Route  Layout        Windows
 │      │              │
 └──────┼──────────────┘
        ▼
   Document/View
        │
        ▼
       619
```

---

# 4. Core Objects

```text
ApplicationShell
NavigationManager
Router
Route
RouteId
RoutePattern
RouteValue
NavigationEntry
NavigationStack
NavigationHistory
NavigationRequest
NavigationResult
NavigationGuard
NavigationTransition
WindowManager
WindowGroup
Window
WindowState
Workspace
WorkspaceId
WorkspaceLayout
DockTree
DockNode
DockPanel
SplitNode
TabGroup
TabItem
FloatingPanel
ToolWindow
DocumentViewHost
ViewPlacement
Presentation
PresentationMode
```

---

# 5. Application Shell

```text
ApplicationShell
```

represents the application-level presentation environment.

It coordinates:

- windows;
- workspace;
- routing;
- commands;
- lifecycle;
- state restoration.

---

# 6. Shell Ownership

The shell owns presentation infrastructure but does not own domain documents unless explicitly configured.

---

# 7. Navigation

Navigation is a transition from one presentation state to another.

---

# 8. Route

A route identifies a destination.

Example:

```text
/editor/document/42
/settings/audio
/project/7/assets
```

---

# 9. Route Identity

```text
RouteId
```

is a stable application-defined identifier.

---

# 10. Route Pattern

A route can contain typed parameters:

```text
/project/{project_id}/document/{document_id}
```

---

# 11. Typed Route Values

Route parameters are strongly typed.

Example:

```text
document_id: DocumentId
```

rather than an unvalidated string.

---

# 12. Route Parsing

Invalid route parameters produce a typed navigation error.

---

# 13. Route Serialization

Routes can serialize to:

- URI;
- application deep-link format;
- workspace state.

---

# 14. URI Boundary

External URI parsing is treated as untrusted input.

---

# 15. Route Registration

Applications register routes explicitly.

---

# 16. No Mandatory Reflection

Route registration can be generated statically by the compiler.

---

# 17. Route Metadata

Compiler metadata may generate:

```text
.axroute
```

containing:

```text
route_id
pattern
parameter_types
required_capabilities
destination
```

---

# 18. Navigation Manager

```text
NavigationManager
```

provides:

```text
navigate
back
forward
replace
reload
reset
```

---

# 19. Navigation Entry

Each navigation entry contains:

```text
NavigationEntry {
    route
    presentation
    state
    timestamp
}
```

---

# 20. Navigation Stack

A stack represents sequential navigation.

```text
A → B → C
```

Back navigation returns:

```text
C → B
```

---

# 21. Navigation History

History is independent from document history.

---

# 22. Document History vs Navigation History

```text
Document History:
edit A → edit B → edit C

Navigation:
document A → settings → document B
```

They must never be conflated.

---

# 23. Back

Back removes the current navigation entry when policy permits.

---

# 24. Forward

Forward restores an entry invalidated by a back operation.

---

# 25. Divergent Navigation

Navigating to a new destination after back clears the normal forward branch.

---

# 26. Navigation Branches

Optional advanced history can retain branches.

---

# 27. Replace

`replace()` changes the current entry without adding a new history item.

---

# 28. Reset

`reset()` replaces the navigation stack with a new root state.

---

# 29. Navigation Request

```text
NavigationRequest {
    destination
    parameters
    presentation
    source
    options
}
```

---

# 30. Navigation Result

```text
NavigationResult {
    Completed
    Rejected
    Cancelled
    Failed
    Deferred
}
```

---

# 31. Navigation Guard

A guard can inspect a navigation request.

---

# 32. Guard Use Cases

Examples:

- unsaved document;
- authentication;
- permission;
- required resource;
- pending transaction.

---

# 33. Guard Must Be Explicit

Navigation must not silently block forever.

---

# 34. Async Guard

Guards may return:

```text
Future<NavigationDecision>
```

through 607.

---

# 35. Guard Cancellation

Navigation requests carry cancellation.

---

# 36. Guard Ordering

Guards execute in deterministic order.

---

# 37. Guard Failure

A failed guard produces a diagnostic and rejected navigation.

---

# 38. Navigation Transaction

Navigation itself can be transactional.

```text
Prepare
Validate
Commit Presentation
```

---

# 39. Presentation Transaction

A navigation transaction must not leave half-created windows or views.

---

# 40. Rollback

If destination creation fails, presentation state returns to its previous valid state.

---

# 41. Destination

A route resolves to a destination provider.

```text
DestinationProvider
```

---

# 42. Destination Provider

Responsible for creating:

- view;
- document view;
- tool panel;
- dialog;
- window;
- workspace.

---

# 43. Lazy Destination

Destinations may be instantiated only when navigated to.

---

# 44. Resource Control

Unused destinations should not remain alive solely because their route exists.

---

# 45. Route State

A route can carry transient presentation state.

---

# 46. Route State Example

```text
/editor/document/42?cursor=100&line=20
```

The application decides which parameters are durable.

---

# 47. Navigation State

Navigation entries may preserve:

- scroll;
- selection;
- focused control;
- query;
- filter;
- zoom.

---

# 48. State Separation

Document content remains in 621.

Presentation state remains in 622/619.

---

# 49. Window Manager

```text
WindowManager
```

controls application windows.

---

# 50. Window Identity

Windows have:

```text
WindowId
WindowGeneration
```

---

# 51. Window Groups

A `WindowGroup` groups windows belonging to one application/session.

---

# 52. Window Roles

```text
Main
Document
Tool
Dialog
Popup
Utility
Inspector
Preview
Floating
```

---

# 53. Window Ownership

A child window can explicitly reference its owner window.

---

# 54. Parent/Owner Relationship

Closing an owner may close owned transient windows according to policy.

---

# 55. Window Lifetime

Window lifetime is separate from document lifetime.

---

# 56. Multi-Window

One document can be displayed in multiple windows.

```text
Document
 ├── Window A
 └── Window B
```

---

# 57. Single-Window

An application can enforce:

```text
one document → one presentation
```

through policy.

---

# 58. SDI

Single Document Interface can be represented as:

```text
Window
 └── DocumentView
```

---

# 59. MDI

Multiple Document Interface can be represented as:

```text
Window
 └── Workspace
      ├── DocumentView A
      ├── DocumentView B
      └── DocumentView C
```

---

# 60. Hybrid

A hybrid application may use:

```text
Main Window
 ├── document tabs
 ├── docked tools
 └── floating inspectors
```

without a special runtime mode.

---

# 61. Presentation Mode

```text
PresentationMode
```

can specify:

```text
Embedded
Tab
Split
Floating
Window
Dialog
Modal
```

---

# 62. Workspace

A workspace is a persistent presentation environment.

---

# 63. Workspace Identity

```text
WorkspaceId
```

is stable.

---

# 64. Workspace Contents

A workspace may contain:

```text
documents
views
windows
dock panels
tabs
splits
navigation
selection
active item
```

---

# 65. Workspace Does Not Own Document Content

Workspace stores references/placements.

---

# 66. Workspace Layout

```text
WorkspaceLayout
```

is a tree.

---

# 67. Layout Tree

```text
Root
 ├── Split
 │    ├── TabGroup
 │    └── DockPanel
 └── FloatingWindow
```

---

# 68. Dock Tree

The dock layout is represented by:

```text
DockTree
```

---

# 69. Dock Nodes

```text
DockNode
SplitNode
TabNode
PanelNode
PlaceholderNode
```

---

# 70. Split Node

A split contains:

```text
orientation
children
ratios
```

---

# 71. Orientation

```text
Horizontal
Vertical
```

---

# 72. Split Ratio

Ratios are normalized.

---

# 73. Ratio Constraints

Minimum and maximum panel sizes are respected.

---

# 74. Tab Group

A tab group contains ordered views.

---

# 75. Tab Identity

Each tab references a stable:

```text
ViewId
```

---

# 76. Tab State

# 261. Architectural Decisions

Axiom adopts:

1. **Navigation is separate from document history.**
2. **Workspace layout is separate from document content.**
3. **Windows are presentation containers, not document owners by default.**
4. **One document can have many views.**
5. **One view can move between presentation containers.**
6. **SDI, MDI and hybrid applications use the same primitives.**
7. **Docking is a data structure, not hard-coded GUI behavior.**
8. **Workspace state is serializable and recoverable.**
9. **Native handles are reconstructed rather than persisted.**
10. **Deep links are typed and capability-aware.**
11. **Navigation guards are explicit.**
12. **Async navigation is cancellable and generation-safe.**
13. **Workspace layouts contain data, never executable code.**
14. **Provider failures do not invalidate the entire workspace.**
15. **Document undo and workspace undo remain separate.**
16. **Autosave and document save remain separate.**
17. **No mandatory MDI framework exists.**
18. **No mandatory routing framework exists.**
19. **No mandatory plugin system exists.**
20. **The entire layer can be dead-stripped from headless applications.**

```text
navigate(B)
back()
```

---

# 251. Divergence Property

---

# 253. Window Property

---

# 254. Workspace Property

---

# 255. Persistence Property

A successfully restored workspace must contain only validated logical state.

---

# 256. Resource Property

Workspace restoration must obey 606 resource limits.

---

# 257. Security Property

Workspace data cannot grant capabilities.

---

# 258. Performance Property

Docking one panel should not require rebuilding unrelated workspace branches.

# 261. Architectural Decisions

Axiom adopts:

1. **Navigation is separate from document history.**
2. **Workspace layout is separate from document content.**
3. **Windows are presentation containers, not document owners by default.**
4. **One document can have many views.**
5. **One view can move between presentation containers.**
6. **SDI, MDI and hybrid applications use the same primitives.**
7. **Docking is a data structure, not hard-coded GUI behavior.**
8. **Workspace state is serializable and recoverable.**
9. **Native handles are reconstructed rather than persisted.**
10. **Deep links are typed and capability-aware.**
11. **Navigation guards are explicit.**
12. **Async navigation is cancellable and generation-safe.**
13. **Workspace layouts contain data, never executable code.**
14. **Provider failures do not invalidate the entire workspace.**
15. **Document undo and workspace undo remain separate.**
16. **Autosave and document save remain separate.**
17. **No mandatory MDI framework exists.**
18. **No mandatory routing framework exists.**
19. **No mandatory plugin system exists.**
20. **The entire layer can be dead-stripped from headless applications.**

# BOOTSTRAP-623 — Native Application Plugin, Extension, Module, Hot-Reload, Package Discovery, Dependency Isolation & Extension Runtime 5.0

**Status:** SPECIFIED  
**Layer:** Application Extension / Module Runtime  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600 → 622

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-623 defines the native extension architecture for Axiom applications:

- modules;
- plugins;
- extensions;
- optional application features;
- package discovery;
- dependency resolution;
- ABI/API boundaries;
- extension lifecycle;
- isolation;
- capability provisioning;
- hot-load;
- hot-unload;
- hot-reload;
- version compatibility;
- extension configuration;
- extension resources;
- extension UI;
- extension commands;
- extension services;
- extension IPC;
- extension diagnostics.

The design must preserve Axiom's primary goals:

- native performance;
- small binaries;
- deterministic behavior;
- no mandatory plugin runtime;
- no mandatory garbage collector;
- no mandatory scripting VM;
- explicit security boundaries;
- static linking when preferred;
- dynamic loading only when explicitly requested.

---

# 2. Core Principle

An Axiom application must be able to exist in three forms:

```text
Static Application
    ↓
all required modules linked into executable

Modular Application
    ↓
modules loaded dynamically

Isolated Extension Application
    ↓
extensions execute out-of-process
```

The language itself does not require dynamic plugins.

---

# 3. Architectural Position

```text
613 Package / CAS
        │
        ▼
623 Extension Runtime
        │
 ┌──────┼───────────────┐
 ▼      ▼               ▼
Module Plugin       Extension
 │      │               │
 └──────┼───────────────┘
        ▼
Application Services
        │
 ┌──────┼─────────────┐
 ▼      ▼             ▼
620    621            622
State  Documents      Workspace
        │
        ▼
       619
```

---

# 4. Definitions

## Module

A compiled unit providing code and metadata.

## Plugin

A module intended to extend an existing application.

## Extension

A plugin plus declared extension points and application integration.

## Provider

A module implementing a runtime-defined service interface.

## Package

The distributable unit defined by 613.

---

# 5. No Mandatory Plugin Model

Axiom applications may contain no plugin system at all.

The compiler must eliminate unused extension runtime components.

---

# 6. Static Module

A static module is linked directly into the executable.

```text
app.exe
 ├── core
 ├── graphics
 └── editor
```

No dynamic loading occurs.

---

# 7. Dynamic Module

A dynamic module is loaded at runtime.

Platform mapping:

```text
Windows  → DLL
Linux    → SO
macOS    → DYLIB
Android  → platform-supported native module
iOS      → statically packaged / restricted dynamic model
WASM     → host module boundary
```

The runtime abstracts the native representation.

---

# 8. Module Identity

Every module has:

```text
ModuleId
PublisherId
ModuleVersion
BuildId
AbiId
TargetId
```

---

# 9. Module ID

`ModuleId` is globally unique within an application's package ecosystem.

Recommended representation:

```text
module.vendor.feature
```

---

# 10. Version

A module version contains:

```text
major
minor
patch
```

Optional prerelease/build metadata may exist.

---

# 11. Compatibility

Compatibility is determined by explicit declarations.

Axiom must not assume that:

```text
1.2.0
```

is ABI-compatible with:

```text
1.3.0
```

without metadata.

---

# 12. ABI Identity

Dynamic modules declare:

```text
AbiId
```

containing:

- target architecture;
- calling convention;
- pointer width;
- endianness;
- compiler ABI revision;
- runtime ABI revision;
- relevant feature ABI.

---

# 13. ABI Boundary

The ABI must use stable primitive/layout definitions.

---

# 14. ABI Rule

No implicit transfer of:

- compiler-private types;
- internal allocator state;
- private runtime objects;
- unstable closures;
- compiler-generated anonymous layouts.

---

# 15. Stable ABI Types

Allowed ABI values include:

```text
integers
floats
bool
UTF-8 slices
byte slices
stable structs
stable enums
opaque handles
function tables
error codes/results
```

---

# 16. Ownership

Every ABI resource has explicit ownership.

Possible policies:

```text
Borrowed
Owned
Shared
Transferred
```

---

# 17. No Raw Cross-Module Pointer Contract

A raw pointer may exist internally but must not be the default public plugin ABI.

Opaque handles are preferred.

---

# 18. Handle Identity

Handles use generation-safe IDs.

```text
Handle {
    index
    generation
}
```

---

# 19. Module Entry Point

Every dynamic module exposes one stable entry point:

```text
axiom_module_entry()
```

The exact binary signature is ABI-defined.

---

# 20. Module Descriptor

The entry point returns a static descriptor:

```text
ModuleDescriptor {
    abi
    metadata
    capabilities
    extension_points
    lifecycle
}
```

---

# 21. Descriptor Immutability

Descriptor memory must remain valid for the lifetime of the loaded module.

---

# 22. Module Initialization

Lifecycle:

```text
Discovered
→ Verified
→ Loaded
→ Initialized
→ Active
```

---

# 23. Shutdown Lifecycle

```text
Active
→ Quiescing
→ Stopping
→ Unloaded
```

---

# 24. Failure States

A module may enter:

```text
Rejected
Failed
Quarantined
Unloading
```

---

# 25. Module Lifecycle API

Conceptually:

```text
module_load()
module_initialize()
module_start()
module_quiesce()
module_stop()
module_unload()
```

---

# 26. Lifecycle Ownership

The extension manager owns module lifecycle.

Application code cannot arbitrarily unload a module still containing active resources.

---

# 27. Quiescence

Before unload:

```text
new calls blocked
active calls drained
tasks cancelled/drained
callbacks disconnected
resources released
```

---

# 28. No Unsafe Unload

If active references remain, unload fails or is deferred.

---

# 29. Extension Context

Every extension receives:

```text
ExtensionContext
```

containing only explicitly granted services/capabilities.

---

# 30. Context Services

Examples:

```text
Logger
Config
Storage
Scheduler
Network
IPC
Commands
Documents
Workspace
GUI
Graphics
Media
```

---

# 31. Capability Boundary

Services are capability-controlled through 603.

---

# 32. No Ambient Privilege

Loading a plugin does not automatically grant:

- filesystem access;
- network;
- process creation;
- camera;
- microphone;
- GPU;
- arbitrary native code execution outside the plugin itself.

---

# 33. Requested Capabilities

Module manifest declares:

```text
requires:
    filesystem.read
    network.connect
```

---

# 34. Granted Capabilities

Runtime computes:

```text
granted =
    declared
    ∩
    application policy
    ∩
    user policy
    ∩
    platform policy
```

---

# 35. Capability Attenuation

An extension may receive a restricted capability derived from the host capability.

---

# 36. Capability Revocation

Long-running extension capabilities may be revoked by 603.

The extension must handle resulting errors.

---

# 37. Trust Levels

A module may be classified:

```text
Trusted
Verified
Sandboxed
Untrusted
Blocked
```

These are security states, not quality rankings.

---

# 38. Signature Verification

Packages may contain publisher signatures through 610/613.

---

# 39. Publisher Identity

Publisher identity is independent from module identity.

---

# 40. Package Discovery

623 discovers extensions from:

```text
application package
installation directory
user extension directory
workspace-local package store
system package store
explicit runtime path
```

Only configured sources are searched.

---

# 41. Search Order

Search order is deterministic and configured by policy.

---

# 42. Path Security

Discovery must prevent:

- path traversal;
- unexpected relative paths;
- unsafe symlink traversal;
- DLL/SO hijacking;
- loading from untrusted directories when prohibited.

---

# 43. Package Integration

Extensions may be distributed through AXPK/613.

---

# 44. Package Manifest

Extension package contains:

```text
.axmanifest
```

with:

```text
module_id
version
publisher
targets
abi
dependencies
capabilities
extension_points
entry
resources
signature
```

---

# 45. Dependency Graph

Modules may depend on other modules.

```text
A
├── B
└── C
    └── D
```

---

# 46. Dependency Resolution

Resolver validates:

- module identity;
- version constraints;
- ABI;
- target;
- architecture;
- capabilities;
- trust;
- package integrity.

---

# 47. Dependency Cycles

Cycles are rejected unless an explicitly supported interface-only cycle is represented without runtime initialization dependency.

---

# 48. Initialization Order

Dependencies initialize before dependents.

---

# 49. Shutdown Order

Dependents stop before dependencies.

---

# 50. Optional Dependencies

Dependencies may be:

```text
Required
Optional
FeatureConditional
```

---

# 51. Feature Dependencies

A module may expose optional features:

```text
feature.audio
feature.video
feature.gpu
```

---

# 52. Capability vs Dependency

Dependency means:

> this module needs another implementation.

Capability means:

> this module is allowed to perform an operation.

They must remain distinct.

---

# 53. Module Resolver

```text
ModuleResolver
```

returns a deterministic dependency graph.

---

# 54. Lock File

Applications may maintain:

```text
.axlock
```

recording resolved package versions and hashes.

---

# 55. Reproducibility

Given identical:

- manifest;
- lock file;
- package store;

resolution must produce the same dependency graph.

---

# 56. Content Verification

Package content hashes are validated through 613/610.

---

# 57. Package Cache

Modules can be stored in the 613 CAS.

---

# 58. Duplicate Modules

Content-identical packages should share CAS objects.

---

# 59. Module Loading

The loader verifies:

```text
target
ABI
signature
hash
dependencies
```

before activation.

---

# 60. Dynamic Loader

Platform adapters provide:

```text
load_library
resolve_symbol
unload_library
```

---

# 61. Symbol Resolution

Public symbols are explicitly exported.

No automatic export of all module symbols.

---

# 62. Symbol Namespace

Module symbols use stable namespaces.

---

# 63. Symbol Versioning

ABI symbols may carry version identifiers.

---

# 64. Function Tables

Preferred ABI mechanism:

```text
HostApiV1
PluginApiV1
```

rather than unrestricted symbol coupling.

---

# 65. ABI Evolution

New API versions are additive.

---

# 66. API Negotiation

Module initialization negotiates supported API version.

---

# 67. Backward Compatibility

Host may expose multiple API versions simultaneously.

---

# 68. Forward Compatibility

---

# 69. Error Boundary

Cross-module failures use stable error/result representations.

---

# 70. Panic Boundary

# 72. Resource Ownership

# 73. Resource Registry

```text
ExtensionResourceRegistry
```

tracks:

- tasks;
- subscriptions;
- windows;
- views;
- commands;
- timers;
- sockets;
- file handles;
- GPU objects;

---

# 74. Automatic Cleanup

Automatic cleanup applies only to runtime-owned registrations.

It must not imply garbage collection.

---

# 75. Resource Cleanup

```text

disconnect
close
release
```

---

# 76. Task Cleanup

# 77. Task Cancellation

# 78. Detached Tasks

---

# 79. Subscription Cleanup

---

# 80. UI Extensions

```text
Control
Panel
ToolWindow
Menu
Toolbar
```

# 81. UI Registration

# 82. UI Unload

# 83. Workspace Integration

# 85. Missing Extension

# 87. Command Extensions

# 88. Command IDs

# 89. Command Collision

---

# 90. Menu Contributions

# 91. No Arbitrary Menu Code

---

# 92. Document Extensions

# 93. Document Provider


# 94. Format Detection

---

# 95. Parser Isolation

---

# 96. Service Extensions

```text
SearchService

```

---

# 97. Service Registry

```text
ServiceRegistry
```

maps stable interface IDs to providers.

---

# 98. Service Versioning

Interfaces have explicit versions.

---

# 99. Service Lifetime

Possible policies:

```text
Singleton
PerApplication
PerWorkspace
PerDocument
PerRequest
```

---

# 100. Provider Selection

Multiple implementations can coexist.

Selection is determined by explicit policy rather than hidden priority.

---

# 101. Extension Points

An application declares:

```text

```

and its expected interface.

---

# 102. Extension Point Descriptor

Contains:

```text
id
api_version
allowed_scope
required_capabilities
lifecycle

```

---

# 103. Extension Registration

An extension registers only against known extension points.

---

# 104. Unknown Extension Point

The extension is not activated for unsupported points.

---

# 105. Optional Extension Point

Applications may expose optional extension points.

---

# 106. Declarative Contributions

Prefer metadata for:

- commands;
- menus;
- file types;
- themes;
- panels;
- routes;
- document providers.

---

# 107. Programmatic Contributions

Allowed when behavior genuinely requires code.

---

# 108. Declarative First

Declarative metadata improves:

- validation;
- startup;
- tooling;
- security;
- AI inspection.

---

# 109. Extension Metadata

Compiler generates:

```text
.axext
```

containing:

```text
module
extension_points
commands
routes
documents
resources
capabilities
dependencies
```

---

# 110. AI-Readable Metadata

Metadata should be deterministic and machine-readable.

---

# 111. Static Extension Registry

For static builds:

```text
StaticExtensionRegistry
```

is generated by the compiler/linker.

---

# 112. Dynamic Registry

For dynamic builds:

```text
DynamicExtensionRegistry
```

loads descriptors from packages.

---

# 113. Static vs Dynamic Equivalence

An extension should expose the same logical API regardless of static/dynamic packaging.

---

# 114. Link-Time Registration

Static extension registration should not require runtime discovery.

---

# 115. Dead Stripping

Unused static extensions must be removable by the linker.

---

# 116. Minimal Build

An application with no extension points should contain zero extension runtime code.

---

# 117. Hot Load

A module may be loaded while the application is running if its extension point permits dynamic loading.

---

# 118. Hot Unload

A module may be unloaded only after successful quiescence.

---

# 119. Hot Reload

Hot reload means:

```text
old module
→ quiesce
→ serialize transferable state
→ unload
→ load new module
→ validate
→ restore state
→ resume
```

---

# 120. Reload Boundary

Only declared transferable state participates.

---

# 121. Code State

Function pointers into the old module cannot survive reload.

---

# 122. Callback Safety

Every callback registered by a module is automatically invalidated during quiescence.

---

# 123. VTable Safety

Old vtables must never remain callable after unload.

---

# 124. Task Safety

Tasks executing old module code must finish/cancel before unload.

---

# 125. Thread Safety

Threads owned by the extension must terminate before unload.

---

# 126. Thread Transfer

Threads cannot silently become host-owned during reload.

---

# BOOTSTRAP-623 — Native Application Plugin, Extension, Module, Hot-Reload, Package Discovery, Dependency Isolation & Extension Runtime 5.0

**Status:** SPECIFIED

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-623 defines the native extension architecture for Axiom applications:

- modules;
- plugins;
- extensions;
- optional application features;
- package discovery;
- dependency resolution;
- ABI/API boundaries;
- extension lifecycle;
- isolation;
- capability provisioning;
- hot-load;
- hot-unload;
- hot-reload;
- version compatibility;
- extension configuration;
- extension resources;
- extension UI;
- extension commands;
- extension services;
- extension IPC;
- extension diagnostics.

The design must preserve Axiom's primary goals:

- native performance;
- small binaries;
- deterministic behavior;
- no mandatory plugin runtime;
- no mandatory garbage collector;
- no mandatory scripting VM;
- explicit security boundaries;
- static linking when preferred;
- dynamic loading only when explicitly requested.

---

# 2. Core Principle

An Axiom application must be able to exist in three forms:

```text
Static Application
    ↓
all required modules linked into executable

Modular Application
    ↓
modules loaded dynamically

Isolated Extension Application
    ↓
extensions execute out-of-process
```

The language itself does not require dynamic plugins.

---

# 3. Architectural Position

```text
613 Package / CAS
        │
        ▼
623 Extension Runtime
        │
 ┌──────┼───────────────┐
 ▼      ▼               ▼
Module Plugin       Extension
 │      │               │
 └──────┼───────────────┘
        ▼
Application Services
        │
 ┌──────┼─────────────┐
 ▼      ▼             ▼
620    621            622
State  Documents      Workspace
        │
        ▼
       619
```

---

# 4. Definitions

## Module

A compiled unit providing code and metadata.

## Plugin

A module intended to extend an existing application.

## Extension

A plugin plus declared extension points and application integration.

## Provider

A module implementing a runtime-defined service interface.

## Package

The distributable unit defined by 613.

---

# 5. No Mandatory Plugin Model

Axiom applications may contain no plugin system at all.

The compiler must eliminate unused extension runtime components.

---

# 6. Static Module

A static module is linked directly into the executable.

```text
app.exe
 ├── core
 ├── graphics
 └── editor
```

No dynamic loading occurs.

---

# 7. Dynamic Module

A dynamic module is loaded at runtime.

Platform mapping:

```text
Windows  → DLL
Linux    → SO
macOS    → DYLIB
Android  → platform-supported native module
iOS      → statically packaged / restricted dynamic model
WASM     → host module boundary
```

The runtime abstracts the native representation.

---

# 8. Module Identity

Every module has:

```text
ModuleId
PublisherId
ModuleVersion
BuildId
AbiId
TargetId
```

---

# 9. Module ID

`ModuleId` is globally unique within an application's package ecosystem.

Recommended representation:

```text
module.vendor.feature
```

---

# 10. Version

A module version contains:

```text
major
minor
patch
```

Optional prerelease/build metadata may exist.

---

# 11. Compatibility

Compatibility is determined by explicit declarations.

Axiom must not assume that:

```text
1.2.0
```

is ABI-compatible with:

```text
1.3.0
```

without metadata.

---

# 12. ABI Identity

Dynamic modules declare:

```text
AbiId
```

containing:

- target architecture;
- calling convention;
- pointer width;
- endianness;
- compiler ABI revision;
- runtime ABI revision;
- relevant feature ABI.

---

# 13. ABI Boundary

The ABI must use stable primitive/layout definitions.

---

# 14. ABI Rule

No implicit transfer of:

- compiler-private types;
- internal allocator state;
- private runtime objects;
- unstable closures;
- compiler-generated anonymous layouts.

---

# 15. Stable ABI Types

Allowed ABI values include:

```text
integers
floats
bool
UTF-8 slices
byte slices
stable structs
stable enums
opaque handles
function tables
error codes/results
```

---

# 16. Ownership

Every ABI resource has explicit ownership.

Possible policies:

```text
Borrowed
Owned
Shared
Transferred
```

---

# 17. No Raw Cross-Module Pointer Contract

A raw pointer may exist internally but must not be the default public plugin ABI.

Opaque handles are preferred.

---

# 18. Handle Identity

Handles use generation-safe IDs.

```text
Handle {
    index
    generation
}
```

---

# 19. Module Entry Point

Every dynamic module exposes one stable entry point:

```text
axiom_module_entry()
```

The exact binary signature is ABI-defined.

---

# 20. Module Descriptor

The entry point returns a static descriptor:

```text
ModuleDescriptor {
    abi
    metadata
    capabilities
    extension_points
    lifecycle
}
```

---

# 21. Descriptor Immutability

Descriptor memory must remain valid for the lifetime of the loaded module.

---

# 22. Module Initialization

Lifecycle:

```text
Discovered
→ Verified
→ Loaded
→ Initialized
→ Active
```

---

# 23. Shutdown Lifecycle

```text
Active
→ Quiescing
→ Stopping
→ Unloaded
```

---

# 24. Failure States

A module may enter:

```text
Rejected
Failed
Quarantined
Unloading
```

---

# 25. Module Lifecycle API

Conceptually:

```text
module_load()
module_initialize()
module_start()
module_quiesce()
module_stop()
module_unload()
```

---

# 26. Lifecycle Ownership

The extension manager owns module lifecycle.

Application code cannot arbitrarily unload a module still containing active resources.

---

# 27. Quiescence

Before unload:

```text
new calls blocked
active calls drained
tasks cancelled/drained
callbacks disconnected
resources released
```

---

# 28. No Unsafe Unload

If active references remain, unload fails or is deferred.

---

# 29. Extension Context

Every extension receives:

```text
ExtensionContext
```

containing only explicitly granted services/capabilities.

---

# 30. Context Services

Examples:

```text
Logger
Config
Storage
Scheduler
Network
IPC
Commands
Documents
Workspace
GUI
Graphics
Media
```

---

# 31. Capability Boundary

Services are capability-controlled through 603.

---

# 32. No Ambient Privilege

Loading a plugin does not automatically grant:

- filesystem access;
- network;
- process creation;
- camera;
- microphone;
- GPU;
- arbitrary native code execution outside the plugin itself.

---

# 33. Requested Capabilities

Module manifest declares:

```text
requires:
    filesystem.read
    network.connect
```

---

# 34. Granted Capabilities

Runtime computes:

```text
granted =
    declared
    ∩
    application policy
    ∩
    user policy
    ∩
    platform policy
```

---

# 35. Capability Attenuation

An extension may receive a restricted capability derived from the host capability.

---

# 36. Capability Revocation

Long-running extension capabilities may be revoked by 603.

The extension must handle resulting errors.

---

# 37. Trust Levels

A module may be classified:

```text
Trusted
Verified
Sandboxed
Untrusted
Blocked
```

These are security states, not quality rankings.

---

# 38. Signature Verification

Packages may contain publisher signatures through 610/613.

---

# 39. Publisher Identity

Publisher identity is independent from module identity.

---

# 40. Package Discovery

623 discovers extensions from:

```text
application package
installation directory
user extension directory
workspace-local package store
system package store
explicit runtime path
```

Only configured sources are searched.

---

# 41. Search Order

Search order is deterministic and configured by policy.

---

# 42. Path Security

Discovery must prevent:

- path traversal;
- unexpected relative paths;
- unsafe symlink traversal;
- DLL/SO hijacking;
- loading from untrusted directories when prohibited.

---

# 43. Package Integration

Extensions may be distributed through AXPK/613.

---

# 44. Package Manifest

Extension package contains:

```text
.axmanifest
```

with:

```text
module_id
version
publisher
targets
abi
dependencies
capabilities
extension_points
entry
resources
signature
```

# 45. Dependency Graph

Modules may depend on other modules.

```text
A
├── B
└── C
    └── D
```

---

# 46. Dependency Resolution

Resolver validates:

- module identity;
- version constraints;
- ABI;
- target;
- architecture;
- capabilities;
- trust;
- package integrity.

---

# 47. Dependency Cycles

Cycles are rejected unless an explicitly supported interface-only cycle is represented without runtime initialization dependency.

---

# 48. Initialization Order

Dependencies initialize before dependents.

---

# 49. Shutdown Order

Dependents stop before dependencies.

---

# 50. Optional Dependencies

Dependencies may be:

```text
Required
Optional
FeatureConditional
```

---

# 51. Feature Dependencies

A module may expose optional features:

```text
feature.audio
feature.video
feature.gpu
```

---

# 52. Capability vs Dependency

Dependency means:

> this module needs another implementation.

Capability means:

> this module is allowed to perform an operation.

They must remain distinct.

---

# 53. Module Resolver

```text
ModuleResolver
```

returns a deterministic dependency graph.

---

# 54. Lock File

Applications may maintain:

```text
.axlock
```

recording resolved package versions and hashes.

---

# 55. Reproducibility

Given identical:

- manifest;
- lock file;
- package store;

resolution must produce the same dependency graph.

# 56. Content Verification

Package content hashes are validated through 613/610.

---

# 57. Package Cache

Modules can be stored in the 613 CAS.

---

# 58. Duplicate Modules

Content-identical packages should share CAS objects.

---

# 59. Module Loading

The loader verifies:

```text
target
ABI
signature
hash
dependencies
```

before activation.

---

# 60. Dynamic Loader

Platform adapters provide:

```text
load_library
resolve_symbol
unload_library
```

---

# 61. Symbol Resolution

Public symbols are explicitly exported.

No automatic export of all module symbols.

---

# 62. Symbol Namespace

Module symbols use stable namespaces.

---

# 63. Symbol Versioning

ABI symbols may carry version identifiers.

---

# 64. Function Tables

Preferred ABI mechanism:

```text
HostApiV1
PluginApiV1
```

rather than unrestricted symbol coupling.

---

# 65. ABI Evolution

New API versions are additive.

---

# 66. API Negotiation

Module initialization negotiates supported API version.

---

# 67. Backward Compatibility

Host may expose multiple API versions simultaneously.

---

# 68. Forward Compatibility

Unknown optional function pointers are treated as unavailable.

---

# 69. Error Boundary

Cross-module failures use stable error/result representations.

---

# 70. Panic Boundary

A plugin panic/unhandled exception must not cross the ABI boundary.

---

# 71. Panic Conversion

It becomes:

```text
PluginFailure
```

and is reported through 602/605.

---

# 72. Resource Ownership

The extension runtime tracks resources associated with each module.

---

# 73. Resource Registry

```text
ExtensionResourceRegistry
```

tracks:

- tasks;
- subscriptions;
- windows;
- views;
- commands;
- timers;
- sockets;
- file handles;
- GPU objects;
- media sessions.

---

# 74. Automatic Cleanup

Automatic cleanup applies only to runtime-owned registrations.

It must not imply garbage collection.

---

# 75. Resource Cleanup

On extension stop:

```text
cancel
disconnect
close
release
```

resources according to ownership rules.

---

# 76. Task Cleanup

Tasks created by an extension are attached to an extension scope.

---

# 77. Task Cancellation

Quiescing cancels extension-owned tasks unless explicitly detached with policy approval.

---

# 78. Detached Tasks

Detached tasks require explicit ownership transfer.

---

# 79. Subscription Cleanup

620/619 subscriptions are automatically disconnected when owned by the extension context.

---

# 80. UI Extensions

Plugins can register:

```text
Control
Panel
ToolWindow
Menu
Toolbar
Command
Dialog
DocumentView
```

---

# 81. UI Registration

UI extensions use 619/622 registration APIs.

---

# 82. UI Unload

Before unload:

```text
views close
panels detach
commands unregister
bindings disconnect
```

---

# 83. Workspace Integration

Extensions can register workspace panels and layout contributions.

---

# 84. Workspace Persistence

Extension-specific workspace state must be namespaced.

Example:

```text
plugin.vendor.tool.settings
```

---

# 85. Missing Extension

If an extension is missing, its persisted state remains available as opaque data where safe.

---

# 86. Extension Restoration

When the extension returns, its state can be restored.

---

# 87. Command Extensions

Plugins can register commands with 620.

---

# 88. Command IDs

Command IDs are globally namespaced.

```text
vendor.plugin.command
```

---

# 89. Command Collision

Duplicate command IDs are rejected.

---

# 90. Menu Contributions

Extensions contribute declarative menu items.

---

# 91. No Arbitrary Menu Code

Menu declarations contain data and command IDs.

---

# 92. Document Extensions

Plugins can register document providers:

```text
*.foo
*.bar
```

---

# 93. Document Provider

Provider implements:

```text
open
load
save
validate
```

according to 621.

---

# 94. Format Detection

File type detection must not execute arbitrary file content.

---

# 95. Parser Isolation

Untrusted document parsers may execute out-of-process.

---

# 96. Service Extensions

Extensions may provide application services.

Example:

```text
SearchService
CompilerService
AssetService
LanguageService
```

---

# 97. Service Registry

```text
ServiceRegistry
```

maps stable interface IDs to providers.

---

# 98. Service Versioning

Interfaces have explicit versions.

---

# 99. Service Lifetime

Possible policies:

```text
Singleton
PerApplication
PerWorkspace
PerDocument
PerRequest
```

---

# 100. Provider Selection

Multiple implementations can coexist.

Selection is determined by explicit policy rather than hidden priority.

---

# 101. Extension Points

An application declares:

```text
ExtensionPointId
```

and its expected interface.

---

# 102. Extension Point Descriptor

Contains:

```text
id
api_version
allowed_scope
required_capabilities
lifecycle
multiplicity
```

---

# 103. Extension Registration

An extension registers only against known extension points.

---

# 104. Unknown Extension Point

The extension is not activated for unsupported points.

---

# 105. Optional Extension Point

Applications may expose optional extension points.

---

# 106. Declarative Contributions

Prefer metadata for:

- commands;
- menus;
- file types;
- themes;
- panels;
- routes;
- document providers.

---

# 107. Programmatic Contributions

Allowed when behavior genuinely requires code.

---

# 108. Declarative First

Declarative metadata improves:

- validation;
- startup;
- tooling;
- security;
- AI inspection.

---

# 109. Extension Metadata

Compiler generates:

```text
.axext
```

containing:

```text
module
extension_points
commands
routes
documents
resources
capabilities
dependencies
```

---

# 110. AI-Readable Metadata

Metadata should be deterministic and machine-readable.

---

# 111. Static Extension Registry

For static builds:

```text
StaticExtensionRegistry
```

is generated by the compiler/linker.

---

# 112. Dynamic Registry

For dynamic builds:

```text
DynamicExtensionRegistry
```

loads descriptors from packages.

---

# 113. Static vs Dynamic Equivalence

An extension should expose the same logical API regardless of static/dynamic packaging.

---

# 114. Link-Time Registration

Static extension registration should not require runtime discovery.

---

# 115. Dead Stripping

Unused static extensions must be removable by the linker.

---

# 116. Minimal Build

An application with no extension points should contain zero extension runtime code.

---

# 117. Hot Load

A module may be loaded while the application is running if its extension point permits dynamic loading.

---

# 118. Hot Unload

A module may be unloaded only after successful quiescence.

---

# 119. Hot Reload

Hot reload means:

```text
old module
→ quiesce
→ serialize transferable state
→ unload
→ load new module
→ validate
→ restore state
→ resume
```

---

# 120. Reload Boundary

Only declared transferable state participates.

---

# 121. Code State

Function pointers into the old module cannot survive reload.

---

# 122. Callback Safety

Every callback registered by a module is automatically invalidated during quiescence.

---

# 123. VTable Safety

Old vtables must never remain callable after unload.

---

# 124. Task Safety

Tasks executing old module code must finish/cancel before unload.

---

# 125. Thread Safety

Threads owned by the extension must terminate before unload.

---

# 126. Thread Transfer

Threads cannot silently become host-owned during reload.

---

# 127. GPU Safety

GPU resources containing module-specific callbacks/shader objects are drained/released or reconstructed.

---

# 128. GUI Safety

Views created by the old module are detached before unload.

---

# 129. State Migration

Reload can specify:

```text
state_schema_version
migration
```

---

# 130. Failed Reload

If the new module fails validation, the old module may remain active when technically possible.

---

# 131. Transactional Reload

Preferred sequence:

```text
prepare new
validate new
quiesce old
transfer state
activate new
commit
```

---

# 132. Rollback

If activation fails after old-module quiescence, rollback is attempted only if the old module remains loaded and valid.

---

# 133. Hard Failure

If rollback is impossible, the extension remains disabled and diagnostics preserve failure information.

---

# 134. Hot Reload Limitations

Some modules cannot safely hot reload:

- ABI providers with persistent external references;
- low-level device drivers;
- process-global hooks;
- platform modules requiring restart;
- modules with unsupported native state.

They must declare:

```text
hot_reload: false
```

---

# 135. Extension State

Extension state may be divided into:

```text
Configuration
PersistentState
SessionState
EphemeralState
```

---

# 136. Persistence

Persistent state uses 600/612/611.

---

# 137. Secret State

Secrets use `Secret<T>` and are excluded from ordinary extension-state serialization.

---

# 138. Session State

Session state may be restored after application restart.

---

# 139. Ephemeral State

Ephemeral state is never required for successful recovery.

---

# 140. State Namespacing

Every extension state key contains its stable module identity.

---

# 141. Configuration

Extension configuration integrates with 601.

---

# 142. Configuration Isolation

An extension cannot overwrite another extension's configuration namespace.

---

# 143. Configuration Capability

Only declared configuration fields are exposed to the extension.

---

# 144. Extension Logging

602 automatically attaches:

```text
module_id
publisher_id
instance_id
```

to extension logs.

---

# 145. Diagnostics

Extension failures include:

```text
module
version
build_id
abi
package_hash
capabilities
dependency_graph
```

1. Dynamic plugins are optional.
2. Static modules are first-class.
3. ABI is explicit.
4. Ownership is explicit.
5. Capabilities are explicit.
6. Loading does not grant arbitrary privilege.
7. Dependencies are deterministic.
8. Dependency cycles are rejected.
9. Lifecycle is explicit.
10. Unload requires quiescence.
11. Old code cannot be called after unload.
12. Callback registrations are invalidated.
13. Task ownership is explicit.
14. Persistent state is versioned.
15. Secret state is protected.
16. Workspace state is namespaced.
17. Extension code cannot modify capabilities implicitly.
18. Package installation does not execute code.
19. Signature verification occurs before activation.
20. Static builds can eliminate extension runtime.
21. Out-of-process extensions have independent failure domains.
22. In-process extensions cannot claim independent crash isolation.
23. Provider precedence is explicit.
24. Registry mutations are transactional.
25. Async operations are cancellable.
26. Stale completions cannot mutate newer state.
27. Extension APIs are versioned.
28. Unknown optional APIs are tolerated.
29. Breaking API changes require new interface versions.
30. Persisted state cannot contain executable code.
31. Workspace restoration cannot grant capabilities.
32. Module resources are tracked.
33. Leaked resources are diagnosable.
34. Hot reload is opt-in.
35. Unsupported hot reload is explicit.
36. Failed activation does not corrupt the host.
37. Failed updates retain rollback information.
38. Extension graph is deterministic.
39. Extension graph has a fingerprint.
40. No mandatory plugin VM exists.
41. No mandatory GC exists.
42. No mandatory scripting engine exists.
43. No mandatory marketplace exists.
44. No mandatory network registry exists.
45. No global mutable extension registry exists.
46. Headless applications can omit GUI extension features.
47. WASM/mobile constraints are represented explicitly.
48. Native handles are never persisted as authoritative state.
49. Extension boundaries are fuzz-testable.
50. Extension runtime is dead-strippable.

# 393. Result

BOOTSTRAP-623 establishes an extension architecture where Axiom applications can grow from:

```text
single native executable
```

to:

```text
large modular desktop application
```

without forcing the language core to contain:

- a VM;
- garbage collector;
- scripting runtime;
- mandatory plugin framework;
- mandatory package registry;
- mandatory dynamic loader.

The architecture preserves a clean distinction between:

```text

application extension
runtime service
package
process
capability
```

while providing a complete path from static linking to dynamically loaded and isolated extensions.

Tiếp tục với **BOOTSTRAP-624**, tập trung vào scripting/automation nhưng giữ nguyên nguyên tắc: **scripting là tầng ứng dụng tùy chọn, không làm phình language core và không biến Axiom thành một VM-first language**.

:::writing{variant="document" id="38154" title="BOOTSTRAP-624 — Native Application Scripting, Embedded Language Boundary, Automation, Macro, Expression Runtime & Sandboxed Dynamic Behavior 5.0"}
# BOOTSTRAP-624 — Native Application Scripting, Embedded Language Boundary, Automation, Macro, Expression Runtime & Sandboxed Dynamic Behavior 5.0

**Status:** SPECIFIED  
**Layer:** Application Automation / Dynamic Behavior  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600 → 623

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-624 defines the optional dynamic-behavior layer for Axiom applications:

- scripting;
- automation;
- macros;
- command sequences;
- expressions;
- user-defined actions;
- embedded DSLs;
- application automation;
- configuration expressions;
- extension scripting;
- dynamic rules;
- sandboxed computation;
- script debugging;
- script persistence;
- script state;
- script package distribution.

The architecture must **not** require scripting for ordinary Axiom applications.

---

# 2. Primary Design Principle

Axiom has three different execution categories:

```text
Native Axiom
    ↓
compiled native machine code

Dynamic Axiom behavior
    ↓
optional interpreter / bytecode / JIT

External automation
    ↓
IPC / command protocol
```

These are intentionally separate.

---

# 3. Non-Goals

BOOTSTRAP-624 does not require:

- a mandatory scripting VM;
- JavaScript compatibility;
- Python compatibility;
- Lua compatibility;
- garbage collection;
- dynamic typing throughout Axiom;
- runtime compilation of arbitrary native code;
- unrestricted `eval`;
- reflection over all application internals.

---

# 4. Architecture

```text id="f7tq3z"
Application
    │
    ├── Native Axiom
    │
    ├── 623 Extensions
    │
    └── 624 Automation
          │
          ├── Expression Engine
          ├── Script Engine
          ├── Macro Engine
          ├── Command Engine
          ├── DSL Runtime
          └── Sandboxed Runtime
```

---

# 5. Three Dynamic Execution Levels

## Level 1 — Expression

Small deterministic expressions.

Example:

```text id="xqz9k1"
width * 0.5 + padding
```

---

## Level 2 — Automation

Structured command/action sequences.

```text id="4x6f4j"
open_document(path)
select_all()
transform(scale = 0.5)
save()
```

---

## Level 3 — Script

General-purpose dynamic program execution.

```text id="d4x6w2"
for document in workspace.documents {
    process(document)
}
```

---

# 6. Why Three Levels

Most application automation does not require a complete programming language runtime.

Therefore:

```text id="k1t6nq"
Expression
    ↓
smallest runtime

Automation
    ↓
command interpreter

Script
    ↓
full optional runtime
```

This minimizes startup cost and binary size.

---

# 7. Script Engine Abstraction

Core interface:

```text id="qz4e3r"
ScriptEngine
```

provides:

```text
compile
load
execute
pause
resume
cancel
inspect
dispose
```

---

# 8. Script Engine Is a Provider

The runtime does not mandate one scripting implementation.

Providers can be:

```text id="8r2f3m"
AxiomScript
ExpressionEngine
ExternalScriptProvider
WASMProvider
ApplicationSpecificDSL
```

---

# 9. Native AxiomScript

The preferred built-in scripting language is a restricted dynamic subset of Axiom.

It should reuse Axiom syntax where practical.

---

# 10. Syntax Compatibility

Example:

```text id="b0k4d8"
let x = 10

for item in items {
    print(item)
}
```

This reduces the number of languages developers and AI systems must learn.

---

# 11. Script ≠ Native Axiom

The same syntax does not imply identical execution semantics.

Script mode may impose:

- runtime checks;
- sandbox restrictions;
- dynamic values;
- resource limits;
- deterministic execution.

---


# 29. No Raw Pointer Exposure

---

# 30. Host Object Model

# 45. Script State Schema

---

# 46. Script Migration

---

# 47. No Arbitrary State Serialization

# 48. Script Resource Budget

A script can be limited by:

```text id="4z2n6q"

memory
execution time
instructions
tasks
handles
IPC
network
storage
GPU
```

# 49. Resource Integration

# 50. Instruction Budget

# 51. Time Budget

```text id="e8n2q4"

  ↓
Binding
  ↓
Capability Check

Native API
```

- type;
- range;

# 57. Error Model

---

# 58. Panic Boundary

---

# 59. Script Exception

```text id="x6q9pa"
ScriptError {
    code

}
```

# 61. Stack Traces

# 62. Source Maps

# 63. Debugging

# 65. Production Mode

---

# 66. Script Inspector

Runtime can expose:

```text id="9j2f0k"

tasks
memory
resource usage
capabilities
```

# 67. Macro Engine

# 70. Macro Recording

Example:

# 72. Macro Sanitization

# 74. Macro Reuse

---

# 78. Macro Failure

# 79. Automation Engine

Automation combines commands, conditions and values.

# 80. Automation Graph

```text id="j5k9r0"

   ↓
Condition
   ↓
Action

Condition
```

Examples:

```text id="8z3m6v"
DocumentOpen
DocumentSave
CommandExecuted
Timer

UserEvent
```

Timers use 607.

---


# 147. Script Device Access

```text id="p3v6z9"
schemas
resources
dependencies
```

# 164. Script Permissions

# 167. Script Profiles

# 266. Design Conclusion

624 deliberately makes dynamic behavior a **layer**, not a fundamental property of every Axiom program.

The resulting model is:

```text
Axiom native code
    ↓
maximum performance

Axiom expression
    ↓
small dynamic behavior

Axiom automation
    ↓
structured application control

AxiomScript
    ↓
general dynamic behavior

623 extension
    ↓
native application integration

IPC
    ↓
strong process isolation
```

This allows a tiny native application to contain almost none of the scripting infrastructure while a large desktop application can expose a powerful automation environment.

Most importantly, **native Axiom does not pay for scripting merely because scripting exists somewhere in the ecosystem**.

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-624 defines the optional dynamic-behavior layer for Axiom applications:

- scripting;
- automation;
- macros;
- command sequences;
- expressions;
- user-defined actions;
- embedded DSLs;

# 2. Primary Design Principle

Axiom has three different execution categories:

```text
Native Axiom
    ↓
compiled native machine code

Dynamic Axiom behavior
    ↓
optional interpreter / bytecode / JIT

External automation
    ↓
IPC / command protocol
```

These are intentionally separate.

# 3. Non-Goals

BOOTSTRAP-624 does not require:

- a mandatory scripting VM;
- JavaScript compatibility;

- Lua compatibility;
- garbage collection;
- dynamic typing throughout Axiom;
- runtime compilation of arbitrary native code;

# 266. Design Conclusion

624 deliberately makes dynamic behavior a **layer**, not a fundamental property of every Axiom program.

The resulting model is:

```text
Axiom native code
    ↓
maximum performance

Axiom expression
    ↓
small dynamic behavior

Axiom automation
    ↓
structured application control

AxiomScript
    ↓
general dynamic behavior

623 extension
    ↓
native application integration

IPC
    ↓
strong process isolation
```

This allows a tiny native application to contain almost none of the scripting infrastructure while a large desktop application can expose a powerful automation environment.

Most importantly, **native Axiom does not pay for scripting merely because scripting exists somewhere in the ecosystem**.
