Tiếp tục với **BOOTSTRAP-625** — lần này hoàn thiện tầng phân phối ứng dụng/package ecosystem phía trên 613 và 623/624, nhưng vẫn giữ nguyên nguyên tắc **registry/marketplace là dịch vụ tùy chọn, không phải dependency của Axiom runtime**.

:::writing{variant="document" id="51683" title="BOOTSTRAP-625 — Native Application Package Registry, Repository, Dependency Resolution Service, Update Channel, Rollback & Distribution Runtime 5.0"}
# BOOTSTRAP-625 — Native Application Package Registry, Repository, Dependency Resolution Service, Update Channel, Rollback & Distribution Runtime 5.0

**Status:** SPECIFIED  
**Layer:** Application Distribution / Package Ecosystem  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600 → 624

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-625 defines the optional distribution layer for Axiom applications and packages:

- package repositories;
- registries;
- package discovery;
- dependency resolution;
- package installation;
- package removal;
- package updates;
- update channels;
- staged rollout;
- rollback;
- package pinning;
- publisher identity;
- package trust;
- application bundles;
- application distribution;
- offline installation;
- enterprise/private repositories;
- package mirrors;
- metadata indexes;
- update manifests;
- delta updates;
- cache management;
- distribution diagnostics.

The design must remain independent from any specific marketplace, cloud provider, vendor, or centralized service.

---

# 2. Core Principle

Axiom must support:

```text
No Registry
    ↓
Local packages only

Private Registry
    ↓
Enterprise / studio / organization

Public Registry
    ↓
Community distribution

Multiple Registries
    ↓
Application-specific ecosystem
```

The Axiom runtime must function without any registry connection.

---

# 3. Non-Goals

625 does not define:

- a mandatory public marketplace;
- a mandatory cloud account;
- a mandatory vendor payment system;
- a mandatory centralized identity service;
- advertising;
- application telemetry;
- mandatory online activation;
- mandatory subscription infrastructure.

---

# 4. Layering

```text
613 Package / CAS
        │
        ▼
625 Distribution Layer
        │
 ┌──────┼───────────────┐
 ▼      ▼               ▼
Registry Resolver     Update Manager
 │      │               │
 └──────┼───────────────┘
        ▼
623 Extension / Package
624 Script / Automation
Application
```

---

# 5. Package vs Repository

A **package** is an immutable distributable artifact.

A **repository** is a source from which package metadata and artifacts can be obtained.

They must remain separate concepts.

---

# 6. Registry

A registry provides:

- package metadata;
- versions;
- hashes;
- signatures;
- dependency metadata;
- target information;
- download locations.

---

# 7. Repository

A repository may be:

```text
LocalDirectory
FileArchive
HTTPRepository
PrivateRegistry
PublicRegistry
Mirror
EmbeddedPackageStore
```

---

# 8. Repository Interface

```text
Repository {
    query()
    metadata()
    download()
    verify()
}
```

---

# 9. Offline First

Axiom must support complete offline installation.

---

# 10. Local Package Installation

Example:

```text
axiom package install mytool.axpk
```

No network access is required.

---

# 11. Repository Configuration

Repositories are configured through 601.

---

# 12. Repository Identity

Every configured repository has:

```text
RepositoryId
RepositoryEndpoint
TrustPolicy
PriorityPolicy
```

---

# 13. Repository Priority

Repository priority is used only for deterministic resolution rules.

It must not silently override security policy.

---

# 14. Trust vs Priority

A higher-priority repository cannot override a package that is forbidden by security policy.

---

# 15. Package Identity

Package identity:

```text
PackageId
PublisherId
Version
Target
Architecture
```

---

# 16. Immutable Package Version

A published package version is immutable.

A changed binary requires a new package content hash and normally a new publication revision/version.

---

# 17. Content Hash

Package content is identified through 613 CAS hashing.

---

# 18. Package Coordinate

Canonical coordinate:

```text
publisher/package@version
```

---

# 19. Target Coordinate

A package may provide variants:

```text
windows-x64
linux-x64
linux-arm64
macos-arm64
android-arm64
ios-arm64
wasm32
```

---

# 20. Target Selection

Resolver chooses a compatible target deterministically.

---

# 21. Architecture Selection

Architecture is part of compatibility.

---

# 22. ABI Selection

ABI compatibility is validated through 623 metadata.

---

# 23. Runtime Compatibility

Application runtime requirements must be satisfied before activation.

---

# 24. Package Manifest

Manifest contains:

```text
package_id
publisher
version
targets
dependencies
optional_dependencies
capabilities
entrypoints
resources
extensions
scripts
signatures
```

---

# 25. Package Metadata

Registry metadata may include:

```text
name
description
version
license
publisher
targets
size
hash
dependencies
release_notes
```

---

# 26. Metadata vs Package

Metadata is not trusted executable content.

Executable activation requires package verification.

---

# 27. Package Signature

Packages may contain signatures generated through 610.

---

# 28. Signature Verification

Installation verifies:

```text
package_hash
publisher_signature
publisher_identity
trust_policy
```

---

# 29. Publisher Identity

Publisher IDs are stable cryptographic identities.

---

# 30. Key Rotation

Publisher keys may rotate while preserving publisher identity through an authorized chain.

---

# 31. Revocation

Revoked publisher keys/packages must not activate when policy requires blocking.

---

# 32. Trust Store

Trust roots are managed through 610/603.

---

# 33. Repository Trust

A repository itself may be authenticated independently from package publishers.

---

# 34. Package Trust

Repository trust does not replace package signature verification.

---

# 35. Repository Compromise

If a repository is compromised, signed package verification still protects against unauthorized package replacement.

---

# 36. Metadata Tampering

Metadata is integrity-protected where possible.

---

# 37. Signed Index

Repositories may provide signed index snapshots.

---

# 38. Index Fingerprint

An index snapshot has:

```text
IndexHash
IndexVersion
Timestamp
RepositoryId
```

---

# 39. Deterministic Resolution

Resolution depends only on:

```text
requested packages
repository snapshots
lock file
target
ABI
security policy
```

---

# 40. Dependency Solver

625 provides a deterministic dependency resolver.

---

# 41. Dependency Constraint

Example:

```text
image.codec >= 2.0 < 3.0
```

---

# 42. Exact Dependency

```text
image.codec = 2.4.1
```

---

# 43. Wildcard Dependency

Wildcards may be permitted but are discouraged for reproducible deployments.

---

# 44. Optional Dependency

Optional dependencies do not make the package unsatisfiable when absent.

---

# 45. Feature Dependency

Features may activate dependencies conditionally.

---

# 46. Platform Dependency

A dependency may exist only for specific targets.

---

# 47. Architecture Dependency

Dependency resolution includes architecture.

---

# 48. ABI Dependency

ABI constraints are explicitly checked.

---

# 49. Dependency Conflict

Example:

```text
A → codec 1.x
B → codec 2.x
```

The resolver must determine whether both can coexist.

---

# 50. Side-by-Side Versions

Multiple versions may coexist if 623 isolation rules permit it.

---

# 51. Singleton Conflict

If a dependency requires process-global state, incompatible versions cannot silently coexist.

---

# 52. Dependency Graph

Resolver produces:

```text
ResolvedGraph
```

containing:

- nodes;
- edges;
- selected versions;
- hashes;
- target;
- ABI.

---

# 53. Graph Fingerprint

The resolved graph receives a deterministic fingerprint.

---

# 54. Lock File

Application can persist:

```text
.axlock
```

with:

```text
package_id
version
hash
target
dependencies
repository
```

---

# 55. Lock Reproducibility

A lock file must be sufficient to reproduce the same package graph while referenced artifacts remain available.

---

# 56. Hash Pinning

Production applications may pin package hashes rather than only versions.

---

# 57. Version Pinning

Applications may pin:

```text
exact
major
minor
range
```

---

# 58. Security Policy

Security policy can impose maximum allowed versions, publishers, capabilities and signatures.

---

# 59. Capability Review

Package installation can display requested capabilities before activation.

---

# 60. Capability Difference

Update manager must detect capability expansion.

Example:

```text
old:
filesystem.read

new:
filesystem.read
network.connect
```

This is a security-relevant update.

---

# 61. Capability Approval

Application policy may require explicit approval before activation.

---

# 62. No Silent Privilege Expansion

An update must not silently grant new capabilities merely because the package version changed.

---

# 63. Package Installation State

```text
Available
Downloaded
Verified
Installed
Activated
Disabled
Quarantined
Removed
```

---

# 64. Installation Transaction

Installation uses an atomic transaction:

```text
download
verify
stage
validate
commit
```

---

# 65. Staging Directory

Temporary package files are stored in a secure staging area.

---

# 66. No Execution During Staging

Package binaries are not executed while staging.

---

# 67. Atomic Activation

Activation switches from old package generation to new package generation atomically where the platform allows.

---

# 68. Generation

Installed package generations are tracked.

---

# 69. Previous Generation

Previous generation remains available until rollback retention policy removes it.

---

# 70. Rollback

Rollback selects a previously verified generation.

---

# 71. Rollback Safety

Rollback must not erase user data.

---

# 72. Application State Compatibility

Package rollback may require state migration compatibility.

---

# 73. State Boundary

Application data is not automatically rolled back with package binaries.

---

# 74. Database Migration

Database/schema migrations must declare forward and rollback capabilities explicitly.

---

# 75. No Fake Rollback

If data migration cannot be reversed, package rollback does not pretend to restore old data.

---

# 76. Update Manager

Core object:

```text
UpdateManager
```

provides:

```text
check()
plan()
download()
verify()
stage()
activate()
rollback()
```

---

# 77. Update Plan

An update plan contains:

```text
current_graph
target_graph
added
removed
changed
capability_changes
migration_requirements
```

---

# 78. Dry Run

Updates can be simulated without modifying the installed state.

---

# 79. Update Preview

Preview reports:

- package changes;
- size;
- dependencies;
- capabilities;
- restart requirements;
- migration requirements.

---

# 80. Restart Requirement

Package metadata may declare whether application restart is required.

---

# 81. Hot Update

Packages compatible with 623 may update without full application restart.

---

# 82. Cold Update

Packages that cannot hot-update require restart.

---

# 83. Hot Update Validation

Hot update follows 623 quiescence and reload rules.

---

# 84. Update Failure

Failure leaves the previous active generation intact where possible.

---

# 85. Interrupted Update

An interrupted update must be recoverable from the staged transaction.

---

# 86. Power Loss

After power loss, installation state is reconciled deterministically.

---

# 87. Crash Recovery

600/611 recovery primitives are used.

---

# 88. Update Journal

Installation may maintain:

```text
.axupdate-journal
```

containing transaction state.

---

# 89. Journal Integrity

Journal state is validated before recovery.

---

# 90. Atomic Pointer

Activation can use an atomic generation pointer:

```text
active → generation_17
```

then:

```text
active → generation_18
```

---

# 91. Update Channels

Packages may publish channels:

```text
stable
beta
preview
nightly
internal
```

---

# 92. Channel Semantics

A channel is a publication policy, not a security boundary.

---

# 93. Channel Pinning

Applications can pin a channel.

---

# 94. Channel Migration

Moving channels is an explicit configuration change.

---

# 95. Downgrade

Downgrade is allowed only if package/state compatibility permits it.

---

# 96. Downgrade Policy

Security policy may prohibit downgrade below a minimum secure version.

---

# 97. Minimum Secure Version

Policy may specify:

```text
min_allowed_version
```

---

# 98. Security Update

A security update can be marked:

```text
security_fix = true
```

This is metadata, not an automatic forced-update requirement.

---

# 99. Emergency Block

Security policy can block known-compromised package versions.

---

# 100. Quarantine

Blocked packages enter:

```text
Quarantined
```

and cannot activate.

---

# 101. Package Removal

Removal transaction:

```text
disable
stop
deactivate
remove registrations
remove package
```

---

# 102. Data Preservation

Removal does not delete application data by default.

---

# 103. Purge

Explicit purge may remove package-owned cache/state where policy allows.

---

# 104. Dependency Removal

A package cannot be removed while required by another active package unless the dependent package is also removed/updated.

---

# 105. Orphan Detection

Resolver identifies unused dependencies.

---

# 106. Garbage Collection of Packages

Package reclamation is distinct from language garbage collection.

---

# 107. Package Reclamation

Unused package generations may be deleted when:

- not active;
- not pinned;
- not required;
- outside rollback retention.

---

# 108. CAS Reclamation

613 handles actual CAS object reclamation.

---

# 109. Cache Layers

```text
Repository Cache
Package Cache
CAS
Compiled Artifact Cache
Runtime Resource Cache
```

---

# 110. Cache Integrity

Caches are verified through hashes.

---

# 111. Corrupted Cache

Corrupted entries are discarded and re-fetched when possible.

---

# 112. Offline Cache

Cached packages remain installable offline.

---

# 113. Mirror

Repositories can use mirrors.

---

# 114. Mirror Selection

Selection can consider:

- configured priority;
- availability;
- locality;
- policy.

---

# 115. Mirror Integrity

All downloaded packages remain independently hash/signature verified.

---

# 116. Partial Download

Large packages support resumable download.

---

# 117. Chunk Verification

613 CAS chunk hashes verify downloaded chunks.

---

# 118. Download Limits

606 resource limits apply to:

- bandwidth;
- disk;
- memory;
- concurrent downloads.

---

# 119. Network

609 provides network transport.

---

# 120. TLS

610 provides TLS/trust.

---

# 121. Authentication

Repository authentication may use:

- TLS certificates;
- tokens;
- signed requests;
- enterprise credentials.

Credentials are managed through 601/610.

---

# 122. Credential Isolation

Repository credentials are not exposed to packages.

---

# 123. Anonymous Repository

Repositories may permit anonymous metadata/download access.

---

# 124. Private Repository

Private repositories require explicit credentials.

---

# 125. Enterprise Repository

Enterprise policy may specify:

```text
allowed_repositories
blocked_repositories
required_signers
allowed_publishers
```

---

# 126. Repository Policy

603 controls access to repository endpoints.

---

# 127. Package Download

Download process:

```text
resolve
→ select artifact
→ download
→ hash verify
→ signature verify
```

---

# 128. Artifact Selection

Selection considers:

- target;
- architecture;
- ABI;
- CPU features;
- graphics capabilities where declared.

---

# 129. CPU Features

A package may publish variants:

```text
baseline
avx2
avx512
neon
```

---

# 130. Runtime Selection

CPU capability detection occurs before selecting an optimized variant.

---

# 131. Fallback

Baseline package remains available when optimized variants are unsupported.

---

# 132. GPU Variants

Packages may provide shader/model/resource variants for different GPUs.

---

# 133. Package Resource Variants

613 handles target-specific resource selection.

---

# 134. Localization

Packages can contain `.axloc` resources from 617.

---

# 135. Theme Resources

Packages can contain theme assets.

---

# 136. Media Resources

Packages can contain 616 media assets.

---

# 137. Shader Resources

Packages can contain 615 shader artifacts.

---

# 138. Model Resources

Packages can contain AI model artifacts.

Large objects should use CAS/chunking rather than duplicating data.

---

# 139. Application Bundle

Application distribution may use:

```text
ApplicationBundle
```

containing:

```text
executable
native libraries
packages
resources
manifest
signatures
```

---

# 140. Platform Bundle

625 maps application bundles to platform-specific packaging:

```text
Windows
Linux
macOS
Android
iOS
WASM
```

---

# 141. Platform Installer

Installer format is platform-specific.

625 defines the logical package model rather than replacing OS-native installers.

---

# 142. Portable Application

An application may be distributed as a self-contained directory/bundle.

---

# 143. Single-File Application

Optional packaging can combine:

```text
executable + resources + package store
```

into a single distributable artifact.

---

# 144. Extraction

Single-file packages may extract resources lazily or at installation time.

---

# 145. Memory Mapping

Uncompressed package resources may be memory mapped through 611/613.

---

# 146. Executable Extraction

Executable components should not be executed directly from unverified temporary locations.

---

# 147. Code Signing

Platform-native signing remains separate from Axiom package signatures.

---

# 148. Dual Verification

Distribution may require:

```text
Axiom package signature
+
OS/platform code signature
```

---

# 149. Application Identity

Application package has:

```text
ApplicationId
PublisherId
Version
BuildId
```

---

# 150. Application Update

Application update follows the same staged-generation model.

---

# 151. Self-Update

An application cannot replace its own running executable directly on platforms that prohibit it.

A separate updater process may perform the operation.

---

# 152. Updater

Optional:

```text
UpdateAgent
```

supervised by 605.

---

# 153. Update Agent Security

Updater receives only the capabilities required for installation.

---

# 154. Updater Isolation

Updater should preferably be a separate executable/process.

---

# 155. Update Agent Failure

A failed update agent must not corrupt the current application generation.

---

# 156. Bootstrap

Applications may use a small bootstrap executable:

```text
bootstrap
    ↓
select generation
    ↓
launch application
```

---

# 157. Generation Selection

Bootstrap chooses the latest valid generation according to policy.

---

# 158. Failed Startup

If the new generation repeatedly fails startup, bootstrap can revert to a known-good generation.

---

# 159. Crash Loop

605 can detect repeated application startup failures.

---

# 160. Rollback Threshold

Rollback requires an explicit configured policy.

---

# 161. Startup Health

Application reports readiness to 605.

---

# 162. Failed Update Detection

An update is considered unhealthy if application readiness is not achieved according to configured policy.

---

# 163. Rollback

Rollback switches to the previous verified generation.

---

# 164. Data Compatibility

Rollback does not automatically revert user data.

---

# 165. Migration Strategy

Applications should use forward-compatible storage migrations where possible.

---

# 166. Database Migration Package

Migration metadata may be included in package manifests.

---

# 167. Migration Transaction

Migration runs transactionally where underlying storage supports it.

---

# 168. Migration Backup

Before irreversible migration, application may create a 600/611 checkpoint/backup.

---

# 169. Backup

Backup is separate from package rollback.

---

# 170. Restore

Restore is an explicit data operation.

---

# 171. Delta Update

Packages may publish binary/content deltas.

---

# 172. Delta Safety

Delta application requires exact source hash matching.

---

# 173. Delta Failure

If delta application fails, full package download remains available.

---

# 174. Delta Verification

Final package hash/signature is verified after reconstruction.

---

# 175. Compression

613 provides package compression.

---

# 176. Encryption

Package encryption is optional and policy-dependent.

---

# 177. Secret Packages

Private packages may be encrypted for authorized deployments.

---

# 178. Package License Metadata

Packages may contain license metadata.

625 stores and exposes it but does not define legal licensing rules.

---

# 179. Publisher Metadata

Publisher metadata may contain:

```text
publisher_id
display_name
key_ids
contact
```

---

# 180. Publisher Verification

Human-readable publisher names are not trust identities.

Cryptographic publisher identity is authoritative.

---

# 181. Package Name Collision

Package IDs, not display names, define identity.

---

# 182. Typosquatting Mitigation

Tooling may warn when package IDs are visually similar to known installed packages.

The warning must not override explicit package identity.

---

# 183. Dependency Confusion Protection

Repository policy can restrict which repositories may satisfy specific package namespaces.

---

# 184. Namespace Ownership

Organizations can reserve package namespaces through repository policy.

---

# 185. Repository Scope

Example:

```text
company.*
```

may be resolved only from an enterprise repository.

---

# 186. Source Locking

Lock file can record the repository that supplied each package.

---

# 187. Source Policy

Resolver can require exact repository identity.

---

# 188. Package Transparency

Repositories may expose immutable publication history.

---

# 189. Reproducible Metadata

Index snapshots should have deterministic serialization.

---

# 190. Repository Snapshot

A snapshot contains a deterministic list of package metadata.

---

# 191. Snapshot Pinning

Production builds can pin a repository snapshot hash.

---

# 192. Build Reproducibility

Build systems can use:

```text
source lock
+
package lock
+
repository snapshot
```

to reproduce dependencies.

---

# 193. Dependency Vendoring

Applications may vendor packages locally.

---

# 194. Vendored Packages

Vendored packages are treated like local immutable packages.

---

# 195. No Network Build

A fully vendored application must build without network access.

---

# 196. Build Cache

Compiler artifacts may be cached through 613.

---

# 197. Binary Cache

Trusted precompiled artifacts can be distributed.

---

# 198. Binary Cache Verification

Binary cache artifacts require:

```text
source_hash
compiler_hash
target
ABI
feature_set
```

matching.

---

# 199. Untrusted Binary Cache

Untrusted binary artifacts are rebuilt locally unless explicitly allowed by policy.

---

# 200. Compiler Trust

Package distribution does not replace compiler/toolchain trust.

---

# 201. Toolchain Packages

Compilers, SDKs and tools can themselves be distributed as packages.

---

# 202. Toolchain Isolation

Different Axiom toolchain versions can coexist.

---

# 203. Toolchain Selection

Project manifest chooses its required toolchain.

---

# 204. Compiler Lock

Project may contain:

```text
toolchain_version
toolchain_hash
```

---

# 205. SDK Packages

Platform SDK metadata can be distributed through package infrastructure.

---

# 206. Cross Compilation

Packages may contain target-specific artifacts.

---

# 207. Native SDK Dependency

Core compiler must not require a public package registry to compile basic Axiom code.

---

# 208. Bootstrap Compiler

Axiom bootstrap toolchain must remain independently distributable.

---

# 209. Package Manager

```text

axiom package info
axiom package install
axiom package remove
axiom package update
axiom package verify
axiom package list
axiom package graph
axiom package cache
```

# 210. Repository Commands

```text
axiom repo remove
axiom repo list
axiom repo sync
axiom repo verify
```

# 211. Update Commands

```text
axiom update plan
axiom update apply
axiom update rollback
```

---

# 212. Offline Commands

```text
axiom package export
axiom package import
axiom repo snapshot
axiom repo restore
```

---

# 213. Package Inspection

Inspection must never execute package code.

---

# 214. Manifest Inspection

Manifest can be parsed without loading binaries.

---

# 215. Binary Inspection

Binary metadata can be inspected without activation.

---

# 216. Capability Inspection

Tools report requested capabilities before installation.

---

# 217. Update Planning

Planning must not modify active package generations.

---

# 218. Download Scheduling

Downloads use 607 and 606.

---

# 219. Concurrent Downloads

Concurrent downloads are bounded by resource policy.

---

# 220. Backpressure

Repository downloads use bounded buffers.

---

# 221. Resume

Interrupted downloads can resume from verified chunks.

---

# 222. HTTP Range

609 may provide HTTP range support.

---

# 223. TLS

Repository traffic uses 610 TLS.

---

# 224. Certificate Policy

Enterprise repositories can use custom trust policies.

---

# 225. Proxy

Repository access can use 609 proxy support.

---

# 226. Authentication Secrets

Credentials use 601/610 secure secret handling.

# 227. Logging

602 logs package operations without exposing credentials.

---

# 228. Diagnostics

Package operations include:

```text
repository_id
package_id
version
hash
operation
duration
result
```

---

# 229. Privacy

Package manager must not transmit unrelated application data.

# 230. Telemetry

No package-management telemetry is mandatory.

# 231. Opt-In Metrics

Applications may enable aggregate package metrics explicitly.

# 232. Audit

# 234. Resource Quotas

```text
                         Package Generation
                                │
              ┌─────────────────┼──────────────────┐
              ▼                 ▼                  ▼
          Native App        623 Extension      624 Script
              │                 │                  │
              └─────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                                ▼
                         Application Runtime
                                │
                         Health / Readiness
                                │
                         605 Supervision
                                │
                         Rollback if required
```

---

# 307. Distribution Profiles

## Minimal

```text
AXIOM_PACKAGE_NONE
```

No package manager.

---

## Local

```text
AXIOM_PACKAGE_LOCAL
```

Local AXPK installation and CAS.

---

## Developer

```text
AXIOM_PACKAGE_DEV
```

## Enterprise

```text
AXIOM_PACKAGE_ENTERPRISE
```

## Full

```text
AXIOM_PACKAGE_FULL
```

Repository synchronization, update channels, staged updates, rollback and package management.

---

# 308. Important Boundary

625 does **not** become part of the fundamental Axiom execution model.

The following remains valid:

```text
hello.ax
    ↓
axiom compiler
    ↓
native executable
```

with:

```text
no registry
no account
no package daemon
no marketplace
no network
no plugin manager
no scripting engine
```

unless the application explicitly chooses those features.

---

# 309. Result

BOOTSTRAP-625 establishes a complete distribution architecture from:

```text
single local .axpk
```

through:

```text
private enterprise repository
```

to:

```text
large multi-platform package ecosystem
```

while maintaining:

- deterministic dependency resolution;
- cryptographic package identity;
- offline operation;
- atomic updates;
- rollback;
- package generations;
- capability-aware installation;
- reproducible builds;
- CAS deduplication;
- target-specific artifacts;
- extension integration;
- scripting integration;
- application recovery.

The key architectural distinction is:

```text
613 = how packages are represented and stored
623 = how native extensions execute
624 = how dynamic behavior executes
625 = how packages are discovered, resolved, installed and updated
```

# BOOTSTRAP-626 — Native Application Networking Services, HTTP Client/Server, Web API, RPC, WebSocket, Service Gateway & Distributed Application Runtime 5.0

**Status:** SPECIFIED  
**Layer:** Application Networking / Service Runtime  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600 → 625

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-609 established Axiom's low-level networking foundation:

- sockets;
- TCP/UDP;
- DNS;
- TLS boundary;
- network buffers;
- asynchronous network I/O.

BOOTSTRAP-626 builds the higher-level **application networking and distributed-service layer** above 609.

It provides:

- HTTP client;
- HTTP server;
- routing;
- middleware;
- request/response handling;
- Web API;
- WebSocket;
- RPC;
- service discovery;
- connection management;
- authentication hooks;
- authorization hooks;
- serialization integration;
- streaming;
- multipart/form-data;
- content negotiation;
- compression;
- retries;
- circuit breakers;
- rate limiting;
- service health;
- distributed tracing;
- API versioning;
- graceful shutdown;
- gateway/proxy primitives;
- reverse proxy;
- service-to-service communication;
- local and remote service abstraction.

The architecture must remain usable for:

```text
Desktop application
CLI tool
Web server
REST API
RPC service
Game backend
AI service
Microservice
Local IPC-like service
Embedded device
WASM host application
```

---

# 2. Core Principle

626 is an **application networking layer**, not a replacement for 609.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
626 Application Networking
    │
    ├── HTTP
    ├── RPC
    ├── WebSocket
    ├── Gateway
    ├── Service Discovery
    └── API Services
    │
    ▼
609 Network Runtime
    │
    ▼
608 / 607
    │
    ▼
OS / Network Device
```

---

# 3. Non-Goals

626 does not mandate:

- REST;
- JSON;
- HTTP;
- microservices;
- service mesh;
- cloud infrastructure;
- centralized service discovery;
- distributed databases;
- Kubernetes;
- a particular RPC protocol;
- a particular authentication provider.

These are implementations/profiles above the core abstractions.

---

# 4. Design Goals

626 must provide:

1. low overhead;
2. type safety;
3. streaming;
4. async-first operation;
5. explicit cancellation;
6. bounded buffering;
7. predictable resource usage;
8. secure defaults;
9. protocol extensibility;
10. easy local development;
11. production scalability;
12. cross-platform behavior;
13. observability;
14. deterministic testing.

---

# 5. Layering

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Application / Business Logic         │
├──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Web API / RPC / Gateway              │
├──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ HTTP / WebSocket / Service Runtime   │
├──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 626 Application Networking           │
├──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 609 Sockets / DNS / TLS Transport    │
├──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 607 Async + 608 Sync                 │
├──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ OS / Device                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

# 6. Core Objects

```text
NetworkApplication
HttpClient
HttpServer
HttpRequest
HttpResponse
HttpHeaders
HttpBody
HttpRoute
HttpRouter
HttpMiddleware
HttpConnection
WebSocket
WebSocketServer
RpcClient
RpcServer
```

```text
struct HttpRequest {
    method: HttpMethod

fn HttpRequest.header(
```

# BOOTSTRAP-627 — Native Distributed Systems Runtime, Cluster Coordination, Membership, Leases, Leader Election, Distributed Locks & Consensus Boundary 5.0

**Status:** SPECIFIED  
**Layer:** Distributed Systems / Coordination Runtime  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600 → 626

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-627 defines the Axiom runtime boundary for applications that operate across multiple processes, machines, nodes, availability zones, or administrative domains.

It provides common primitives for:

- node identity;
- cluster membership;
- service membership;
- health state;
- leases;
- heartbeats;
- failure detection;
- leader election;
- distributed locks;
- fencing;
- distributed coordination;
- replicated state-machine boundaries;
- consensus-provider abstraction;
- quorum;
- cluster configuration;
- membership epochs;
- topology;
- distributed clocks;
- logical clocks;
- causal metadata;
- distributed request identity;
- cluster diagnostics;
- deterministic testing.

The design deliberately distinguishes **coordination primitives** from **distributed application semantics**.

---

# 2. Core Principle

627 must not pretend that distributed systems can provide the same guarantees as local memory.

The runtime explicitly models:

```text
latency
partial failure
message loss
reordering
duplication
partition
node crash
clock skew
restart
stale membership
```

---

# 3. Layering

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Distributed Application
    │
    ▼
627 Distributed Runtime
    ├── Membership
    ├── Failure Detection
    ├── Lease
    ├── Election
    ├── Lock
    ├── Coordination
    ├── Cluster State
    └── Consensus Boundary
    │
    ▼
626 RPC / Service Networking
    │
    ▼
609 Network
```

---

# 4. Non-Goals

627 does not provide a mandatory:

- database;
- distributed filesystem;
- service mesh;
- cloud control plane;
- Kubernetes replacement;
- consensus algorithm implementation in every build;
- distributed transaction manager;
- global shared-memory abstraction;
- exactly-once distributed execution.

---

# 5. Fundamental Rule

No distributed primitive may silently convert an uncertain network event into a certainty.

For example:

```text
timeout != proof of node death
```

and:

```text
connection lost != proof that remote operation failed
```

---

# 6. Node Model

```text
Node {
    node_id
    generation
    incarnation
    endpoint_set
    capabilities
    labels
    metadata
}
```

---

# 7. NodeId

`NodeId` is globally unique within the configured cluster domain.

---

# 8. Node Generation

Every node process instance has a generation.

```text
NodeId + Generation
```

uniquely identifies a running incarnation.

---

# 9. Restart

Restart increments generation/incarnation.

Old messages cannot automatically apply to the new generation.

---

# 10. ClusterId

A cluster has a stable:

```text
ClusterId
```

distinct from its current membership.

---

# 11. Cluster Epoch

Membership-changing operations advance:

```text
ClusterEpoch
```

where supported.

---

# 12. Epoch Rule

Operations carrying an older epoch may be rejected as stale.

---

# 13. Membership

```text
Membership {
    join()
    leave()
    members()
    watch()
}
```

---

# 14. Membership States

```text
Joining
Alive
Suspect
Leaving
Left
Failed
Unknown
```

---

# 15. Membership Semantics

Membership is a view, not absolute truth.

---

# 16. Failure Detector

```text
FailureDetector {
    observe()
    suspect()
    status()
}
```

---

# 17. Failure Detector Inputs

May include:

- heartbeat;
- RPC response;
- local process state;
- transport failures;
- lease expiration;
- indirect probes.

---

# 18. Failure Detector Output

```text
Healthy
Suspected
Unreachable
Failed
Unknown
```

---

# 19. Suspicion

Suspicion must remain distinguishable from confirmed failure.

---

# 20. Phi Accrual

An optional statistical failure detector may expose a suspicion score.

It is never treated as absolute proof.

---

# 21. Heartbeat

Heartbeats contain:

```text
node_id
generation
membership_epoch
sequence
timestamp
```

---

# 22. Heartbeat Frequency

Configurable and bounded by 606 resource budgets.

---

# 23. Heartbeat Transport

Uses 626 service/network transport.

---

# 24. Failure Detection

Failure detector must tolerate transient packet loss.

---

# 25. Network Partition

A partition can produce:

```text
Node A believes B unreachable
Node B believes A unreachable
```

without either node being crashed.

---

# 26. Split Brain

Systems requiring a single active leader must use fencing/quorum/consensus.

---

# 27. Quorum

For an odd-sized voting set:

```text
quorum = floor(N / 2) + 1
```

---

# 28. Quorum Safety

A minority partition must not independently claim exclusive leadership when quorum is required.

---

# 29. Quorum Availability

A system requiring quorum may become unavailable during a partition.

This is an intentional safety tradeoff.

---

# 30. Lease

```text
Lease {
    lease_id
    holder
    expiration
    epoch
}
```

---

# 31. Lease Semantics

A lease grants authority only while its validity conditions remain satisfied.

---

# 32. Lease Renewal

```text
renew()
```

must happen before expiration.

---

# 33. Lease Expiration

After expiration, holder must stop relying on the lease.

---

# 34. Clock Safety

Wall-clock time alone must not be used as proof of remote lease expiration unless the protocol explicitly provides clock-bound guarantees.

---

# 35. Lease Provider

Lease implementations may use:

```text
ConsensusStore
Database
ExternalCoordinator
StaticAuthority
```

---

# 36. Fencing Token

Every exclusive lease may produce a monotonically increasing:

```text
FenceToken
```

---

# 37. Fencing

Resource owners should reject operations carrying an older fencing token.

---

# 38. Example

```text
Node A owns token 41
Node A becomes partitioned

Node B obtains token 42

Storage accepts:
    token >= 42

Storage rejects:
    token 41
```

---

# 39. Distributed Lock

```text
DistributedLock {
    acquire()
    renew()
    release()
}
```

---

# 40. Lock Identity

A lock has:

```text
LockName
LeaseId
FenceToken
Owner
Epoch
```

---

# 41. Lock Safety

A distributed lock is not equivalent to a local mutex.

---

# 42. Lock Expiration

Expiration can occur without explicit release.

---

# 43. Lock Usage

Critical resources should use fencing rather than trusting lock ownership alone.

---

# 44. Lock Fairness

Distributed lock fairness is optional and must not compromise safety.

---

# 45. Reentrant Lock

Reentrant distributed locks are not required by the core runtime.

---

# 46. Leader Election

```text
LeaderElection {
    campaign()
    resign()
    leader()
    watch()
}
```

---

# 47. Leader Identity

Leader identity includes:

```text
NodeId
Generation
Epoch
FenceToken
```

---

# 48. Leadership

Leadership is valid only within its protocol-defined epoch/term.

---

# 49. Stale Leader

A node that loses leadership must stop performing leader-exclusive operations.

---

# 50. Fencing Leader

Leader-controlled external resources should validate the current fencing token.

---

# 51. Election Algorithms

627 defines an abstraction.

Possible providers:

```text
Raft
Paxos-family
external consensus service
database-backed election
platform coordinator
```

---

# 52. No Mandatory Algorithm

Axiom applications do not depend on a single consensus algorithm at the language/runtime level.

---

# 53. Consensus Boundary

Consensus provider exposes:

```text
propose()
read()
watch()
term()
commit_index()
```

where supported.

---

# 54. Replicated State Machine

Applications may build:

```text
StateMachine {
    apply(command)
    snapshot()
    restore()
}
```

above the consensus provider.

---

# 55. Determinism

A replicated state machine must produce deterministic results for identical committed commands.

---

# 56. Forbidden State

Consensus-applied state must not depend on:

- local wall clock;
- random numbers;
- local filesystem state;
- network timing;

unless explicitly modeled as replicated input.

---

# 57. Snapshot

Consensus providers may create snapshots.

---

# 58. Snapshot Version

Snapshots contain:

```text
state_machine_version
log_index
term
schema_fingerprint
```

---

# 59. Log

Replicated logs consist of ordered entries.

---

# 60. Log Entry

```text
LogEntry {
    index
    term
    command
    schema
}
```

---

# 61. Commit

Only committed entries become authoritative state.

---

# 62. Apply

Application state is updated only according to provider commit semantics.

---

# 63. Read Consistency

Distributed reads must explicitly declare consistency.

---

# 64. Consistency Modes

Possible:

```text
Local
Leader
Quorum
Linearizable
BoundedStale
Eventual
```

subject to provider support.

---

# 65. No Fake Linearizability

The API must not label a read linearizable unless the provider actually supplies the required guarantee.

---

# 66. Eventual Consistency

Applications may explicitly select eventual-consistency models.

---

# 67. Read-Your-Writes

Optional session-level consistency token:

```text
ConsistencyToken
```

---

# 68. Causal Metadata

Optional causal metadata may use logical clocks.

---

# 69. Lamport Clock

```text
LamportClock {
    value
    tick()
    observe()
}
```

---

# 70. Vector Clock

Optional:

```text
VectorClock
```

for systems requiring richer causality.

---

# 71. Hybrid Logical Clock

Optional HLC provider may combine physical and logical time.

---

# 72. Physical Time

627 never assumes synchronized physical clocks without explicit bounds.

---

# 73. Distributed Timestamp

Distributed timestamps carry their clock domain/version.

---

# 74. Request Identity

Distributed calls use:

```text
RequestId
TraceId
AttemptId
```

---

# 75. Duplicate Detection

Applications may use request IDs to detect duplicate operations.

---

# 76. Exactly-Once Boundary

Duplicate suppression is application/storage-specific.

627 does not claim universal exactly-once execution.

---

# 77. Idempotent Command

Distributed commands should declare whether they are idempotent.

---

# 78. Retry

Retries must preserve:

```text
RequestId
```

while changing:

```text
AttemptId
```

---

# 79. Retry Budget

Distributed clients inherit 626 retry-budget semantics.

---

# 80. Membership Watch

Applications can subscribe to membership changes.

---

# 81. Watch Semantics

Watch streams may experience:

- duplicate events;
- reconnect;
- compaction;
- missed events.

Consumers must handle resynchronization.

---

# 82. Snapshot + Watch

Preferred pattern:

```text
snapshot()
+
watch(from_version)
```

---

# 83. Watch Version

Each membership/state update has a monotonic version where provider semantics permit.

---

# 84. Resync

When history is unavailable:

```text
watch → resync snapshot → watch
```

---

# 85. Cluster Configuration

Cluster configuration contains:

```text
ClusterId
members
roles
protocol_version
epoch
security_policy
```

---

# 86. Configuration Changes

Membership/config changes should be transactional where consensus is available.

---

# 87. Membership Roles

Possible roles:

```text
Voter
Observer
Learner
Worker
Witness
Client
```

---

# 88. Observer

Observer does not participate in quorum unless explicitly configured.

---

# 89. Learner

Learner receives replicated state without voting authority.

---

# 90. Witness

Witness may participate in quorum without holding full application state, depending on provider.

---

# 91. Node Labels

Nodes may expose labels:

```text
region
zone
rack
device
platform
capacity
```

---

# 92. Labels

Labels are descriptive metadata, not automatically trusted authorization attributes.

---

# 93. Capability

Distributed capability authorization remains controlled by 603.

---

# 94. Node Trust

Membership does not imply full application trust.

---

# 95. Secure Membership

Node authentication uses:

```text
610 TLS
mTLS
signed identity
platform identity
```

---

# 96. Join

Joining a cluster requires explicit admission policy.

---

# 97. Join Token

Join credentials are treated as secrets.

---

# 98. Join Bootstrap

A node may obtain:

```text
cluster identity
membership configuration
trust roots
protocol version
```

---

# 99. Join Verification

Cluster verifies node identity before admission.

---

# 100. Rejoin

A restarted node joins with a new generation.

---

# 101. Removed Node

Removed nodes must not automatically regain authority.

1. Distributed state is not shared memory.
2. Network timeout is not proof of failure.
3. Membership is a view.
4. Suspicion is not failure proof.
5. Node generation identifies process incarnation.
6. Cluster epoch identifies membership/configuration generation.
7. Consensus term is distinct from cluster epoch.
8. Fence token is distinct from leadership term.
9. Quorum is explicit.
10. Minority cannot silently claim quorum authority.
11. Lease is time/protocol bounded.
12. Expired lease cannot authorize protected work.
13. Fencing protects external resources.
14. Distributed locks are not local mutexes.
15. Leader status is epoch/term scoped.
16. Stale messages are rejected.
17. Exactly-once execution is not universally promised.
18. Retry must consider idempotency.
19. Request identity survives retry.
20. Attempt identity changes per attempt.
21. Consensus state must be deterministic.
22. Physical clock is not consensus.
23. Wall clock is not a monotonic timer.
24. Membership does not imply trust.
25. Discovery does not imply authentication.
26. Authentication does not imply authorization.
27. Authorization cannot bypass 603.
28. Credentials use 601/610.
29. Network transport uses 626/609.
30. Durable state uses 611/612.
31. Resource limits use 606.
32. Scheduling uses 607.
33. Synchronization uses 608.
34. Supervision uses 605.
35. Diagnostics use 602.
36. Unused distributed modules can be stripped.
37. No mandatory external coordinator.
38. No mandatory cloud.
39. No mandatory service mesh.
40. No mandatory database.
41. No automatic consensus membership mutation after timeout.
42. Split-brain safety requires protocol support.
43. Recovery must revalidate authority.
44. Rejoining node receives a new generation.
45. Old credentials can be revoked.
46. Watch streams require bounded resources.
47. Snapshots require explicit consistency semantics.
48. Schema changes require compatibility handling.
49. Rolling upgrades preserve quorum.
50. Administrative changes are capability-protected.

```text
       ┌───────────────────┐
       │       626         │
       │ RPC / HTTP / WS   │
       └─────────┬─────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
       ┌───────────────────┐
       │       609         │
       │ Network Transport │
       └─────────┬─────────┘
                 │
          ┌──────┴──────┐
          ▼             ▼
        610           611/612
        TLS         Durable State
```

---

# 323. Final Design Decision

Axiom's distributed runtime deliberately uses a **layered capability model**:

```text
609 = transport
626 = application networking
627 = distributed coordination
```

Consensus is a provider boundary rather than an unavoidable dependency.

This allows:

```text
tiny local application
        ↓
HTTP client

small server
        ↓
HTTP + RPC

distributed application
        ↓
HTTP/RPC + discovery

clustered service
        ↓
membership + lease + election

strongly consistent cluster
        ↓
consensus provider
```

without forcing the smallest Axiom executable to contain distributed-systems machinery.

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-627 defines the Axiom runtime boundary for applications that operate across multiple processes, machines, nodes, availability zones, or administrative domains.

It provides common primitives for:

- node identity;

The design deliberately distinguishes **coordination primitives** from **distributed application semantics**.

# 2. Core Principle

627 must not pretend that distributed systems can provide the same guarantees as local memory.

The runtime explicitly models:

```text
latency
partial failure

duplication
partition
```

2. Network timeout is not proof of failure.
3. Membership is a view.

41. No automatic consensus membership mutation after timeout.

45. Old credentials can be revoked.

# 323. Final Design Decision

Axiom's distributed runtime deliberately uses a **layered capability model**:

```text
609 = transport
626 = application networking
627 = distributed coordination
```

Consensus is a provider boundary rather than an unavoidable dependency.

This allows:

```text
tiny local application
        ↓
HTTP client

small server
        ↓
HTTP + RPC

distributed application
        ↓
HTTP/RPC + discovery

clustered service
        ↓
membership + lease + election

strongly consistent cluster
        ↓
consensus provider
```

without forcing the smallest Axiom executable to contain distributed-systems machinery.

# BOOTSTRAP-628 — Native Distributed Data, Replicated Storage, Consistency Models, Distributed Cache, CRDT Boundary, Event Log & Data Replication Runtime 5.0

**Status:** SPECIFIED  
**Layer:** Distributed Data / Replication Runtime  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600 → 627

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-628 defines the Axiom runtime foundation for distributed data.

It provides standardized boundaries for:

- replicated data;
- distributed key/value storage;
- replicated logs;
- distributed caches;
- consistency models;
- replication streams;
- conflict detection;
- conflict resolution;
- CRDT providers;
- event logs;
- change feeds;
- snapshots;
- data synchronization;
- offline replicas;
- anti-entropy;
- version vectors;
- causal metadata;
- quorum reads/writes;
- read repair;
- hinted handoff;
- compaction;
- tombstones;
- distributed garbage collection of obsolete replicas;
- replica placement;
- replication policies.

It builds on:

```text id="fcz7o6"
611 Storage
612 Serialization
613 Package/CAS
627 Distributed Coordination
626 Networking
610 Cryptography
606 Resource Governance
```

---

# 2. Core Principle

Axiom must never hide the consistency model.

Every distributed data API must make its consistency semantics explicit.

For example:

```text id="6j2x8a"
Eventual
Causal
Session
Quorum
Linearizable
```

are different guarantees.

The runtime must not expose all of them through one ambiguous `get()` operation without a declared policy.

---

# 3. Layering

```text id="k86h7u"
Application
    │
    ▼
Distributed Data
    │
    ├── Replicated Store
    ├── Distributed Cache
    ├── Event Log
    ├── Change Feed
    ├── CRDT
    └── Replication
    │
    ▼
628
    │
    ├── 627 Coordination
    ├── 612 Serialization
    ├── 611 Storage
    └── 626 Networking
```

- globally synchronized clocks;
- exactly-once delivery.

# 275. Final Design Decision

Axiom's distributed-data architecture deliberately separates:

```text

612 = structured data
627 = distributed coordination
628 = distributed data
626 = network services
```

This produces an important property:

```text
local application
      │
      └── local storage only

distributed cache
      │
      └── 628 cache

event-driven system
      │
      └── 628 event log

eventually consistent system
      │
      └── 628 replication/CRDT

strongly consistent service
      │
      └── 627 consensus
             +
          628 replicated state
```

Axiom therefore does not force one universal distributed-storage model onto every application.

# 275. Final Design Decision

Axiom's distributed-data architecture deliberately separates:

```text
611 = local durable storage
612 = structured data
627 = distributed coordination
628 = distributed data
626 = network services
```

This produces an important property:

```text
local application
      │
      └── local storage only

distributed cache
      │
      └── 628 cache

event-driven system
      │
      └── 628 event log

eventually consistent system
      │
      └── 628 replication/CRDT

strongly consistent service
      │
      └── 627 consensus
             +
          628 replicated state
```

Axiom therefore does not force one universal distributed-storage model onto every application.

# BOOTSTRAP-629
## Native Distributed Workflow, Jobs, Scheduling, Orchestration, Durable Tasks, Sagas, Compensation & Long-Running Process Runtime 5.0

**Status:** COMPLETE  
**Layer:** Distributed Application Runtime  
**Depends on:** BOOTSTRAP-600 → BOOTSTRAP-628  
**Primary dependencies:** 605, 607, 612, 626, 627, 628  
**Optional integrations:** 619, 622, 623, 624  
**Core principle:** durable distributed execution without requiring Kubernetes, a cloud provider, a message broker, a GC runtime, or a third-party workflow engine.

---

# 1. Purpose

BOOTSTRAP-629 defines Axiom's native runtime for:

- workflows;
- jobs;
- scheduled jobs;
- durable tasks;
- task queues;
- worker pools;
- orchestration;
- long-running processes;
- durable timers;
- signals;
- retries;
- timeouts;
- cancellation;
- compensation;
- Sagas;
- human tasks;
- workflow recovery;
- deterministic replay;
- distributed execution;
- workflow versioning;
- execution history;
- workflow migration;
- failure recovery.

The system is designed for workloads ranging from:

```text
single-machine scheduled task
        ↓
local durable workflow
        ↓
multi-process workflow
        ↓
multi-node distributed workflow
        ↓
months-long business process
```

The runtime must remain useful even when only a small subset is enabled.

---

# 2. Non-Goals

629 does not define:

- a general-purpose distributed database;
- a new network protocol replacing 626;
- a new consensus algorithm replacing 627;
- a new storage engine replacing 611/628;
- a general-purpose actor model;
- a cloud-specific orchestration platform;
- Kubernetes compatibility as a core requirement;
- mandatory GUI tooling;
- mandatory human workflow functionality;
- exactly-once distributed execution;
- distributed ACID transactions.

---

# 3. Architectural Position

```text
                    AXIOM APPLICATION
                           │
                           ▼
              ┌────────────────────────┐
              │       629 WORKFLOW      │
              │        RUNTIME          │
              ├────────────────────────┤
              │ Workflow Engine         │
              │ Job Engine              │
              │ Scheduler               │
              │ Task Queues             │
              │ Workers                 │
              │ Durable Timers          │
              │ Signals                 │
              │ Retry Engine            │
              │ Saga/Compensation       │
              │ Replay/Recovery         │
              └────────────┬───────────┘
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼────────────────────┐
       ▼                   ▼                    ▼
    627                  628                   626
Coordination        Distributed Data       Network/RPC
       │                   │                    │
       └───────────┬───────┴────────────┬───────┘
                   ▼                    ▼
                  611                  607
              Local Storage         Scheduler
                   │                    │
                   ▼                    ▼
                  605                  606
             Supervision         Resource Governor
```

629 orchestrates execution.

It does **not** own the underlying distributed consensus, network transport, or durable storage mechanisms.

---

# 4. Fundamental Design Principle

Axiom distinguishes:

```text
Workflow decision
Activity execution
Persistent state
Distributed coordination
Worker execution
```

These must never be implicitly conflated.

For example:

```text
workflow:
    if account.balance >= amount:
        charge_card()
```

The `if` decision belongs to the deterministic workflow.

`charge_card()` is an external side effect and therefore belongs to an activity.

Conceptually:

```text
Workflow
    │
    ├── deterministic decision
    │
    └── Activity
            │
            └── external side effect
```

This distinction is fundamental to deterministic replay.

---

629 defines:

```text
Workflow

```

Every externally visible identity is generation-safe where required.

---

# 6. Workflow Definition

A workflow is a deterministic executable state machine.

A workflow may contain:

```text
sequence
branch
loop
parallel
join
wait
timer
signal
activity
sub-workflow
compensation
failure handler
retry policy
timeout
cancellation
```

Example:

```text
workflow OrderProcess(order):

    reserve_inventory(order)

    charge_payment(order)

    ship(order)

    notify_customer(order)
```

A more complex workflow:

```text
workflow OrderProcess(order):

    reserve_inventory(order)

    parallel:
        charge_payment(order)
        validate_shipping_address(order)

    join

    if payment_failed:
        compensate_reservation()
        return Failed

    ship(order)

    wait for delivery_confirmation

    notify_customer()
```

---

# 7. Workflow State Machine

Every workflow instance has an explicit lifecycle.

```text
Created
  ↓
Starting
  ↓
Running
  ├── Waiting
  ├── Suspended
  ├── Compensating
  ├── Cancelling
  ├── Failed
  └── Completed
```

Terminal states:

```text
Completed
Failed
Cancelled
Terminated
Abandoned
```

State transitions must be durable.

Invalid transitions must be rejected.

---

# 8. Workflow Identity

A workflow instance is identified by:

```text
WorkflowId
WorkflowVersion
WorkflowInstanceId
WorkflowRunId
Generation
```

These have different meanings.

```text
WorkflowId
    logical workflow definition

WorkflowVersion
    immutable definition version

WorkflowInstanceId
    durable business/process instance

WorkflowRunId
    execution generation

Generation
    fencing/recovery generation
```

A retry or worker restart must not silently create a new logical workflow instance.

---

# 9. Workflow Version

Workflow definitions are immutable after publication.

Example:

```text
OrderWorkflow@1
OrderWorkflow@2
OrderWorkflow@3
```

Running instances are normally pinned to their original version.

Migration requires explicit policy.

```text
WorkflowVersionPolicy:
    Pinned
    Compatible
    Migratable
```

No implicit source-code replacement is allowed to alter running workflows.

---

# 10. Deterministic Workflow Execution

Workflow decision code must be deterministic.

Forbidden inside deterministic workflow code:

```text
random()
system_time()
read_file()
network_request()
database_write()
environment_variable()
process_id()
thread_id()
GPU query
OS device query
```

Instead:

```text
now()
random()
activity(...)
signal(...)
```

must pass through deterministic runtime boundaries.

For example:

```text
t = workflow.now()
```

returns a workflow time derived from recorded execution state.

---

# 11. Side Effects

All external side effects are activities.

Examples:

```text
send_email()
charge_payment()
write_file()
publish_event()
call_http()
invoke_gpu()
access_camera()
start_process()
```

The workflow engine records:

```text
ActivityScheduled
ActivityStarted
ActivityCompleted
ActivityFailed
```

Replay uses the recorded activity result rather than executing the activity again.

---

# 12. Activity Model

An activity is executable work outside deterministic workflow evaluation.

Conceptual signature:

```text
activity<TInput, TOutput>(
    input: TInput,
    context: ActivityContext
) -> Result<TOutput, Error>
```

Activities may:

- access network;
- access files;
- access devices;
- access databases;
- call other services;
- perform CPU work;
- perform GPU work.

Activities are subject to:

- capabilities;
- resource budgets;
- timeouts;
- retries;
- cancellation;
- worker policies.

---

# 13. Activity Idempotency

Default distributed execution semantics are:

```text
AT_LEAST_ONCE
```

Therefore an activity may execute more than once.

Every retryable side-effecting activity should support an idempotency key.

Example:

```text
idempotency_key =
    hash(WorkflowInstanceId, StepId, ActivityAttemptGroup)
```

The external service may use that key to deduplicate operations.

Axiom does not claim exactly-once execution merely because an operation has an idempotency key.

---

# 14. Exactly-Once Semantics

629 explicitly does **not** guarantee global exactly-once execution.

Instead:

```text
durable state
+
at-least-once delivery
+
idempotent activity
+
deduplication
+
fencing
```

provide practical exactly-once *effects* where the external system supports them.

This distinction must be visible in the API and documentation.

---

# 15. Workflow History

Every durable workflow maintains an append-only logical history.

Example:

```text
WorkflowStarted
ActivityScheduled
ActivityStarted
ActivityCompleted
TimerCreated
TimerFired
SignalReceived
StepCompleted
WorkflowCheckpointed
WorkflowCompleted
```

History is stored through:

```text
629
 ↓
628
 ↓
612
 ↓
611
```

The workflow runtime does not require a proprietary storage engine.

---

# 16. Workflow Snapshot

Long workflows cannot replay unlimited history forever.

Therefore 629 supports:

```text
History
+
Snapshot
+
History after snapshot
```

A snapshot contains:

```text
WorkflowVersion
SchemaFingerprint
State
CompletedStepSet
PendingTimers
PendingActivities
PendingSignals
CompensationState
ReplayPosition
```

Snapshots must be immutable once committed.

---

# 17. Replay

Recovery process:

```text
load latest snapshot
        ↓
load subsequent history
        ↓
replay deterministic decisions
        ↓
reconstruct pending work
        ↓
resume execution
```

Replay must not repeat external side effects.

---

# 18. Replay Determinism Rule

For identical:

```text
WorkflowVersion
InitialState
History
```

the workflow engine must produce identical:

```text
next state
next commands
next timers
next activities
```

Any nondeterministic API used inside a workflow is a compiler/runtime error where statically detectable.

---

# 19. Durable Timer

Timers must survive:

- process crash;
- worker restart;
- machine restart;
- coordinator restart;
- node failure.

Example:

```text
workflow.wait(Duration.days(30))
```

must not require a process to remain alive for 30 days.

The runtime stores:

```text
TimerId
Deadline
WorkflowInstanceId
Generation
Status
```

---

# 20. Timer Semantics

Timer clock domain must be explicit.

Supported:

```text
MonotonicDuration
WallClockInstant
CalendarTime
```

Long-running schedules use wall-clock/calendar semantics.

Timeouts use monotonic time where possible.

This avoids confusing:

```text
"run after 10 minutes"
```

with:

```text
"run at 09:00 local time"
```

---

# 21. Job Model

A job is a unit of independently schedulable work.

```text
Job:
    JobId
    Payload
    Queue
    Priority
    Schedule
    RetryPolicy
    TimeoutPolicy
    ResourcePolicy
    CapabilityPolicy
```

Jobs may be:

```text
one-shot
periodic
scheduled
event-triggered
manually triggered
workflow-generated
```

---

# 22. Task Model

A task is a concrete execution request.

```text
Task:
    TaskId
    JobId
    WorkflowInstanceId?
    StepId?
    QueueId
    Attempt
    Lease
    Deadline
    Priority
```

A job can create many tasks.

A workflow step can create one or more tasks.

---

# 23. Task Queue

629 defines durable task queues.

Operations:

```text
enqueue()
receive()
lease()
ack()
nack()
delay()
dead_letter()
requeue()
```

Queue properties:

```text
durable
bounded
partitioned
ordered
priority-aware
backpressure-aware
```

---

# 24. Queue Delivery

Supported semantics:

```text
AtLeastOnce
AtMostOnce
BestEffort
```

Exactly-once queue delivery is not a core semantic.

The default is:

```text
AtLeastOnce
```

because durability and failure recovery are more important than pretending duplicates cannot occur.

---

# 25. Task Lease

A worker receives a lease.

```text
TaskLease:
    TaskId
    WorkerId
    LeaseId
    Expiration
    Generation
```

A worker must renew long-running tasks.

If the lease expires:

```text
task becomes eligible for reassignment
```

unless a fencing mechanism prevents stale execution from committing results.

---

# 26. Fencing

Every worker execution receives a fencing token.

Example:

```text
FenceToken = 9182
```

A newer execution may receive:

```text
FenceToken = 9183
```

Storage or service-side commit operations can reject stale tokens.

This prevents:

```text
old worker
    ↓
network partition
    ↓
new worker executes
    ↓
old worker returns
    ↓
old worker overwrites new result
```

---

# 27. Worker Model

A worker advertises:

```text
WorkerId
Generation
Version
Capabilities
Target
Architecture
ResourceGroup
ConcurrencyLimit
Health
Queues
```

Example:

```text
Worker:
    target = x86_64-windows
    capabilities = [gpu, ffmpeg-provider, filesystem]
    queues = ["video"]
    max_concurrency = 4
```

Workers must never gain capabilities merely by claiming them.

Actual capabilities come from 603.

---

# 28. Worker Registration

Lifecycle:

```text
Discovered
Registering
Ready
Serving
Draining
Stopping
Disconnected
Failed
```

Worker registration is lease-based.

Expired registrations are removed automatically.

---

# 29. Worker Selection

Task routing considers:

```text
queue
capability
target
architecture
resource availability
priority
locality
affinity
worker health
tenant policy
```

The scheduler must not route work to a worker that lacks required capability.

---

# 30. Worker Affinity

Optional affinity:

```text
None
Workflow
Partition
DataLocality
Device
Session
```

Affinity is a preference unless explicitly marked mandatory.

Mandatory affinity can cause a task to remain queued when no matching worker exists.

---

# 31. Retry Policy

Retry configuration:

```text
max_attempts
initial_delay
max_delay
backoff
jitter
retryable_errors
non_retryable_errors
retry_budget
```

Example:

```text
RetryPolicy:
    max_attempts = 5
    backoff = Exponential
    initial_delay = 1s
    max_delay = 60s
    jitter = Full
```

---

# 32. Retry Budget

Retry storms are prohibited.

Budgets can be applied to:

```text
workflow
job
queue
tenant
service
worker
application
```

The Resource Governor 606 supplies quota/budget primitives.

---

# 33. Timeout Model

Separate timeout types:

```text
ScheduleToStartTimeout
StartToCloseTimeout
HeartbeatTimeout
WorkflowTimeout
QueueVisibilityTimeout
LeaseTimeout
```

They must not be conflated.

---

# 34. Heartbeats

Long-running activities can emit:

```text
heartbeat(progress)
```

Heartbeat state can contain:

```text
progress
checkpoint marker
estimated stage
custom status
```

Heartbeat data is bounded and rate-limited.

---

# 35. Cancellation

Cancellation propagates through:

```text
Workflow
    ↓
Step
    ↓
Task
    ↓
Activity
```

Cancellation is cooperative unless the platform provides safe termination.

A cancellation request does not imply that external side effects have been undone.

---

# 36. Cancellation Policy

Each workflow may specify:

```text
CancelImmediately
CancelAtCheckpoint
FinishCurrentActivity
Compensate
ManualResolution
```

The policy must be explicit.

---

# 37. Saga Model

A Saga represents a sequence of business operations with compensating operations.

Example:

```text
reserve_inventory
charge_payment
create_shipment
```

Compensations:

```text
release_inventory
refund_payment
cancel_shipment
```

A compensation is not a database rollback.

It is another business operation.

---

# 38. Compensation Ordering

Default order:

```text
reverse dependency order
```

Example:

```text
A
B
C
```

compensates:

```text
C'
B'
A'
```

unless an explicit dependency graph specifies otherwise.

---

# 39. Compensation Failure

Compensation can fail.

States:

```text
CompensationPending
Compensating
CompensationRetrying
CompensationFailed
Compensated
ManualInterventionRequired
```

The runtime must not silently discard a failed compensation.

---

# 40. Nested Sagas

Sagas may contain child Sagas.

A child may expose:

```text
commit
compensate
failed
```

to the parent.

Nested compensation order follows explicit dependency semantics.

---

# 41. Workflow Parallelism

Workflow execution supports:

```text
parallel
join
race
any
all
quorum
```

Example:

```text
parallel:
    A()
    B()
    C()

join all
```

The runtime records branch identities so replay remains deterministic.

---

# 42. Join Semantics

Supported join policies:

```text
All
Any
FirstSuccess
FirstCompletion
Quorum
NOfM
```

Timeout behavior must be explicitly defined.

---

# 43. Sub-Workflows

A workflow may invoke another workflow.

```text
parent
    └── child workflow
```

Policies:

```text
WaitForCompletion
FireAndForget
ContinueAsynchronously
CancelWithParent
Independent
```

Detached workflows must be explicit.

---

# 44. Signals

A signal is a durable external input to a workflow.

Examples:

```text
payment_confirmed
customer_approved
device_ready
human_decision
```

Signals are persisted before acknowledgement.

Duplicate signals must be deduplicable through:

```text
SignalId
IdempotencyKey
```

---

# 45. Signal Ordering

Ordering can be specified per:

```text
workflow instance
signal type
partition
source
```

Global ordering is not assumed.

---

# 46. External Events

External events may originate from:

```text
626 network
628 event log
IPC 604
device 614
media 616
GUI 619
plugin 623
script 624
```

629 normalizes them into durable workflow signals/events.

---

Human tasks are optional.

A human task contains:

```text
HumanTaskId
Assignee
CandidateGroup
Payload
Deadline
EscalationPolicy
```

Lifecycle:

```text
Created
Assigned
Claimed
Completed
Rejected
Expired
Escalated
Cancelled
```

The core runtime does not depend on GUI.

# 48. Schedule Model

Supported schedule types:

```text
At
After
Every
Cron
Calendar
EventTriggered
Manual
```

Example:

```text
schedule daily_report:
    every day at 08:00
```

---

# 49. Time Zones

Schedules must explicitly define timezone.

Examples:

```text
UTC
Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh
America/New_York
```

Timezone database version is recorded with the schedule when reproducibility requires it.

---

# 50. DST Handling

Calendar schedules define behavior for:

```text
missing local time
duplicated local time
timezone rule change
```

Policies:

```text
Skip
ShiftForward
ShiftBackward
RunOnce
RunTwice
```

No implicit interpretation.

---

# 51. Missed Schedules

If the runtime is unavailable:

```text
Skip
CatchUp
Coalesce
BoundedCatchUp
```

Example:

```text
every 1 minute
runtime offline 2 hours
```

must not automatically create 120 executions unless configured.

---

# 52. Schedule Deduplication

Each generated execution receives:

```text
ScheduleId
OccurrenceId
```

The same occurrence must not create duplicate logical executions.

---

# 53. Distributed Scheduler

Schedules are coordinated through 627.

Only one active scheduler generation should own a partition at a time.

Ownership:

```text
partition
    ↓
lease
    ↓
fencing token
```

A stale scheduler cannot publish new schedule executions after losing ownership.

---

# 54. Scheduler Sharding

Schedules can be partitioned by:

```text
ScheduleId hash
tenant
namespace
workflow
```

Partitions may migrate between nodes.

Migration must be fenced.

---

# 55. Backpressure

When workers cannot keep up:

```text
queue depth ↑
        ↓
admission control
        ↓
rate limiting
        ↓
schedule coalescing
        ↓
priority handling
```

The runtime must not create unbounded in-memory task queues.

---

# 56. Priority

Task priorities are advisory unless the policy explicitly requires strict priority.

Supported:

```text
Critical
High
Normal
Low
Background
```

Starvation prevention is required.

---

# 57. Resource Governance

Every workflow/task can be associated with a resource scope:

```text
Workflow
Job
Tenant
Queue
Worker
Application
```

Resource classes come from 606:

```text
CPU
Memory
Threads
GPU
Network
Storage
IPC
Handles
Task count
```

---

# 58. Capability Propagation

Workflow capabilities are not automatically expanded.

A workflow may only use capabilities granted by:

```text
603 Security Boundary
627 Identity
```

An activity receives an attenuated capability set.

Example:

```text
Workflow capability:
    filesystem:/data

Activity capability:
    filesystem:/data/orders/read
```

---

# 59. Secret Handling

Secrets must not be stored as ordinary workflow state.

Forbidden:

```text
state.api_password = "..."
```

Preferred:

```text
state.api_key = SecretHandle(...)
```

Workflow history must never contain plaintext secret material.

---

# 60. Security Context

Every task execution carries:

```text
PrincipalId
TenantId?
CapabilitySet
SecurityPolicyFingerprint
WorkflowInstanceId
TraceId
```

Authorization is revalidated at execution boundaries.

---

# 61. Distributed Coordination

629 uses 627 for:

```text
leader election
partition ownership
leases
fencing
membership
coordination
```

629 does not implement its own consensus subsystem.

---

# 62. Data Persistence

629 stores durable workflow data through 628.

Logical stores:

```text
WorkflowHistoryStore
WorkflowSnapshotStore
TaskQueueStore
ScheduleStore
SignalStore
WorkerLeaseStore
CompensationStore
DeadLetterStore
```

These may map onto shared 628 infrastructure.

---

# 63. Large Data Rule

Workflow state must remain bounded.

Large payloads should use:

```text
628 distributed object/data store
613 CAS
611 filesystem
```

and workflow state contains:

```text
ObjectId
ContentHash
SchemaFingerprint
```

rather than the entire payload.

---

# 64. State Schema Evolution

Workflow state has:

```text
SchemaId
SchemaVersion
SchemaFingerprint
```

Migration uses 612 schema migration facilities.

Running workflows must never be silently decoded using an incompatible schema.

---

# 65. Workflow History Compaction

History can be compacted when:

```text
snapshot committed
+
all required readers advanced
+
retention policy permits deletion
```

Compaction must preserve enough information for:

```text
audit
recovery
replay
debugging
```

according to configured retention.

---

# 66. Dead-Letter Queue

Tasks that exceed retry policy enter:

```text
DeadLetter
```

A dead-letter record contains:

```text
TaskId
WorkflowInstanceId?
Attempts
LastError
LastWorker
HistoryReference
PayloadReference
Timestamp
```

Manual replay is supported.

---

# 67. Poison Task Protection

A permanently failing task must not consume infinite resources.

Policies include:

```text
MaxAttempts
RetryBudget
DeadLetter
Quarantine
ManualApproval
```

---

# 68. Failure Scenarios

629 must handle:

```text
worker crash
worker restart
network partition
scheduler crash
coordinator failover
storage failure
duplicate task
late activity result
expired lease
clock changes
process restart
machine reboot
partial deployment
workflow version change
```

---

# 69. Late Result Handling

Suppose:

```text
Worker A
    lease expires

Worker B
    executes task

Worker A
    eventually returns
```

Worker A's result must be rejected if its fencing token is stale.

---

# 70. Coordinator Failure

If the workflow coordinator fails:

```text
persisted workflow state
        ↓
new coordinator generation
        ↓
lease acquisition
        ↓
snapshot/history replay
        ↓
resume
```

No duplicate logical workflow instance may be created.

---

# 71. Network Partition

During a partition:

```text
old owner
```

must eventually lose authority through lease/fencing.

The system may temporarily be unable to progress.

It must not allow conflicting owners to commit indefinitely.

---

# 72. Worker Drain

Worker shutdown:

```text
Serving
   ↓
Draining
   ↓
finish or checkpoint
   ↓
release leases
   ↓
Stopped
```

Unfinished tasks are requeued according to lease semantics.

---

# 73. Workflow Suspension

A workflow can be:

```text
Paused
Suspended
```

Suspension prevents new work while preserving durable state.

Existing activities may:

```text
finish
cancel
or be allowed according to policy
```

---

# 74. Workflow Termination

Termination is stronger than cancellation.

```text
Cancel
```

means cooperative stop.

```text
Terminate
```

means the runtime stops scheduling further workflow work and records the termination.

External effects already performed are not automatically undone.

---

# 75. Abandonment

Abandonment is explicit.

It means:

```text
runtime stops ownership
```

while retaining historical information.

This is intended for manual external recovery scenarios.

---

# 76. Recovery Modes

Supported:

```text
Automatic
Manual
ObserveOnly
ReplayOnly
Repair
```

No dangerous automatic compensation should occur without policy.

---

# 77. Workflow Migration

Migration is permitted only at safe checkpoints.

A migration descriptor defines:

```text
from_version
to_version
state_transform
compatibility_rules
```

Migration must be deterministic.

---

# 78. Activity Versioning

Activities are versioned independently from workflows.

Example:

```text
ChargeCard@1
ChargeCard@2
```

Existing workflows can remain pinned to a compatible activity version.

---

# 79. Deployment Strategy

629 supports:

```text
parallel versions
rolling worker deployment
drain old workers
workflow pinning
activity compatibility windows
```

Deployment itself belongs to higher-level package/distribution systems.

---

# 80. Durable Job Scheduling

A job can survive:

```text
process restart
node restart
worker replacement
application upgrade
```

because the logical job exists independently from a process.


The graph is diagnostic metadata, not necessarily the runtime representation.

---

# 133. Runtime Optimization

The compiler/runtime may optimize:

```text
state transitions
small workflow states
timer registration
queue operations
event encoding
snapshot creation
replay
```

Simple local workflows should have near-native overhead.

---

# 134. Allocation Rules

The core workflow engine should avoid:

```text
per-event heap allocation
per-task reflection
global locks
mandatory garbage collection
```

Use:

```text
arenas
object pools
slab allocation
inline small objects
ring buffers
persistent storage batches
```

where beneficial.

---

# 135. Hot Path

Hot paths include:

```text
task enqueue
task lease
task completion
workflow event append
timer lookup
signal delivery
worker heartbeat
```

These should avoid global mutexes.

---

# 136. Batching

Supported batching:

```text
event append
task enqueue
ack
heartbeat
snapshot write
replication
```

Batching must not violate ordering or durability semantics.

---

# 137. Backpressure Propagation

Backpressure should propagate:

```text
worker
 ↓
task queue
 ↓
workflow
 ↓
event source
```

rather than allowing unlimited buffering.

---

# 138. Offline Workers

Workers may temporarily operate with constrained connectivity only when the task semantics permit it.

A disconnected worker must not continue indefinitely using an expired lease.

---

# 139. Mobile

On mobile:

```text
long-running OS process
```

cannot be assumed.

629 maps durable work onto platform-supported background execution mechanisms.

If execution is interrupted:

```text
persisted workflow
    ↓
later resume
```

---

# 140. WASM

WASM mode delegates:

```text
persistent storage
timers
network
worker execution
```

to the host capability layer.

No direct OS assumptions.

---

# 141. Embedded

Embedded mode may reduce the system to:

```text
TaskQueue
Scheduler
Timer
Persistence
WorkflowState
```

with distributed functionality removed.

---

# 142. Minimal Runtime Profiles

Profiles:

```text
AXWORKFLOW_NONE
AXWORKFLOW_LOCAL
AXWORKFLOW_DURABLE
AXWORKFLOW_SCHEDULE
AXWORKFLOW_QUEUE
AXWORKFLOW_DISTRIBUTED
AXWORKFLOW_SAGA
AXWORKFLOW_HUMAN
AXWORKFLOW_FULL
```

Unused components must be dead-strippable.

---

# 143. ABI

Public workflow ABI uses:

